items.statement: Knowing the Cognitive Faculty is impossible through ordinary cognition; it can only be achieved by complete psychic merger into It.
items.title: Rádhá's Devotion – Excerpt D

items.quote: Now in this march of life – and particularly in human life – there are three kinds of expression; and those three expressions, or those three factors, are jiṋána, karma and bhakti. Bhakti is the supreme one. And how to acquire bhakti, how to get bhakti? The simple formula is, karma minus jiṋána is equal to bhakti.
items.statement: Spiritual devotion is quantitatively attained through selfless service devoid of intellectual vanity, formulated as karma minus jnana equals bhakti.
items.title: Rádhiká Shakti

items.quote: And when this desire to do something practical is created in the mind, this created force is called hládinii shakti or Rádhiká shakti. With the help of this Rádhiká shakti one can move towards that Cosmological Nave.
items.statement: Radhika shakti is the active devotional force arising from conscience that impels a spiritual aspirant towards the Cosmological Nucleus.
items.title: Rádhiká Shakti

items.quote: In rágánugá samádhi the unit mind retains its existence and feels blissful owing to the close proximity of Parama Puruśa.
items.statement: Raganuga samadhi maintains the unit mind's separate identity near Parama Purusa, whereas ragatmika samadhi seeks complete identity and merger.
items.title: Rágánugá and Rágátmiká Samádhi

items.quote: After a long time this very terrain, this nameless mountainous terrain, was given the name Ráŕh. The word ráŕh originated in the ancient Austric language and means a land of red (laterite) soil. In the world of those days there was no Áryyávartta; ( 3 ) there were none of the plain lands of Bengal and the Deccan, nor were there the deserts of Rajasthan and Gujarat.
items.statement: The ancient Austric name 'Rarh' designates a land of red laterite soil that existed before the formation of the Himalayas and the Gangetic plains.
items.title: Ráŕh – 1.

items.quote: What is mysticism? Mysticism is the never-ending endeavour to find out a link between finite and infinite. So the people of Ráŕh are all mystical by birth.
items.statement: Mysticism is the ceaseless psychic longing and effort to discover the connecting link between the finite and the infinite.
items.title: Ráŕh – 10.

items.quote: In short, in the depths of their minds the people of Ráŕh were all followers of Shaeva Dharma. It was like an enamelled ornament; the gold underneath was Shaeva Dharma and the enamel was Digambara Jaena Dharma.
items.statement: The deep-seated Shaiva traditions of Rarh were surfaced by Digambara Jainism, leading to the depiction of Shiva as an unclothed deity.
items.title: Ráŕh – 11.

items.quote: At this juncture, ( 1 ) Raghunandan came and attempted to solve the problem. Being unable to trace the complicated lines of descent underlying the caste divisions, he gave his decision that Ráŕh should not follow the four-caste system of India, rather it should recognize a two-tier system of Vipra and Shúdra.
items.statement: Raghunandan imposed a rigid two-tier caste classification of Vipra and Shudra on Rarh, destroying social equality and fostering kuliina polygamy.
items.title: Ráŕh – 16.

items.quote: There being profuse coal beneath the riverbed, the river is known as Dámodar (dám + udar). In the Sanskrit language dám means “fire”. The river which has dám in its udar [belly], or fire, is the Dámodar.
items.statement: The Damodar River was named from the underground coal deposits formed from ancient dense forests embedded beneath its bed.
items.title: Ráŕh – 18.

items.quote: Though the inhabitants of Ráŕh are a mixed race of Austric and Negro (and in a few cases Mongolian), there is an abundance of Sanskrit words in the language of Ráŕh. The language is replete with tatsama words [Sanskrit words used in unchanged form in the Bengali language], bhagnatatsama words [Sanskrit words used in changed form in Bengali language], tadbhava words [Bengali words derived from Sanskrit root but used in a corrupted form in the Bengali language] and semi-tadbhava words [Bengali words derived from Sanskrit root but corrupted to the point of their roots being unrecognizable]. About ninety-two percent of the words are directly or indirectly related to the Sanskrit language. Ráŕh is situated in the extreme east of India. If Sanskrit were a foreign language and if it were thought to have come into India across its north-west border, then how could so many Sanskrit words have entered the colloquial language of the remote outpost Ráŕh?
items.statement: Approximately 92% of the colloquial vocabulary of Rarh is derived from Sanskrit, proving Sanskrit was not an imported northwest Aryan tongue.
items.title: Ráŕh – 19. Language, Literature and Culture of Ráŕh

items.quote: Some think that Devanagari is the script of Sanskrit, but this idea is totally wrong. Sanskrit has no script of its own. The Shriiharśa script is much older than Devanagari, and it facilitates swift writing (as one can write for a long time without raising one’s hand).
items.statement: Sanskrit has no native script of its own; it was historically recorded across eastern India in the ancient Shriiharsa script.
items.title: Ráŕh – 20. The Script of Ráŕh

items.quote: Sáhitya means all those [literary] manifestations of the human minds that always move along the path of welfare [hita], that are associated with [with = sa] welfare. Hitena saha ityarthe sáhitya, that is, sáhitya is a reflection of social movement on the mirror of welfare.
items.statement: Sahitya refers strictly to literary creations aligned with collective welfare that elevate and mirror societal movement.
items.title: Ráŕh – 21.

items.quote: Hence the Bengalee civilization represents the confluence of the three civilizations. The mixture of the three is Báḿlá civilization – Báuṋálii culture. Bengal is not an appendage of Áryyávartta [northern India], nor is it an annex to greater China; nor is it only the flag-bearer of the Austric-Dravid [legacy]. So in trying to give an identity of Bengal, I am left with no alternative but to say that Bengal owes that identity to its river-based existence only.
items.statement: Bengalee culture arose as an independent river-based synthesis of Ráŕhiiya, Gangetic Aryan, and Brahmaputra Mongolian civilizations.
items.title: Ráŕh – 26.

items.quote: The three gharáńás [styles] of the cho dance are: 1) The Manbhum style. It is prevalent in Manbhum and Bankura Districts. One of the many characteristics of this dance is that the dancers are to sport masks (mohará in Ráŕhii Bengali, rather than mukhośa). 2) The Seraikela style. It is prevalent in Singhbhum District and the western part of Midnapur District. In this style, masks are used as needed. 3) The Bhanjabhum style. It was (and is) prevalent in Mayurbhanja and in the Nayabasan regions of Midnapur. This style does not use masks.
items.statement: The Cho dance of Rarh is categorized into three regional gharanas: Manbhum (masked), Seraikela (partially masked), and Bhanjabhum (unmasked).
items.title: Ráŕh – 26.

items.quote: It goes without saying here that the custom of wearing veils appeared in Ráŕh at the beginning of the Mughal Age.
items.statement: The custom of wearing veils in Ráŕh emerged at the beginning of the Mughal Age.
items.title: Ráŕh – 27.

items.quote: The four styles basically used in the building of temples in India are: 1) The Rajput style of north-western India, in which the roof tapers upwards to a point. 2) The Dravidian style, in which there is a small roof atop the temple, along with a special type of gopuram [a special kind of decoration]. 3) The Utkal style. 4) The thatched-hut style of Ráŕh.
items.statement: There are four primary styles utilized in Indian temple architecture: the Rajput style of north-western India, the Dravidian style, the Utkal style, and the thatched-hut style of Ráŕh.
items.title: Ráŕh – 28. The Temples of Ráŕh

items.quote: Why does leprosy break out in such an incomparably healthy place as this? In no way is the soil, water, climate or nature responsible for this. It is only a defective man-made socio-economic system that is at fault. People cannot live on water and air alone. Ráŕh is trapped in extreme poverty. A large part of the population cannot fill their stomachs with nutritious food. It is due to this malnutrition that they contract leprosy.
items.statement: Leprosy in Ráŕh is caused by severe malnutrition resulting from a defective man-made socio-economic system, rather than local natural, climatic, soil, or water conditions.
items.title: Ráŕh – 29. The Climate of Ráŕh

items.quote: The ancient calculations of the Suryasiddhánta ( 6 ) could not keep pace with the passage of time. Calculations were becoming prone to error. It was under the auspices of Shalibahan, the king of Dańd́abhukti (of southern Ráŕh, i.e., of the Midnapur area) that Jayanta Panigrahi, an outstanding son of Ráŕh, introduced a new system of calculation. This resulted in a new system of calculation based on the solar year.
items.statement: Under the patronage of King Shalibahan of Dańd́abhukti, Jayanta Panigrahi formulated a revised system of astronomical calculations based on the solar year because the ancient Suryasiddhánta had become error-prone.
items.title: Ráŕh – 2. Outstanding Personalities of Ráŕh

items.quote: It was at that time that Devibar Ghatak (of Birbhum) introduced the melbandhan (pat́ibandhan as it was called in the Barendra caste) system ( 4 ) among those outcastes. As a result, the tendency to convert to other religions came to a halt.
items.statement: Devibar Ghatak introduced the melbandhan system among outcastes in Ráŕh to prevent excommunicated individuals from converting to other religions.
items.title: Ráŕh – 3.

items.quote: The excessive ahimsá in Digambara Jainism and a type of excessive ahimsá in the Gaoŕiiya Vaeśńava Dharma prevalent in Ráŕh did a lot of damage to the spirit of valour of the people of Ráŕh. Notwithstanding their strength, capability, courage and diligence, they were not easily able to leap into a struggle.
items.statement: The excessive practice of ahimsa in Digambara Jainism and Gaoŕiiya Vaeśńavism severely diminished the martial spirit and fighting capacity of the people of Ráŕh.
items.title: Ráŕh – 30. History of the Regions of Ráŕh

items.quote: The fundamental difference between the exploitation by the local vaeshyas and that by the outsiders is this: though both are exploiters and the exploitation of both causes people to cry aloud for relief, the local exploiters mostly keep their exploitation-gotten wealth within the territory of the land, and hence there is a chance for that wealth to be utilized in future in the service of the people. But the outsider exploiters will in most cases transfer outside all the wealth that they have ruthlessly squeezed out of the land.
items.statement: Local capitalist exploitation retains acquired wealth within the land enabling future utilization for the public, whereas outsider exploitation transfers extracted wealth outside the territory entirely.
items.title: Ráŕh – 31. Socio-Economic Exploitation in Ráŕh

items.quote: There is no proof as to whether Shiva upheld idol worship. But it was after His passing away that a special kind of worship known as phallus worship came into being. In this phallus worship there was a nice combination of spirituality and earthly need. At that time the different groups remained locked in continual fighting with one another. All the groups wanted to increase their own populations. So they first introduced phallus worship to symbolize the increase of their numerical strength. Later this phallus worship became subtilized by infusing it with spiritual ideations.
items.statement: Phallus worship originated after Shiva's passing as a symbolic attempt by clashing groups to promote population growth, and was later subtilized with spiritual ideation.
items.title: Ráŕh – 4.

items.quote: Shankaracharya came to Ráŕh only [not the rest of Bengal]. Hence many Buddhists and Jains of Ráŕh embraced Paoráńika Dharma. D́abák being marshy land, neither Shankaracharya nor any of his disciples with leadership qualities visited there much. So the inhabitants of that land remained Buddhists and later embraced Islam on a large scale.
items.statement: Because the marshy terrain of D́abák deterred Shankaracharya and his prominent disciples from visiting, its population remained Buddhist and later converted to Islam on a large scale.
items.title: Ráŕh – 5.

items.quote: Mokśa [emancipation, non-qualified liberation of the soul] and nirváńa are not synonymous. Because Tantra, which is based on mokśa, is the sádhaná [spiritual practice] of absolute expansion, the sádhaná of moving at lightning speed from the cimmerian darkness of staticity to the fullness of divine effulgence; while the pursuit of nirváńa is the sádhaná of knowingly extinguishing one’s most precious treasure, one’s lamp of life – it is nothing but to let the radiance of one’s inner and outer world become dimmer and dimmer and to lose oneself in the deepest abyss of darkness – not only to lose oneself, but to deny one’s existence under the impact of utter ignorance.
items.statement: Mokśa is the spiritual practice of absolute expansion toward divine effulgence, whereas nirváńa represents a negative pursuit aimed at extinguishing one's lamp of life.
items.title: Ráŕh – 7.

items.quote: There are mainly two types of mentality at work behind an inclination towards spirituality: the selfish mentality, or átmá-sukha tattva [theory of selfish pleasure], and sama-samája tattva [the theory of social equality]. When utter self-centredness manifests itself in people, when someone thinks only “I shall eat and dress well, ride luxury cars and fulfil all my desires,” that is the dualistic or selfish mentality, that is, to take shelter in a dogma and exploit others.
items.statement: Átma-sukha tattva is a dogma-sheltered selfish mentality driving religion for self-centred gain, whereas sama-samája tattva is true dharma establishing beings in both objective and noumenal spheres without caste discrimination.
items.title: Ráŕh – 8.

items.quote: The movement of spirituality is never pulsative in character, but rather linear: it flows in a straight line. Due to this straightness, it has no positive curvature or negative curvature. Yet for the sake of convenience we can call it the supreme positivity; and its farthest extremity, the point where resides all human existence, the starting-point of all intellectuals and non-intellectuals, can be termed the supreme negativity.
items.statement: Material reality and intellectuality are intrinsically ambiguous and defective because they are based on pulsative, systaltic waves, whereas spirituality is absolute because its movement is linear.
items.title: Reality and Intellectuality

items.quote: Time is the mental measurement of the motivity of action. Where there is no action or where there is no mind to measure, there cannot be any time either.
items.statement: Time is not an absolute entity or eternal reality, but the mental measurement of the motivity of action.
items.title: Relativity and the Supreme Entity

items.quote: (In Saḿskrta, an action whose cause is known to human beings is called kriirá, and an action whose cause is not known is called liilá. The actions of the Supreme Consciousness are called liilá because we do not know their cause.)
items.statement: An action whose causal factor is known to humans is termed kriirá, whereas an action whose cause is unknown is termed liilá.
items.title: Relativity and the Supreme Entity

items.quote: Movement which is devoid of logic and reason is called “dogma,” and a collection of dogma is called an “ism.”
items.statement: Movement that is completely devoid of logic and reason is defined as dogma, and a collection of dogmas constitutes an ism.
items.title: Religious Dogma – Excerpt A

items.quote: A charter of principles or bill of rights should be included in such a constitution and encompass at least the following four areas. First, complete security should be guaranteed to all the plants and animals on the planet. Secondly, each country must guarantee purchasing power to all its citizens. Thirdly, the constitution should guarantee four fundamental rights – spiritual practice or Dharma; cultural legacy; education; and indigenous linguistic expression. Fourthly, if the practice of any of these rights conflicts with cardinal human values then that practice should be immediately curtailed. That is, cardinal human values must take precedence over all other rights.
items.statement: A world constitution under a World Government must guarantee animal and plant security, guarantee purchasing capacity, ensure four fundamental rights, and establish that cardinal human values override any conflicting rights.
items.title: Requirements of an Ideal Constitution

items.quote: The causes of this disease are just like those of acidity. That is to say, rheumatism occurs when the váyu bodily air is disturbed due to excess of poisonous acids in the body.
items.statement: Rheumatism is caused by an excess of poisonous acids creating an acid-dominated bodily system that disturbs bodily air (váyu).
items.title: Rheumatism

items.quote: In original civilizations (maolik sabhytá), people are physically strong. In blended civilizations, people are strong in the psychic stratum and the civilization is complicated as well as forceful. In the simple Gangá civilization people are simple and physically strong; in the delta stage people are complicated, less physically strong and strong psychically.
items.statement: People belonging to original civilizations are physically strong, whereas in blended deltaic civilizations people become psychically strong, complicated, and intellectually developed.
items.title: River and Civilization – Excerpt A

items.quote: In the opinion of the yogic scriptures there is an ideological difference between rta and satya. That which is a fact, which has happened or happens, is called rta. And the ideation used for the welfare of the people is called satya. Parahitárthaḿ váunmanaso yathárthatvaḿ satyam. “Using one’s mind or speech out of a spirit of welfare for others is satya.”
items.statement: Rta refers to factual occurrences that have happened or happen, whereas satya refers to thought and speech employed specifically for the benevolent welfare of others.
items.title: Rk to Rkśa (Discourse 11)

items.quote: Since the Rgvedic age, rśis have been mainly divided into four categories: maharśi, devarśi, rájarśi and brahmarśi.
items.statement: Since the Rgvedic period, rśis have been classified into four categories: maharśi, devarśi, rájarśi, and brahmarśi.
items.title: Rk to Rkśa (Discourse 11)

items.qualifiers: Applicable to targeted application by a Sadguru; widespread waves of positive microvita influence everyone without harm
items.quote: So, positive microvita should never be applied to children, animals, birds and plants. Similarly, positive microvita should never be applied to the bodies of women. When the waves of positive microvita are widespread, they influence everyone and help in their all-round development.
items.statement: Positive microvita must never be applied to children, women, animals, birds, or plants because their nerve structures cannot withstand the vibrations.
items.title: Sadguru and Microvita

items.quote: The parallelism between the sentimental flow of the microcosm and the perennial flow of spirituality is what is called “bháva”.
items.statement: Bháva is the state of parallelism established between the sentimental flow of the unit being and the perennial flow of spirituality.
items.title: Sadguruḿ Taḿ Namámi

items.quote: Hence, as each of these fifty vrttis can be expressed both internally and externally, there are one hundred possible expressions. These hundred expressions can be expressed in ten directions: six “pradisha” directions: north, south, east, west, above, and below; and four “anudisha” directions: northeast, southeast, northwest and southwest. So the total number of expressions comes to (100 x 10 =) 1,000! That is why the pineal gland is called sahasrara cakra or “that which expresses itself in one thousand directions.”
items.statement: Human beings possess fifty psychic propensities (vrttis), which, by being expressed either internally or externally in ten distinct directions, yield a total of one thousand potential expressions corresponding to the sahasrara cakra.
items.title: Sádhaná, Abhidhyána and Kiirtana

items.qualifiers: Specifically applies when fasting for mental purification
items.quote: When you fast for mental purification, you should give your food to a needy passerby, and use the drinking water to water the plants.
items.statement: When fasting for mental purification, one must give their food to a needy passerby and use the drinking water to water plants.
items.title: Sádhaná (Intuitional Practice)

items.quote: In Ananda Marga there are three particular stages of sádhaná which can be fused into one, or can remain separate: Shákta, Vaeśńaviiya, and Shaeva. True spiritual practice is a happy combination of these three stages.
items.statement: Spiritual practice integrates three distinct stages: Shákta (struggling against staticity and acquiring strength), Vaeśńava (surrendering ego and floating in Cosmic bliss), and Shaeva (merging into the non-attributional stance of Nirguńa Brahma).
items.title: Sádhaná

items.quote: Pratyáhára has four stages: yatamána, vyatireka, ekendriya and vashiikára.
items.statement: Pratyáhára yoga comprises four sequential stages: yatamána (conscious effort to control propensities), vyatireka (partial or alternating control), ekendriya (intermittent suppression of propensities), and vashiikára (complete control of mind and senses).
items.title: Sádhaná

items.quote: Mysticism is a never-ending endeavour to find out the link between finite and infinite.
items.statement: Mysticism is the never-ending endeavour to discover and establish the link between the finite and the infinite.
items.title: Salvation and Corporeal Beings

items.quote: The conscious mind functions with the help of both nerve-cells and nerve-fibres, while the subconscious and the unconscious function with the help of nerve-cells only.
items.statement: The conscious mind operates via both nerve-cells and nerve-fibres, whereas the subconscious and unconscious minds operate using nerve-cells only.
items.title: Samádhi, Senselessness and Sleep

items.qualifiers: Requires holding the status continuously for two years (four half-years); the title is non-hereditary
items.quote: A bhukti pradhána retaining the status of samájamitram continuously for two years (four half-years) can permanently prefix the title to his/her name (but this will not be hereditary). A permanent samájamitram can no longer hold the post of bhukti pradhána.
items.statement: A bhukti pradhána who retains the status of samájamitram or jiivamitram continuously for two years permanently prefixes the title to their name but can no longer hold the post of bhukti pradhána.
items.title: Samájamitram, Smártta, Jiivamitram and Dharmamitram

items.qualifiers: Identifies three specific structural factors behind lack of prestige
items.quote: There are three main factors due to which they are denied social prestige: First, society did not recognize them; society did not want to give them recognition. Secondly, as they are economically crippled, economically destroyed, they are forced to remain in perpetual subservience. Thirdly, a want of education, a want of knowledge, in them.
items.statement: Social prestige is denied to ninety-nine percent of people due to lack of social recognition, economic destitution leading to perpetual subservience, and lack of education.
items.title: Samatábháva

items.qualifiers: Distinguishes three precise categories of destruction and transformation
items.quote: What we call “destruction” in ordinary language is called násha. When an object is transformed and cannot be brought back to its original form it is called vinásha. For example, when a five-year-old boy grows into a twenty-five-year-old man it signifies a major change. Where has the growing body of the five-year-old gone? It has been annihilated. When an object returns to its original source after being annihilated, it is called prańásha.
items.statement: Destruction is categorized into ordinary destruction (násha), irreversible transformation (vinásha), and transformation where an annihilated object returns to its original source (prańásha).
items.title: Sambhúti and Mahásambhúti

items.qualifiers: Distinguished categorically from jiivakot́i and Iishvarakot́i
items.quote: This pessimism in collective life cannot be solved by one particular sambhúti; it requires the appearance of a special structure through which the Supreme Entity can fully express Himself. This special manifestation is called Mahásambhúti [“Great Sambhúti”]. The role of Mahásambhúti is to properly guide all other sambhútis and, by enforcing proper discipline, to bring about proper harmony and coordination amongst them. This special manifestation does not come within the purview of jiivakot́i or that of Iishvarakot́i.
items.statement: Mahásambhúti is the special manifestation through which the Supreme Entity fully expresses Himself to guide, discipline, and bring harmony among all individual creations when collective life suffers irremediable disequilibrium.
items.title: Sambhúti and Mahásambhúti

items.quote: Just to represent the spirit of “saḿgacchadhvam”, I propounded the theory of PROUT. So the entire theory of PROUT stands upon this Vaedika sermon of “saḿgacchadhvam”.
items.statement: The socio-economic theory of PROUT is founded directly upon the Vedic collective principle of saḿgacchadhvam.
items.title: Saḿgacchadhvaḿ

items.qualifiers: Requires both components for aesthetic validity
items.quote: If one looks at the characteristics of dance, one must admit that both gestures and rhythm are important components of a dance: the gestures give expression to the inner sentiment, and the rhythm gives it dynamism. If dance has only gestures but is devoid of rhythm, it is called pantomime, not dance. And dance devoid of gestures is merely a form of physical exercise – it is not art.
items.statement: Dance is defined by the integration of gestures and rhythm; gestures devoid of rhythm constitute pantomime, while rhythm devoid of gestures is mere physical exercise.
items.title: Saḿgiita As Soft Expressions of Art

items.qualifiers: Traces transition from folk to classical status
items.quote: When kiirtana first began to develop, it did not have any hard and fast rules, just as folk songs do not conform to hard and fast rules. [[ Kiirtana adopted hard and fast rules later on.]] Just as the different schools ( gharáńá ) of rága and ráginii evolved out of various rhythmic expressions, similarly, as soon as kiirtana was brought within the framework of fixed rules, it came to be elevated from folk music to classical music.
items.statement: Kiirtana originally lacked fixed rules like folk songs, but was elevated to classical music once it adopted a systematic framework of fixed rules.
items.title: Saḿgiita – Excerpt B

items.qualifiers: Operates at the disembodied soul and saḿskára level
items.quote: When there is dominance of saḿyojanii shakti in one’s latent saḿskáras, the disembodied soul attains a female body for its outward expression, and conversely where there is a dominance of vibhájanii shakti, it attains a male body. Where there is an approximate balance between the two, the disembodied soul attains the body of a hermaphrodite.
items.statement: Biological sex assignment is caused by the balance of latent mental forces: dominance of the attractive force (saḿyojanii shakti) results in a female body, dominance of the attracted force (vibhájanii shakti) in a male body, and approximate balance in a hermaphroditic body.
items.title: Saḿskára and Gender Differences

items.qualifiers: Philosophical qualification of the doctrine of reincarnation
items.quote: To be more precise it is the saḿskáras which are reborn. Philosophically speaking, it is not correct to say that the átman [unit consciousness] is reborn, because átman is neither body, intellect, nor mind; it is just the witnessing entity, the subject witnessing the metamorphoses of its object, sometimes into another finite form and sometimes into an infinite form.
items.statement: Rebirth applies strictly to saḿskáras and not to the unit consciousness (átman), which serves solely as a non-reborn witnessing entity.
items.title: Saḿskára and Gender Differences

items.qualifiers: Defines karma in terms of physical-positional transformation
items.quote: The true definition of Karma (action) is the relative change of position of an object. That is a particular object has changed its location from one place to another at a given time. How does this change occur? The faculty which causes this trans-shipment of objects is Karma (action).
items.statement: Action (karma) is defined scientifically as the relative change in an object's spatial position over time, caused by an active faculty.
items.title: Samyak Karmánta (Perfect Finish)

items.qualifiers: Contingent on specific regional literacy and starvation thresholds
items.quote: The upabhukti pramukha of any particular region within whose jurisdiction there is the maximum number of functioning producers’ and consumers’ cooperatives in any half-year - provided that the percentage of literacy in the upabhukti is more than 25 per cent (although the purodhá pramukha may change this whenever necessary) and nobody in that upabhukti has died of starvation or malnutrition during the concerned half-year - will be known as sándhivigráhika [organizer of service centres].
items.statement: An upabhukti pramukha earns the rank of sándhivigráhika by having the highest number of functioning producers' and consumers' cooperatives in a half-year, provided literacy exceeds 25 percent and no starvation or malnutrition deaths occurred.
items.title: Sándhivigráhika, Janamitram and Lokamitram

items.qualifiers: Attributed to textual misinterpretation and lack of trained philosophic guidance
items.quote: For instance, it was written Vidhavá agre gamiśyati. [“A widow should go (die) before (her husband)”]. But later, due to a defective interpretation, this was misread as Vidhavá agne gamiśyati. [“A widow should go into the fire”]. As a result, hundreds of thousands of innocent widows were burnt alive on the funeral pyres of their husbands.
items.statement: The historical burning of widows on funeral pyres arose from a misreading of 'Vidhavá agre gamiśyati' ('A widow should go before her husband') as 'Vidhavá agne gamiśyati' ('A widow should go into the fire').
items.title: Sati and Widowhood – Excerpt A

items.qualifiers: Encompasses both intellectual awakening and environmental/circumstantial abolition
items.quote: Kriyálopa is when a ritual, observance, rule or regulation is abolished due to an awakening of or a development in the faculties of judgement, intellect or wisdom. Kriyálopa is also when some old, worn-out customs and mores are done away with because of environmental pressures or under the impact of natural circumstances.
items.statement: Kriyálopa refers to the obsolescence and abolition of rituals, customs, or regulations caused by awakening intellect/judgement or circumstantial environmental pressures.
items.title: Sati and Widowhood – Excerpt C

items.qualifiers: External association without internal recollection is ineffective
items.quote: There are two types of satsauṋga – external and internal. Just as the best medicine is Parama Puruśa Himself, the best satsauṋga is also Parama Puruśa. Internal satsauṋga is the satsauṋga of Parama Puruśa, that is, the thought of Parama Puruśa during all the [waking] hours of the day, even when the bodily organs are engaged in worldly activities.
items.statement: Satsauṋga operates on internal and external levels; internal satsauṋga is continuous mental contemplation of Parama Puruśa during all waking hours and is considered essential, whereas external association alone is insufficient.
items.title: Satsaunga

items.qualifiers: Refutes common philosophic identification of deep sleep with pure vacuity
items.quote: The opinion that the state of sleep is the state of the sense of vacuity is unacceptable to a subtle philosophical judgement, because at that time the works of both the conscious and the subconscious minds are done by the unconscious mind. The real state of vacuity is verily the state of utter destruction of the mind, and so even savikalpa samádhi is not a state of vacuity. Only the state of nirvikalpa is the state of vacuity.
items.statement: Sleep is not a state of vacuity because the unconscious mind performs the work of conscious and subconscious layers; true vacuity occurs only in the state of nirvikalpa samádhi.
items.title: Savikalpa and Nirvikalpa Samádhi

items.qualifiers: Applies strictly to the Vedic chanting system
items.quote: In the Vedic system whenever there is any clash between grammar and rhythm the rhythm is to be supported and not the grammar. Here, for the sake of rhythm, the correct pronunciation should be, “Tatsavitur vareńi-yam”. It has been cut into two portions.
items.statement: In the Vedic system, when a conflict arises between grammatical rules and metrical rhythm, the poetic rhythm takes precedence over grammar.
items.title: Savitr Rk

items.quote: Sterilization brings glandular changes and changes in the hormone secretion of the glands which ultimately affects mental expression. Due to these changes a man may become like a eunuch. According to Prout only severely handicapped people and born criminals should be sterilized.
items.statement: Under Prout, artificial sterilization is restricted exclusively to severely handicapped individuals and born criminals due to its adverse endocrine and psychological consequences.
items.title: Science and Population Control – Excerpt D

items.quote: Ananda Marga philosophy lays down that punishment can be given only in the social sphere, not in the spiritual sphere.
items.statement: According to Ananda Marga philosophy, punitive measures may be applied strictly in the social sphere and never in the spiritual sphere.
items.title: Scope for Environmental Adjustment

items.qualifiers: Definitional distinction of types of jiṋána
items.quote: Mundane knowledge may be defined as the internal projection of the external physicality. And Pará-jiṋána or spiritual knowledge is the internal projection of the internal or cosmic spirituality. This is all jiṋána.
items.statement: Apará-jiṋána is the internal projection of external physicality, whereas Pará-jiṋána is the internal projection of cosmic spirituality.
items.title: Self-Realization Is the Real Knowledge

items.qualifiers: Characterized by total control over recollection and unbroken spiritual ideation
items.quote: And that condition of never forgetting anything, is called Dhruvásmrti. And memory then stands firm and sure. Then you have full control over your memory according to your wish. Such people are called Dhruvásmrti – they can always remember God and thus feel a special kind of Ánanda or bliss in their minds. That Ánanda is called Dharmameghánanda.
items.statement: Dhruvásmrti is that perfected state of memory where continuous, unbreached mental recollection of God is established, producing Dharmameghánanda.
items.title: Self-Realization Is the Real Knowledge

items.qualifiers: Sádhaná cannot progress without concurrent social service
items.quote: Remember, you have come to this world to render service to it – to render service to the world, and to practise the sádhaná of self-realization. [But] those who do only the sádhaná of self-realization, and refrain from social service, cannot make any headway in their sádhaná. The two are invariably dependent upon each other.
items.statement: Spiritual practice for self-liberation and active social service to the universe are mutually interdependent; pursuing self-realization while ignoring service is condemned as hypocritical escapism.
items.title: Self-Realization and Service to Humanity

items.quote: Spiritual practice is the means for the expansion of the soul, not for its annihilation; so samádhi does not mean suicide but self-transcendence. One who has known Brahma becomes Brahma Itself, for the unit entity takes on the very form of its object of ideation.
items.statement: Samádhi represents the expansion and self-transcendence of the soul into Brahma, rather than the destruction or annihilation of individual consciousness.
items.title: Self-Transcendence

items.qualifiers: Contrasts directionality of neurological and psychic disruption
items.quote: Epilepsy is also transmitted from the psychic level, that is, from the nerve cells to the nerve fibres. But this disease, hysteria, first occurs in the nerve fibres and then agitates the nerve cells. After this, it remains imprinted in the nerve cells as a psychic disease and expresses itself in a particular place and time.
items.statement: Epilepsy originates in nerve cells and transmits downward to nerve fibres, whereas hysteria originates from long-term suppression in nerve fibres and subsequently agitates the nerve cells.
items.title: Sentimentality: A Special Quality in Women – Excerpt D

items.qualifiers: Devotion prioritizes pure service over realization or attainment
items.quote: On the paths of action and knowledge, Parama Puruśa is the goal, the entity to be realized, and there is a definite cult to attain Him, to realize Him. But on the path of Bhakti (devotion), it is the goal itself and not a cult. This is the fundamental difference between devotion on the one hand and knowledge and action on the other.
items.statement: Knowledge and action view Parama Puruśa as a goal to be attained through practice, whereas devotion (bhakti) is itself the ultimate stance and goal rather than a mere practice.
items.title: Service to God Is Devotion

items.quote: In the first phase, sadhana is physico-psychic, and in the second stage it is only psychic. In the third stage psycho-spiritual and in the fourth stage it is entirely spiritual – These are the different stages of physico-psycho Spiritual practice.
items.statement: Spiritual practice evolves through four distinct stages: physico-psychic in the first stage, purely psychic in the second, psycho-spiritual in the third, and entirely spiritual in the fourth stage.
items.title: Service to Humanity Is the Supreme Ideology of Life

items.qualifiers: Categorizes human striving across trifarious existence
items.quote: Human success in physical strata is called Pratiśt́há in Saḿskrt. Human success in psychic strata is called Sarvajiṋatá in Saḿskrt, and human success in spiritual strata is called Siddhi in Saḿskt.
items.statement: Human success is categorized into three strata: physical success (pratiśt́há), psychic success (sarvajiṋatá), and spiritual success (siddhi).
items.title: Seven Secrets

items.qualifiers: contrasting abstract energy with materialized matter
items.quote: When form remains in the abstract realm it is called energy; when it comes into the material realm it is called matter. Energy is not one of the fundamental factors, but a stage prior to the metamorphosis of the Cosmic Citta into the five fundamental factors.
items.statement: Energy is defined not as a fundamental factor, but as an abstract stage prior to the metamorphosis of the Cosmic Citta into the five fundamental factors.
items.title: Shakti and Its Proper Application

items.qualifiers: internal dynamic of consciousness and operative principles
items.quote: The resultant flow created due to clash between the waves of the Cognitive Faculty, and those of the three principles of Prakrti, is called the spiritual flow. And the special resultant created in microcosms by this spiritual flow is called spiritual inspiration.
items.statement: Spiritual flow is defined as the resultant flow arising from the clash between the waves of the Cognitive Faculty and those of the three principles of Prakrti.
items.title: Shakti and Its Proper Application

items.qualifiers: historical attribution regarding the origin of music
items.quote: Based on the sounds of seven creatures, Shiva evolved the surasaptaka. This seven-note scale, which made the rhythm sweeter and more graceful, includes the sounds of śad́aja [peacock], rśabha [ox], gándhára [goat], madhyama [horse], paiṋcama [cuckoo], dhaevata [ass] and niśáda [elephant].
items.statement: Shiva formulated the seven-note musical scale (surasaptaka) based on the specific sounds produced by seven distinct birds and animals.
items.title: Shiva – Both Severe and Tender (Discourse 2)

items.quote: He observed that in the bodies of different creatures, the various glands were either over-active or under-active, either over-secreting or under-secreting. As a result, these creatures expressed themselves in various ways. Shiva intensively researched all these factors, and finally invented mudrá. Each and every mudrá affects certain human glands in a particular way and thus influences people’s minds accordingly.
items.statement: Mudrás in classical dance were designed to influence human mental states by directly stimulating and regulating the secretion of body glands.
items.title: Shiva – Both Severe and Tender (Discourse 2)

items.quote: Harati pápán ityarthe Hari [“One who steals otherśsins is called Hari”], and Harati bandanaḿ ityarthe Hara [“One who cuts asunder the knots of bondages is called Hara”]. That great personality who lays out the spiritual path which leads to liberation from all kinds of bondages is called Hara.
items.statement: Hari refers to an entity that steals sins, whereas Hara designates a personality who severs the knots of worldly bondages.
items.title: Shiva in the Song of Shiva (Discourse 19)

items.quote: The bird in a cage eating little morsels of food can be likened to lokáyata sádhaná, and the restless, intense psychic urge to soar freely into the vast distant blue sky can be compared with lokottara sádhaná. Shaeva Dharma in Ráŕh is Tantra-oriented; and as I have said, Tantra means all-round expansion.
items.statement: Lokáyata sádhaná is like a caged bird eating grains, whereas lokottara sádhaná represents the intense psychic urge to soar freely into the vast sky.
items.title: Shiva Tantra in Ráŕh

items.qualifiers: historical transition spanning roughly 2500 years ago
items.quote: Thus the worship of Shiva-liuṋga was introduced about 2500 years ago. But the phallic worship of the pre-historic age, and the worship of Shiva-liuṋga in medieval India (around 2250 years ago), were not the same. The latter, invested with a novel philosophical and spiritual significance, awakened a new trend of human thought.
items.statement: Shiva-liuṋga worship was transformed from prehistoric phallic multiplication rites into a philosophical cult representing the ultimate culmination point of cosmic vibrations during the Jain and Buddhist Tantric ages.
items.title: Shiva Throughout the Ages (Discourse 5)

items.quote: Time is nothing but the mental measurement of the motivity of action. Whenever there is action, there is motivity. Time is not an unbroken flow, but consists of disjointed elements. These elements are so closely connected that they seem to become one integral whole although actually it is not continuous.
items.statement: Time is an imaginary aggregate consisting of disjointed moments of motivity of action rather than an unbroken continuous flow.
items.title: Shiva Throughout the Ages (Discourse 5)

items.quote: Another Sanskrit equivalent for “woman” is nárii, which is feminine gender. But Shiva used the term kalatra, in the neuter; for to her husband a woman is a wife, but to her children and other members of the society, she is as dignified as her male counterpart. So by declaring a married lady to be kalatra, Shiva gave her special status, and addressed her in neuter terms.
items.statement: Shiva designated married women as 'kalatra' in the neuter gender to indicate equal dignity with men in relation to children and society.
items.title: Shiva Upholds the Dignity of Women – Excerpt C

items.quote: The idea of the five-faced Shiva is purely a symbol of the five expressions of one and the same face. The central face, the real face, of Shiva, is Kalyáńasundaram. The face on the extreme right is Dakśińeshvara, and the face between Kalyáńasundaram and Dakśińeshvara is Iishána. The face on the extreme left is Vámadeva, and the face between Kalyáńasundaram and Vámadeva is Kálágni.
items.statement: The five faces of Shiva represent five distinct behavioral expressions of a single countenance: Kalyáńasundaram, Dakśińeshvara, Iishána, Kálágni, and Vámadeva.
items.title: Shiva in the Dhyána Mantra (Discourse 20)

items.quote: I was referring to the three weapons of philosophy – váda, jalpa and vitańd́á. One of those is váda, to strengthen one’s position through logic; the second is jalpa, to demolish the structures of the other philosophy or doctrine through logic; and the third, vitańd́á, is to capture the zone of intellectual influence of the defeated philosophy.
items.statement: Comprehensive philosophical debate relies on three methodological weapons: váda to establish logic, jalpa to dismantle rival doctrines, and vitańd́á to capture intellectual influence.
items.title: Shiva in the Light of Philosophy (Discourse 17 (continued))

items.quote: All these glands need regular and proper exercise. Food alone is not enough; people need a special kind of exercise. The systematic and rhythmic dances invented by Shiva constitute those useful exercises. Now, all dances do not equally exercise all glands, and there are some glands which are not at all influenced by dances. In the absence of the proper exercise of those glands, people lose many capacities at an early age – especially the capacities of deep thinking and of sustained recollection.
items.statement: Táńd́ava dance exercises internal bodily glands through sustained jumping, which promotes hormonal secretion necessary for deep thinking and sustained recollection.
items.title: Shiva – the Focal Point of Everything (Discourse 3)

items.qualifiers: attributed directly to Shiva in reply to Parvati
items.quote: Phaliśyatiiti vishvása siddherprathama lakśańam Dvitiiyaḿ shraddhayá yuktaḿ Trtiiyaḿ gurupújanam. Caturtho samatábhávo Paiṋcamendriya nigraha, Śaśt́haiṋca pramitáhárah Saptamaḿ naeva vidyate.
items.statement: The seven secrets of success taught by Shiva consist of firm determination, shraddhá, guru pújana, mental equipoise, self-restraint, balanced diet, and the non-existence of any seventh factor.
items.title: Shiva's Seven Secrets

items.quote: What is shraddhá ? Shraddhá is a very old Vedic term. Shrat ” means “recognized status of veracity”, and “ dha ” means “movement towards it”. That is, when the ideological goal has been accepted, all my might, all my propensities, should move unto that goal. This is shraddhá .
items.statement: Shraddhá denotes the mental movement of all propensities toward an ideological goal once its status of veracity is recognized.
items.title: Shiva's Seven Secrets

items.qualifiers: fourth factor is the resultant of the first three
items.quote: The very essence of mánava dharma [human dharma], lies in three factors, plus a fourth factor which is the resultant of the first three: (1) vistára, the principle of expansion; (2) rasa, the principle of total surrender to Parama Puruśa; (3) sevá, selfless service to Parama Puruśa and His creation; and (4) tadsthiti, the final ensconcement in Parama Puruśa.
items.statement: Human dharma (Bhágavata Dharma) comprises four distinct factors: vistára (expansion), rasa (flow/surrender), sevá (selfless service), and tadsthiti (final ensconcement in Parama Puruśa).
items.title: Shiva's Teachings – 1 (continued) (Discourse 11)

items.quote: This expressed world of ours includes these three factors: sadvastu-in-fact, sadvastu-in-essence and sadvastu-in-appearance. Of these, sadvastu-in-essence is beyond the scope of perception and conception. Sadvastu-in-appearance is within the scope of perception. We can convert it into substance by our intellectual analysis and scientific research. And sadvastu-in-fact, although it comes within the scope of mind, does not come within the scope of perception; though we can experience it, we cannot convert it into substance.
items.statement: The expressed world manifests three ontological states of matter: sadvastu-in-fact, sadvastu-in-essence, and sadvastu-in-appearance.
items.title: Shiva's Teachings - 2 (Discourse 11 (continued))

items.quote: Now what is the process of knowledge? It is said, “Subjectivization of objectivities is the faculty of knowing.” The external entity or entities which are being subjectivized are known as objectivity or objectivities.
items.statement: Knowing is defined as the subjectivization of objectivities.
items.title: Shivas Teachings – 2 (continued) (Discourse 12)

items.quote: There are mainly two divisions, parávidyá [subjective knowledge] and aparávidyá [objective knowledge]. Parávidyá is that branch of knowledge which leads from analytical descent (from the infinite to the finite) to synthetic ascent (from the finite to the infinite). It helps human beings to reach the golden line of self-knowledge – the line which is the dividing line between objective knowledge and self-knowledge; the line beyond which is the sweet ideation of the all-pervasive Cognitive Faculty.
items.statement: Parávidyá conducts synthetic ascent from finite to infinite leading to self-knowledge, while aparávidyá governs objective, analytical mundane study for practical welfare.
items.title: Shivas Teachings – 2 (continued) (Discourse 12)

items.quote: People make efforts to get rid of these triple bondages and that which leads to temporary success in these efforts is called artha. That which leads to temporary success, but on a larger scale, is called madhyártha. And that which leads to permanent success is called Paramártha.
items.statement: In relieving the triple bondages, artha brings temporary relief, madhyártha provides broader temporary systemic relief, and Paramártha delivers permanent liberation.
items.title: Shivas Teachings – 2 (continued) (Discourse 13)

items.qualifiers: classification based on internal motive and external paraphernalia
items.quote: When a person, with or without any selfish motive, offers his or her deep reverence to an entity with undivided concentration, with or without external paraphernalia such as flowers, bel leaves, sandalwood paste, Ganges water, basil, bananas, rice, etc., that is called pújá or pújana. And the type of worship which is performed with selfish motive and external paraphernalia is called arcá or arcaná. The type of worship which is performed with or without selfish motive, but certainly without any specific external paraphernalia, is called prárthaná. And the special type of pújá which is performed without any selfish motive or external paraphernalia is called Brahmasadbháva [ideation of Brahma].
items.statement: Four distinct levels of worship are categorized: arcá (with selfish motive and paraphernalia), prárthaná (without specific paraphernalia), pújana (deep reverence with single-pointed focus), and Brahmasadbháva (unselfish ideation of Brahma without paraphernalia).
items.title: Shiva's Teachings – 2 (continued) (Discourse 14)

items.quote: Thoughts are also of various types: first, thoughts regarding the existing environment; second, thoughts regarding the past environment; third, thoughts without any environment; and fourth, fantastic thoughts.
items.statement: Thoughts are classified into four types: those of the existing environment, those of past environments, those without environment, and fantastic thoughts combining unrelated components.
items.title: Shiva's Teachings – 2 (continued) (Discourse 16)

items.quote: For if a person takes one step towards worldliness, one is likely to be entangled in all sorts of worldly allurements, and if one takes a step towards the “water of spirituality,” one will be carried away by its current. That very point, which is the connecting link between worldliness and spirituality, is tiirtha: Tiirasthaḿ tiirthamityáhuh.
items.statement: The geographical tiirtha represents the meeting line of land and water, and symbolically signifies the psychic junction point between worldliness and spirituality.
items.title: Shivas Teachings – 2 (continued) (Discourse 17)

items.quote: And the second thing you will see, or you will feel, is that they do not require these things. The microcosm, or unit spirit, does not require any food or clothes or sesame or utensils. All these ideas are scoundrels’ philosophy. And they have been doing this type of exploitation for the last five thousand years, since the time of the Atharva Veda.
items.statement: A departed unit spirit requires neither physical food nor material offerings, rendering ritualistic ancestral feeding a form of exploitation.
items.title: Shráddha

items.quote: N.B.: The departed soul does not get any advantage from the shráddha ceremony [memorial ceremony]. It is only meant for the psychic satisfaction of the person performing it.
items.statement: The memorial shráddha ceremony provides no objective benefit to the departed soul, serving exclusively the psychic satisfaction of the living performer.
items.title: Shráddha Ceremony

items.qualifiers: philosophical axiom cited from Ananda Sutram
items.quote: In Ananda Sútram it has been said, Bádhá sá yuśamáná shaktih sevyaḿ sthápayati lakśye “Obstacles are the helping forces which establish people in their cherished goal.”
items.statement: Obstacles are defined as helping forces that serve to establish people in their cherished goal.
items.title: Shrávańii Púrńimá

items.quote: Revolution takes place when, from the economic perspective, only two classes remain in society: the exploiting vaeshyas and the exploited shúdras. But if there are no vipras and kśatriyas from a mental standpoint – in other words if there are no people who, though shúdras from an economic standpoint, are vipras or kśatriyas from a mental standpoint – shúdra revolution will not be possible. It is not the work of people who have a shúdra mentality to bring about revolution.
items.statement: A shúdra revolution cannot be executed by purely shúdra-minded labourers; it requires vikśubdha shúdras who possess kśatriya or vipra mentalities.
items.title: Shúdra Revolution and Sadvipra Society

items.qualifiers: practical organizational protocol to combat hypocrisy
items.quote: The Acárya Board may take two months, four months, or a year to make a decision about this ácárya/á. But why should you wait that long for the decision? Under such circumstances you should take silent action – that is, do not accept the person’s ácárya-ship. It is a question of human rights, because Acárańát pát́hayati yah sah ácáryah – “One who teaches through one’s conduct is an ácárya.” If you cannot learn anything from the conduct and behaviour of a certain person, why should you accept that person as an ácárya/á?
items.statement: If an ácárya acts contrary to moral principles, practitioners should apply 'silent action' by immediately refusing to recognize their ácárya-ship without waiting for formal board rulings.
items.title: Silent Action

items.quote: Pátaka is divided into two categories. One category is Papa or sin. If something is done which should not be done it is called Papa. That which is not done but should be done is called Pratyaváya. Papa and Pratyaváya are both undesirable things. But according to the ancient saints and sages, Pratyaváya was more abominable than Papa.
items.statement: Pápa constitutes performing forbidden actions, whereas pratyaváya represents failing to execute duties that ought to be done.
items.title: Sin, Crime and Law

items.quote: That which is inherent or intrinsic in the mind and expresses itself in the external world is called Ripu or enemy. There are six Ripus – lust, anger, avarice, blind attachment, vanity and jealousy. That which originates in the external world and influences the mind is called Pasha. Thus Ripu is intro-external and Pasha is extro-internal.
items.statement: Ripus are internal psychic enemies that express outward, whereas páshas are external fetters that bind and influence the mind inward.
items.title: Sin, Crime and Law

items.qualifiers: affirmation of spiritual equality across genders
items.quote: In the spiritual and psycho-spiritual or supra-mental spheres, there is no difference between men and women. That is to say, the highest spiritual realization accessible to men is also accessible to women. There is no reason whatsoever to deprive women of the highest spiritual experiences or to impede their spiritual progress. Those who say that only men are entitled to liberation or salvation and that women will have to be reborn as males are saying something totally irrational.
items.statement: Spiritual realization in the supramental sphere is fully identical for men and women, despite physiological differences in lower propensities.
items.title: Smell and Microvita – Excerpt C

items.qualifiers: critical ideological critique of Gandhian trusteeship
items.quote: In Gandhism we find two defects: psychological and material. Although Gandhism is not pure capitalism, it undoubtedly protects capitalism. Capitalists find complete protection in this system. Gandhism claims that the capitalists are the trustees of the people, but how is that possible? Can those who thrive on human blood be the protectors of the people? How can the exploited masses believe that their exploiters will be their saviours? We can therefore see that Gandhism directly contradicts psychology.
items.statement: Gandhism contains major material and psychological defects by attempting to eliminate struggle and positing capitalists as trustees of the exploited.
items.title: Social Defects in Gandhism

items.quote: From the first expression of moralism, to the establishment in cosmic humanity, there is a gap. The concerted effort to negotiate this gap is termed as social progress, and the collective body of those who are engaged in this concerted effort I shall call the “society.”
items.statement: Social progress is defined as the concerted effort to negotiate the gap between the first expression of moralism and establishment in cosmic humanity, and 'society' is the collective body engaged in this effort.
items.title: Social Discourses

items.quote: In my opinion, sentencing people to capital punishment just because one cannot cure their ills is as much a crime as killing them oneself. Why is nothing done to remedy their ills? Is it not tantamount to beheading oneself to escape a headache? Rather it is the bounden duty of civilized society to cure the ills of these criminals. We shall have to deal with criminals with a humane heart and guide them out of their ills.
items.statement: Sentencing individuals to capital punishment instead of curing their ailments is considered criminal, and the penal system should eliminate punitive measures in favor of corrective rehabilitation camps.
items.title: Social Discourses

items.quote: The first cause of sin is: shortage of physical and psychic resources. If there is lack of physical necessities, people are not able to follow the higher pursuits of life. A person’s discrimination is easily disturbed; with a little anger even an intellectual utters crude words. Hence, due to a shortage of physical wealth, people become restless, lose their discrimination, and become brutal. It is because of this that communism has tended toward brutality. Likewise, if there is a dearth of intellectual resources and the intellectual standard of the people is not high, they may confuse dos and don’ts. An example is a riot in which an innocent little boy is killed. The one who encourages the riot becomes the people’s leader. Because the intellectual standard of the people is low, they commit blunders prompted by these leaders and become beasts.
items.statement: Sin originates from three main causes: shortage of physical and psychic resources, non-utilization of over-accumulated resources, and stagnancy.
items.title: Social Discourses

items.quote: Everyone should realize that to construct or preserve anything, there must be close cooperative action among the constituent parts. Human beings are not lifeless matter, so not only should all of their collective structures be based on cooperation, but that cooperation must be of a special type. It should not be based on the relation of master and servant, but on mutual cordiality. It should be a coordinated cooperation and not a subordinated one.
items.statement: True cooperative social structures between human beings must be founded on coordinated cooperation rather than subordinated master-servant relations.
items.title: Social Justice

items.quote: To make people conscious of their rights in every sphere of life – social, economic, psychic and spiritual – is called [[jiṋána vistára; and to exercise these rights fully is called vijiṋána sádhaná. ( 3 ) ]] Neglected people, who have remained ignorant of different branches of knowledge for whatever reason, should be given maximum opportunities to develop. There should not be any discrimination as far as these rights are concerned.
items.statement: Jiṋána vistára is defined as making people conscious of their rights in every sphere of life, while vijiṋána sádhaná is the full exercise of those rights.
items.title: Social Justice

items.quote: (21) Sevá (service) is of four kinds – shúdrocita, vaeshyocita, kśatriyocita and viprocita. This is known as nr yajiṋa.
items.statement: Service (sevá) or nr yajiṋa is classified into four distinct types based on social faculties: shúdrocita (physical labour), vaeshyocita (economic/material relief), kśatriyocita (protective/courageous physical rescue), and viprocita (spiritual/intellectual upliftment).
items.title: Society

items.quote: While forming socio-economic units, several factors should be considered. These include same economic problems; uniform economic potentialities; ethnic similarities; the sentimental legacy of the people; and similar geographical features.
items.statement: The formation of self-sufficient socio-economic units requires analysis of five specific criteria: common economic problems, uniform economic potentialities, ethnic similarities, sentimental legacy, and similar geographical features.
items.title: Socio-Economic Groupifications

items.qualifiers: regardless of colour, creed, race, mother tongue, or birthplace
items.quote: Local people are defined as those who have merged individual socio-economic interests with the socio-economic interests of the socio-economic unit they live in. The primary consideration is whether or not people have merged their individual interests with their socio-economic unit, regardless of their colour, creed, race, mother tongue, birthplace, etc. Those who earn their livelihood in a particular socio-economic unit but spend their earnings in another socio-economic unit should be considered as outsiders or non-local people, as this practice is not in accordance with the interests of the socioeconomic unit in which they are employed. It results in the drainage of the capital necessary for the continued growth of that unit and undermines its economic development.
items.statement: Local people are defined as those who have merged their individual socio-economic interests with the socio-economic interests of the unit they inhabit, rather than by race, creed, or birthplace.
items.title: Socio-Economic Movements

items.quote: It is worth mentioning that microvita do not belong to the category of krimi. However, like krimi and all other organic and psychic beings, microvita exist, multiply and die. But unlike krimi and other organic and psychic beings, they are not directly related to carbon atoms or carbon molecules.
items.statement: Microvita differ fundamentally from krimi (germs/unicellular life) because microvita are not directly related to carbon atoms or molecules and operate beyond barometric constraints.
items.title: Some Examples of Microvita in Daily Life – Excerpt A

items.quote: Why does microvita research need to be done in physical laboratories? Because atoms have two parts – the cruder part and the subtler part. Microvita also have two parts – the cruder part and the subtler part. So far atomic research has been done taking into account the cruder part of atoms. The subtler part of atoms has not been investigated. For research into the subtler part of atoms, psycho-spiritual practice is needed. When the cruder part of atoms could give energy for atom bombs, nuclear bombs, etc., much more can be achieved by exploring the subtler part of atoms. You will utilize the cruder part for the physical development of society, but many great things can be achieved by using the subtler part of atoms. This is yet to be seen. When research into the crude and the subtle part of atoms proceed together, then only will there be great benefit for the entire creation. The subtler part is closer to idea and the cruder part is closer to matter.
items.statement: Atoms and microvita contain both crude and subtle aspects; research on the crude portions belongs to physical laboratories, whereas exploration of the subtle portions closer to idea requires psycho-spiritual practice.
items.title: Some Guidelines for Commencing Microvita Research – Excerpt A

items.quote: Dhárańá and Dhyána are therefore quite different from each other although both take place in the citta. Dhárańá is process of the citta taking the shape of external objects, while dhyána concerns internal objects only. Dhárańa is static, while dhyána is full of dynamic form. Dhárańá is non-continuous and momentary, while dhyána is continuous. Dhárańá may result in action, but dhyána results only in the cessation of actions. Dhárańá is purely a creation of citta and is tamoguńi or static, where as dhyána is full of dynamism and is rajoguni or mutative by nature. The resultant cessation of action in dhyána shows that its final goal is Sattvaguńii Samádhi through the principle of sattvaguńa.
items.statement: Dhárańá is static, momentary, and shaped by external sensations arriving in discrete intervals, whereas dhyána is continuous, dynamic, internal, and culminates in the complete cessation of action (karma samádhi).
items.title: Some Questions and Answers on Ananda Marga Philosophy – Excerpt A

items.quote: Similarly, manomaya kośa or pure mental body can also be influenced by the Atimánasa kośa. This is known as Paeshácii Vidyá in Sanskrit; there is no English equivalent. By means of this influence a person can convert mental force into physical force and carry out physical actions by mental force only, without the use of the annamaya kośa of another person. When vijiṋánamaya kośa of an individual influences the atimánasa kośa of another person or persons it is called Gándharva vidyá. By this influence other persons can be enchanted and attracted. This is the influence which is expressed in arts like music, dancing, painting, etc. In music and dancing the annamaya and kámamaya kośas of others are attracted, while in painting the attraction is purely mental; hence painting is said to be a higher art than dancing and music. This influence can hold any audience spellbound if used in speech, music, dancing or painting. When vijiṋánamaya kośa of a person is influenced by the hirańmaya kośa of another is called Daevii vidya. It is by this influence and also by Gandharva vidyá that lesser Gurus guide their disciples. Gandharva vidyá is used in this way in the form of kiirtana and bhajana, etc.
items.statement: The occult psychic influences over the mental sheaths (kośas) are classified as Bhútavidyá, Paeshácii Vidyá, Gándharva vidyá, Daevii vidyá, Bráhmii vidyá, and Bráhmii Ákarśańa.
items.title: Some Questions and Answers on Ananda Marga Philosophy – Excerpt A

items.qualifiers: under extreme fear, stupefaction, crudity, or intense mental concentration
items.quote: In a dream, due to the dormant state of kámamaya kośa, the thought-vibrations of manomaya kośa appear real (this we call a dream when we wake up). When, due to extreme fear, stupefaction, crudity, or an excessive expression of any ripu or pásha, the kámamaya becomes temporarily suspended in the next higher kośa and the imagined objects appear real. This is also the case when a person sees various gods and goddesses. Psychologically, seeing a ghost, god or goddess is the same thing; none of them actually exist.
items.statement: Apparitions such as ghosts or visions of deities in a waking state are auto- or outer-positive hallucinations produced when the crude mind (kámamaya kośa) is temporarily suspended and concentrated into higher sheaths due to fear, stupefaction, or intense sentiment.
items.title: Some Questions and Answers on Ananda Marga Philosophy – Excerpt B

items.quote: Cooperative managers should be elected from among those who have shares in the cooperative. Members of agricultural cooperatives will get dividends in two ways – according to the amount of land they donated to the cooperative, and according to the amount of their productive manual or intellectual labour. To pay this dividend, initially the total produce should be divided on a fifty-fifty basis – fifty percent should be disbursed as wages and fifty percent should be paid to the shareholders in proportion to the land they donated. Local people should get first preference in participating in cooperative enterprises.
items.statement: Agricultural cooperatives should divide total produce on a fifty-fifty basis, distributing half as wages for manual or intellectual labour and half as dividends according to donated land shares.
items.title: Some Specialities of Prout's Economic System

items.quote: Now, how do these mudrás originate? The source of all sound is Paráshakti [primordial desire for expression], which is such a vast entity that it cannot be explained in words. Next comes madhyamá shakti , in which we try to translate the bháva or mental form into action. The next stage is vaekharii shakti . When translating bháva into action, we need to take the help of our vocal cords. Then comes dyotamáná shakti . At first we try to express something: we may or may not be able to do so. In your own life, sometimes you might have experienced that you are unable to exactly remember a person, for instance Hari Babu, whom you have seen numerous times: you feel that you have something in your mind to express, but you cannot give any outward expression to your mental image. This is dyotamáná shakti, that is, feelings that you actually want to express.
items.statement: The evolution of sound and psychic expression proceeds through five developmental stages: Paráshakti, madhyamá shakti, vaekharii shakti, dyotamáná shakti, and shrutigocará shakti.
items.title: Song, Dance and Instrumental Music

items.quote: Now, while rising upwards, the first step is the solid factor, where it rests. When, just after diikśá [initiation], the kulakuńd́alinii begins to move, it rises to the kśititattva. [We can then say] Devena saha; where deva means one’s abode, the ádi kśititattva [primordial solid factor]. So [changing the order of the words] the name “Sahádeva” [youngest of the Pandava brothers] means the solid factor. The kulakuńd́alinii continues to move upwards. What is above the solid factor? Apatattva. In which cakra? The svádhiśt́hána. What does apa mean? Liquid, kúlaḿ násti yasya – “that which has no kúla [limit]”. The universe exists within the vast liquid factor. That which has no limit is “Nakúla” [the liquid factor and name of the next-youngest Pandava brother]. What is above the nakúla? Tejastattva. Tejastattva means “universal energy”. The kulakuńd́alinii rise there. “Arjuna” [the middle Pandava brother] means “energy, power”. What is above this? The váyaviitattva [aerial factor], the anáhata cakra, ( 2 ) also called pavana. What was Bhima [the next-oldest of the Pandava brothers]? Pavananandana [the child of pavana]. The pavanatattva, the váyutattva. The kulakuńd́alinii rises still higher. Where does it go? To the ákáshatattva, the ethereal factor. This represents a state midway between matter and consciousness, between mind and body, between abstract and matter. It is the [lowest] point in the abstract-matter scale, and the [highest] point in the matter-abstract scale. A little higher is the region of the mind, and a little lower the region of váyutattva, which comes under the category of matter.
items.statement: In the esoteric interpretation of the Mahábhárata, the five Pandava brothers correspond to the five ascending fundamental factors: Sahadeva (solid), Nakula (liquid), Arjuna (luminous/energy), Bhima (aerial), and Yudhisthira (ethereal).
items.title: Spiritual Lessons of the Giitá – 3

items.quote: Sálokya means that the sádhaka feels that in the stratum, or sphere, where he or she is, where that person’s exalted mind is, he or she is not alone; the Supreme Father is also there. This samádhi, where the feeling is that in the stratum, or status, where the person is, that person’s Supreme Father is also there, gives the person very much pleasure. This first pleasure is called sálokya samádhi.
items.statement: The upward elevation of the coiled serpentine force (kulakuńd́alinii) across the bodily plexi produces distinct hierarchical stages of samádhi: sálokya, sámiipya, sáyujya, sárúpya, sárśt́hi, and ultimately nirvikalpa samádhi/kaevalya.
items.title: Stages of Samádhi

items.qualifiers: post-death state determined by reactive momenta
items.quote: A devayoni is actually a human spiritual aspirant who after death, due to his or her saḿskáras, undergoes a transformation in which “… he gives up his physical structure, that is, the solid body, and gives up his aquatic structure, that is, apatattva, also, but the other three factors – tejas (luminous), marut (aerial) and vyoma (ethereal) remain with him, with his detached mind.” ( 13 ) At the same time, devayonis are also the “singular or collective structures” of subtle positive microvita – beings forming the boundary between the physical and psychic worlds, and between the animate and inanimate creation. ( 14 ) They exert a profound influence upon the mind, and under certain circumstances, may become visible or otherwise perceivable. For a proper understanding of the subject of microvita, please consult the author’s Microvita in a Nutshell.
items.statement: A devayoni is defined as an entity with divine qualities resulting from a departed human aspirant retaining only the luminous, aerial, and ethereal factors with a detached mind, representing subtle positive microvita structures.
items.title: Appendices

items.quote: Dhanátmaka bhránti o cittáńavika srśt́i [Literally, “Positive hallucination and the creation of an ectoplasmic structure”]
items.statement: A visual occurrence resembling a deceased individual appearing in reality or in a photograph is explained as a positive hallucination combined with an ectoplasmic creation.
items.title: Strange Experiences – Chapter 13

items.quote: Bhayasrśt́a cittáńavika shakti-sampáta [Literally, “External projection of ectoplasmic force triggered by fear” bhayasrśt́a = bhaya + srśt́a; shaktisampáta = shakti + sampáta]
items.statement: A bodily phenomenon or projection triggered under extreme fear is classified as an external projection of ectoplasmic force.
items.title: Strange Experiences – Chapter 14

items.quote: Ekajaner saḿskáraja ávesha, bákider pratisáḿvedanika bhrántidarshana [Literally, “One person’s self-hypnotism arising from reactive momenta (saḿskára), and the remaining peoples’ psycho-reactive hallucination” Ekajaner = eka + janer; bhrántidarshana = bhránti + darshana]
items.statement: Apparitions witnessed collectively can involve self-hypnotism rooted in reactive momenta by one person, coupled with psycho-reactive hallucination in observers.
items.title: Strange Experiences – Chapter 5

items.quote: Pratisáḿvedanika tathyánubhu’ti – jágradavastáy [Literally, “Psycho-reactive perception of real events in the waking state” tathyánubhúti = tathya + anubhúti]
items.statement: Perceptions of distant crises or fatal occurrences experienced during the waking state operate as psycho-reactive perceptions of real events.
items.title: Strange Experiences – Chapter 9

items.quote: In this connection it should be understood that the philosophical term bhúta is different from the scientific term “element”. The Saḿskrta equivalent for element is maolika padártha. Philosophically, bhúta means that which has been created, that which is recognized as a factor (tattva). In the world there are many elements, but only five bhútas, five fundamental factors.
items.statement: In cosmological philosophy, a fundamental factor (bhúta) represents that which is created and recognized as a tattva, distinctly different from a chemical element (maolika padártha).
items.title: Struggle and Progress

items.quote: Through physical clash the kámamaya and manomaya Kośas can be developed, and through psychic clash the higher kośas can be developed.
items.statement: Physical clash between bodily components and mind develops the kámamaya and manomaya kośas, whereas cultivating psychic clash develops the higher kośas.
items.title: Struggle and Progress

items.quote: To become one with the Macrocosm is called liberation, and to transcend the periphery of the Cosmic Cycle and becomes one with the Non-attributional stance is called salvation. The Tangential Entity which connects the path of liberation and the path of salvation, who, although infinite, comes within the domain of the finite, is called Táraka Brahma.
items.statement: Liberation is the attainment of oneness with the Macrocosm within Saguna Brahma, whereas salvation is transcending the Cosmic Cycle entirely to merge into the Non-attributional stance.
items.title: Struggle and Progress

items.quote: All human approaches and all human emanations are of four stages.
