That is, we may say that all human expressions are four-staged expressions: the physical world and all physical activities concerned in the physical world, which is known as “Káma” in Saḿskrta; all psychic expressions, including the cruder psychic expressions, including the subtler psychic expressions, are limited within the jurisdiction of the psychic world, both conscious, sub-conscious and unconscious strata, known as “Artha” in Saḿskrta: the third world, the third stage is psycho-spirituality, that is, that which starts from the point situated within the scope of unit psychic world and touches the extremity, lowermost extremity, of the spiritual stratum. This third stage is known as the stage “Dharma”; and the fourth world – the progress, never-ending progress, in the realm of spirituality, known as “Mokśa”, the stage of “Mokśa”.
items.statement: Human expressions occur across four distinct stages: physical action (Káma), mental expression (Artha), psycho-spirituality (Dharma), and spiritual progress (Mokśa).
items.title: Subjective Approach and Objective Adjustment

items.quote: These questions, that is, the question portion, was known as nigama, and the answer portion, ágama. The collective name of ágama and nigama is Tantra.
items.statement: Tantra scripture is formally defined as the combination of questions posed by Párvatii (nigama) and the explanatory answers delivered by Sadáshiva (ágama).
items.title: Subjective Approach through Objective Adjustment

items.quote: It is that whatever you are doing, whatever you are thinking, you should always remember that that action of yours, those thoughts of yours, are being witnessed by Him. If you remember this, He remains the subject and you remain the object.
items.statement: Self-knowledge occurs when the unit mind realizes it is the witnessed object of Parama Puruśa, thereby bringing the witnessing subject within mental ideation.
items.title: Subjective Approach through Objective Adjustment

items.quote: Nara means the Operative Principle, and ayana means “shelter”. Parama Puruśa is the shelter of the Operative Principle, ( 7 ) is the shelter of Avyaktam . And that’s why Parama Puruśa is superior to, is greater than, Avyaktam, the Operative Principle.
items.statement: Parama Puruśa is designated Náráyańa because Nara denotes the Operative Principle and ayana signifies shelter, making Consciousness the ultimate refuge of the Operative Principle.
items.title: Subtler than the Subtlest Mind

items.quote: Immediately after the death of a creature, be it insect or human, the search for a new body starts afresh. Wherever it finds an appropriate environment, it will get a new body. Until it finds the new body, is the mind suspended? No, Even then it is engaged in action, the action of search. Search, search, effort, effort.
items.statement: Upon physical death, the mind cannot remain in a suspended state; it immediately engages in active search for a new body matching its stored reactive momenta.
items.title: Superstitions about Death

items.quote: Everyone’s nerve cells continue to function for at least some time after so-called death. In some such instances, as you have seen, I have saved persons from death.
items.statement: A person's nerve cells may continue to function for a period after clinical respiration, heart function, and nerve fibres stop, meaning irreversible death is not instantaneous.
items.title: Superstitions about Death

items.quote: Suppression occurs when the mind is prevented from expanding and all its outlets are closed, sealed and blocked. The nature of the human mind is that it wants to expand. Even if some force does not want the mind to expand, still the mind must try to expand. In Saḿskrta suppression is called “pradamana”.
items.statement: Pradamana (suppression) blocks mental expansion, avadamana (repression) damages the subconscious creating inferiority complexes, and damana (oppression) punishes actions to extinguish worthwhile aspirations.
items.title: Suppression, Repression and Oppression

items.quote: From the word brhat the word Brahma has come. Brahma literally means the Entity who is Himself very vast, and whose ideation makes others vast like Him. Brhattvád Brahma Brḿhanatvád Brahma. Brḿhanatvád means making others vast. He himself is very great, and hence he is called Brahma; but this is not enough. Besides that He has the capacity to make others equally great like Him, and that is why He is Brahma.
items.statement: Brahma is defined by two intrinsic Sanskrit derivations: brhattva (immeasurably vast Himself) and brḿhanatva (possessing the capacity to expand and make others vast).
items.title: Supramundane Heritage and Supramundane Desideratum

items.quote: “Artha” means that which causes the cessation of pain. This cessation is of two kinds – one is the momentary or temporary and the other is permanent. In temporary cessation, the possibility of the recurrence of pain has not been extinguished; with the removal of the temporary cause of the cessation, the previous state of pain comes back again. That which causes momentary or temporary cessation is called artha, and that which causes its permanent cessation, which destroys pain at the root or consumes it with seed, is called Paramártha.
items.statement: Artha represents the temporary or momentary cessation of pain, whereas Paramártha represents permanent cessation that eradicates pain at the root.
items.title: Supreme Benevolence and Mundane Pleasure (Shreya and Preya)

items.quote: Those objects of preyas which are enjoyable by the unit mind, are fragmentary. Such attraction for fragmentary objects of pleasure is called káma or mundane longing. And the attraction for the integral One, for the Great “I”, is called Prema or Divine Love. The movement of káma is towards unit entities and hence it is extroversial; the movement of prema is towards the Soul, towards Supreme Peace, and thus it is introversial.
items.statement: Káma (passion) is extroversial attraction directed toward fragmentary unit entities for ego gratification, while Prema (divine love) is introversial attraction directed toward the integral Soul.
items.title: Supreme Benevolence and Mundane Pleasure (Shreya and Preya)

items.quote: The realization that “I am Brahma” is called Pańd́á and the one who has attained pańd́á is called pańd́ita. Hence nástika pańd́ita or “atheist-pandit” is a contradiction in terms.
items.statement: A pańd́ita is strictly defined as one who has achieved pańd́á—the direct cognitive realization that 'I am Brahma'—making the term 'atheist-pandit' an inherent contradiction.
items.title: Supreme Benevolence and Mundane Pleasure (Shreya and Preya)

items.quote: The best prayer therefore is, “O Lord, do whatever You think fit and best for me. I do not know in which way lies my good – You know.”
items.statement: Spiritual surrender is compromised when asking for specific personal boons; authentic prayer requests only that the Lord do whatever He determines best.
items.title: Surrender

items.quote: Bhágavata dharma is quadruped: (1) Paramátmá, (2) vistára, (3) rasa and (4) sevá.
items.statement: Bhágavata dharma consists of four structural components: Paramátmá (Supreme Soul), vistára (infinite expansion), rasa (cosmic flow), and sevá (service).
items.title: Svábhávika Dharma and Bhágavata Dharma

items.quote: Aeshvaryaiṋca samagraiṋca viiryaiṋca yashasah shriyah; Jiṋána vaerágyayoshca tu śańńáḿ bhaga iti smrtam.
items.statement: The attribute bhaga comprises six specific faculties: aeshvarya (occult powers), viirya (commanding authority), yashah (fame), shrii (attraction/charm), jiṋána (knowledge), and vaerágya (renunciation of mundane coloration).
items.title: Svadharma and Paradharma – 2

items.quote: The root verb rańj means “to colour” something. When a person is not affected or swayed by the colour of any object whatsoever of the world, that person is said to have attained vaerágya. He or she moves among various colours, yet no colour of any object can spread its influence over the person’s mind. This is vaerágya.
items.statement: Vaerágya is the mental state in which an individual remains uninfluenced and uncolored by any mundane object or worldly vibration despite interacting with them.
items.title: Svadharma and Paradharma – 2

items.quote: So it is evident that humans’ svadharma is to practise this Bhágavata dharma, this mánava dharma. (Here the term dharma does not mean “religion”. It means guńadharma, or “property”, it means svabháva dharma [the characteristics of one’s own nature].)
items.statement: Dharma refers to intrinsic natural properties (svabháva/guńadharma), not religion, distinguishing human spiritual realization from lower animal sustenance drives.
items.title: Svadharma and Paradharma – 3

items.quote: Ananda Marga [[dharma]] scriptures means Subháśita Saḿgraha (all parts), Ánanda Vacanámrtam (all parts), and the books Namámi Krśńasundaram and Namah Shiváya Shántáya . The rest of the Ananda Marga literature is considered the associate scriptures. Ánanda Sútram is our philosophical treatise, and Caryácarya (all parts) is our social treatise.
items.statement: The core dharma scriptures of Ananda Marga are defined as Subháśita Saḿgraha, Ánanda Vacanámrtam, Namámi Krśńasundaram, and Namah Shiváya Shántáya, while Ánanda Sútram is philosophical and Caryácarya is social.
items.title: Svádhyáya

items.quote: You know, the measure of sacrifice is not its quantity or its grandeur. A sacrifice should always be measured in terms of the circumstances in which it has been rendered.
items.statement: The true spiritual measure of a sacrifice is evaluated not by its material volume or splendour, but by the circumstances and personal stakes under which it was rendered.
items.title: Svarńanakula Kathá

items.quote: Grammar must be formulated according to the way people speak; that is, grammar is a systemized form of dialogue – the accepted structure for the rules and regulations of conversation.
items.statement: Grammar is not an infallible fixed authority over speech, but rather an evolving systemized framework that must adjust to changes in spoken human dialogue.
items.title: Syntax (Discourse 11)

items.quote: Had physical clash not existed, the creation and evolution of the human mind would never have been possible. The emergence of subtle human intellect as we know it today would never have happened.
items.statement: Physical clash in the environment drove the creation and biological evolution of the human mind and subtle intellect.
items.title: Synthesis and Analysis

items.quote: However, science can never change people’s saḿskáras . Therefore, for the development of their personalities, there is no alternative for human beings other than to perform sadhana.
items.statement: While biological and glandular changes can alter future actions, scientific and physiological alterations can never modify a mind's stored reactive momenta (saḿskáras).
items.title: Synthesis and Analysis

items.quote: Remember that it is injurious to health to suppress the secretion of fluid, blood or pus of any skin sores by external application of medicines. So in the preliminary stage of the disease, no external ointments should be used. Only after the disease is fully developed should neem oil or any other external medicine be applied.
items.statement: Suppressing the discharge of fluid, blood, or pus from syphilitic sores via early external ointments harms health; ointments must wait until sores fully develop.
items.title: Syphilis

items.quote: Yesterday[see beginning] I told you that there are three types of pátaka [sin]. The first type is where atonement is possible. Suppose, for instance, that someone has stolen five rupees. Certainly that is a sin. But if the thief returns the money to its owner, and apologizes for his or her conduct, then it must be considered that the sin has been atoned for. The second type of pátaka is called atipátaka, and for that there is no social atonement. Suppose someone has brutally cut off someone else’s leg. To atone for that sort of sin will mean completely giving up all sorts of ease, comforts and pleasures of life for the sake of social welfare. The third category of sin is called mahápátaka. For that also there is no atonement. That kind of sin brings recurring harm to society. An example is the adulteration of black pepper with papaya seeds; because, if one businessman does this, another will see the first and be encouraged to imitate the first.
items.statement: Sin (pátaka) is classified into three tiers: pátaka (atonable socially), atipátaka (no social atonement, requires complete personal sacrifice), and mahápátaka (recurrent social contagion without atonement).
items.title: “Tadátmánaḿ Srjámyaham”

items.quote: I said before that pápa is also of two types – pátaka and pratyaváya . An action that should not be done but that is nevertheless done, is called pátaka . And an action that should be done but is not done, is called pratyaváya .
items.statement: Pápa is divided into pátaka (sin of commission, doing what should not be done) and pratyaváya (sin of omission, failing to perform required duty).
items.title: “Take Refuge in Parama Puruśa with Unswerving Attention”

items.quote: Akkodhena jine kodhaḿ asádhuḿ sádhuná jine Jine kadariiyaḿ dánena sattyena aliikavádinam.
items.statement: To overcome opponents and negative mental states in conflict, one must systematically adopt the reverse stance: patience against anger, honesty against deceit, charity against greed, and truth against falsehood.
items.title: Taking the Opposite Stance in Battle

items.quote: Chanting the name of Parama Puruśa aloud is called kiirtana; For, the vibration created in the atmosphere by kiirtana will influence others also. But if one’s mental ideation is conveyed only to Parama Puruśa without affecting other human beings, this is called bhajana. So bhajana is purely personal; it has no collective aspect. Kiirtana is more beneficial than bhajana
items.statement: Bhajana is purely personal mental ideation directed toward Parama Puruśa, whereas Kiirtana is vocal chanting that generates collective elevating environmental vibrations.
items.title: Taking the Opposite Stance in Battle

items.quote: The original name of the Bengali community was “Kaebarta” meaning “a community of fishermen”. They were divided into five groups – the Namashudras in the east; the Rajabangshir in the north; the Mahisyas in the south; the Sadgopes in the northern part; and the Mahatos in the west. Mahato came from “Mahatma”. These original five communities were not tribals.
items.statement: The indigenous non-tribal population of Bengal was historically known as the Kaebarta (fishermen community), which formed five regional groups: Namashudras, Rajabangshis, Mahisyas, Sadgopes, and Mahatos.
items.title: Talks on Bengal – Excerpt E

items.quote: A pure and subtle physical body or Annamaya Kosa is the best medium for a subtle psycho-spiritual manifestation. The purity of the Annamaya Kosa depends upon the food we eat and other rules such as bathing, fasting, etc.
items.statement: The purity of the physical body (Annamaya Kośa) directly governs subtle psycho-spiritual manifestation, depending on dietary discipline and physical conduct.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt A

items.quote: The words práńa dharma mean the cardinal characteristic of a person which differentiates one person from another.
items.statement: Práńa dharma is defined as the cardinal characteristic of an individual or the vital expression of an entire race developed through mode of living and internal discipline.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt B

items.quote: Now, the best way of enmity against a person or a race is to deprive the person or the race of the freedom to cultivate their práńa dharma, and to prevent them from channelizing their potentiality accordingly.
items.statement: Depriving an individual or race of the freedom to cultivate their práńa dharma is the subtlest and most effective method of enmity against them.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt B

items.quote: We can build up an ideal society only on the basis of a happy adjustment between the subjective and the objective approaches.
items.statement: An ideal society requires a synthetic adjustment balancing the East's subjective spiritual outlook and the West's objective material development.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt C

items.qualifiers: all four factors must be present together
items.quote: To be learned in the real sense mentioned above, all four factors are necessary. A person who has one of these points missing is not a learned person.
items.statement: Being truly learned requires fulfilling four simultaneous criteria: extensive reading, understanding, retention in memory, and appropriate practical action.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt D

items.quote: Singing, the playing of instruments and dancing are together called “ saḿgiita ”. Where there is only singing and the playing of instruments but no dance, it is called “ giita ”.
items.statement: Saḿgiita is defined as the combination of singing, playing instruments, and dancing, whereas giita includes only singing and instruments without dance.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt D

items.quote: The first is that education must always be based on factuality. There must not be the injection of any dogma or fanaticism or any type of geographical or racial chauvinism in the education system.
items.statement: True education must be built on three fundamentals: grounding in factuality without dogma, awakening a burning thirst for knowledge, and maintaining a balanced mind.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt E

items.qualifiers: must be fully independent from political authority
items.quote: The framing of educational policies, the control of the educational system, and all other activities concerned with education should be managed by a board comprised of efficient teachers. This board should enjoy full freedom and authority to carry out its duties. Education must be free from all political interference.
items.statement: The framing of educational policy and institutional management should be controlled entirely by efficient teachers without political interference.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt F

items.qualifiers: applies specifically to human beings due to their psychic wont
items.quote: But because of this psychic wont, they exploit others in the psychic level as well as the physical level, and this exploitation in the psychic level is more dangerous than in the physical one.
items.statement: Human expansion occurs both physically and psychically, making psychic exploitation potentially far more dangerous than physical subjugation.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt H

items.quote: Try to find a link between this finite and that infinite. That endeavour of yours is known as ‘mysticism’.
items.statement: Mysticism is defined as the human endeavour to establish a link between the finite unit and the infinite cosmic entity.
items.title: Talks on Education – Excerpt I

items.quote: The approach of PROUT is subjective approach through objective adjustment. This presupposes a connecting link between intuition and intellect. This connecting link or touching point is called “Bodhi Jiṋána”.
items.statement: Bodhi Jiṋána is the connecting link between transcendental intuition and empirical intellect, enabling intuitional knowledge to solve mundane problems.
items.title: Talks on Prout

items.quote: Payment for the time saved in doing a particular piece of work is called the bonus system of work. That is, a particular amount earned by labourers from the profit of the organization on the basis of their labour is called a bonus. Piece work payments are something else. If a piece of work is completed before the fixed time, and in the remaining portion of time extra work is done, then labourers will get extra payment for that extra work.
items.statement: In industrial management, a bonus system pays for time saved on a task, whereas piece work pays extra for additional work executed during remaining saved time.
items.title: Talks on Prout

items.quote: There are six stages in the process of expression. The seed of expression is called Parashakti and lies in the Muládhára Cakra (or basic plexus). In the Svádhisthána Cakra (or fluidal plexus), a person mentally visualises the expression. The mental vision of one’s expression is called Pashyanti Shakti. In the Mańipura Cakra (or solar plexus) this mental vision is transformed into mental sound which is called Madhyamá Shakti. The person now wants to express that feeling. This endeavour to express the feeling is called Dyotamáná Shakti. It works between the navel area and the throat. In the vocal cord it transforms an idea into language. This is called Vaekharii Shakti. After Vaekharii it is transformed into actual spoken language and is termed Shrutigocará.
items.statement: Vocal linguistic expression develops across six sequential stages, starting from the basic plexus up through the vocal cord to audible speech.
items.title: Talks on Prout

items.qualifiers: in exchange for productive work according to capacity
items.quote: Hence PROUT’s view is that people should be guaranteed the provision of sufficient purchasing power to meet these requirements. In that case the state need not adopt control measures.
items.statement: To prevent lethargy and bureaucratic overreach, the state should guarantee minimum necessities through sufficient purchasing power rather than direct distribution of commodities.
items.title: Talks on Prout

items.qualifiers: prohibited for women due to its physiological effects
items.quote: The hormones secreted through táńd́ava generate greater manliness and courage in the person. That is why hormones are secreted from the lymphatic glands and greater manliness is produced in those who practise táńd́ava .
items.statement: Táńd́ava dance stimulates the secretion of hormones from the lymphatic, pineal, and pituitary glands, enhancing courage, manliness, and memory.
items.title: Táńd́ava Dance – What and Why?

items.quote: very recently, perhaps on 6th September, I invented kaośikii, because for ladies there was a necessity for a dance similar to táńd́ava, and kaośikii will serve the purpose
items.statement: Kaośikii is a dance-exercise invented specifically to provide women with physical, mental, and spiritual benefits similar to those derived from táńd́ava.
items.title: Táńd́ava Is a Fight

items.quote: That which teaches discipline to human beings is called shástra. It usually deals with the dos and don’ts, that is, with what should be followed and what should not be followed, what should be practised and what should not be practised.
items.statement: Shástra refers to authoritative guidelines and disciplines that liberate human beings through systematic regulation.
items.title: Táńd́ava, Shástra, and the Teachings of Shiva

items.quote: Hence, in the course of sadhana, when a sádhaka achieves full control over objects (an object is nothing but a collection of inferential vibrations) he or she is said to have attained “tanmátrika samádhi”.
items.statement: Tanmátrika samádhi is attained when a spiritual aspirant achieves full one-pointed mental control over the inferential vibrations constituting objects.
items.title: Tanmátrika Samádhi

items.qualifiers: differs from the Vedic practices across the rest of India
items.quote: Women, though belonging to a new gotra [clan] after marriage, were entitled to observe the funeral rites of their departed parents. They would observe ashaoca [mourning] for three days and three nights after their father’s or mother’s death, and on the fourth day would perform the shráddha ceremony [in commemoration of the departed].
items.statement: Ancient Bengali society was Tantric and matrilineally inclined, granting married women the rights to retain parental surnames and perform ancestral shráddha rites.
items.title: Tantra in Bengal – Excerpt B

items.qualifiers: inner spirit of both derivations is identical
items.quote: So the root verb tan means to expand, and thus Tantra is the scientific process which leads to liberation through the process of expansion.
items.statement: Tantra carries two complementary meanings: the practical process that eliminates static dullness, and the scientific process leading to liberation through mental expansion.
items.title: Tantra Is Sádhaná, Sádhaná Is Tantra

items.qualifiers: historical assessment of Shiva around 5000 BCE
items.quote: It was He who systematized the science of Tantra and thus He was the guru or the father of Tantrics and yogis. To this Self-realized Mahápuruśa there was no distinction of high and low.
items.statement: Shiva systematized Tantra into a universal way of life and overcame racial antagonisms between Aryans and non-Aryans in prehistoric India.
items.title: Tantra and Indo-Aryan Civilization

items.quote: There are many who try to make a distinction between Hindu Tantra and Buddhist Tantra. This is absolutely wrong, for as I have said earlier, Tantra is one and only one. It is based on one sentiment, on one idea. The Buddhist and Hindu Tantras express the same thing in different words.
items.statement: Hindu Tantra and Buddhist Tantra share identical philosophical substance, differing solely in external terminology and deities.
items.title: Tantra and Indo-Aryan Civilization

items.qualifiers: hormones from lower glands cannot regulate upper glands
items.quote: Since the sahasrára cakra [corresponding to the pineal gland] is the highest cakra, or plexus, hormones secreted by that plexus can control all other glands of the human body.
items.statement: The sahasrára cakra functions as the master controlling station whose secretions regulate the hormones and propensities of all lower bodily plexuses.
items.title: Tantra and Its Effect on Society

items.qualifiers: both systems were formulated by Sadáshiva for different levels of aspirants
items.quote: The practice of the Five M’s was formulated for those people who harboured secret desires for crude physical enjoyment. But for those guided by subtle propensities, the subtle Paiṋcamakára, or yoga márga, was prescribed.
items.statement: The crude Five M's (Paiṋcamakára) were designed to gradually restrain crude physical desires, while the subtle Five M's represent internal yogic practices.
items.title: Tantra and Sádhaná

items.qualifiers: must include both diipanii and mantra caetanya
items.quote: “The process which produces the capacity to realize the inner import of mantra and which expedites the requital of the saḿskáras, or reactive momenta, is called diikśá.”
items.statement: Diikśá is the initiation process that imparts the spiritual realization of a mantra's inner meaning and expedites the exhaustion of reactive momenta (saḿskáras).
items.title: Tantra and Sádhaná

items.qualifiers: avidyá practices lead to psychic degradation
items.quote: Through Vidyá Tantra one “binds” [wins] Paramátmá, while through Avidyá Tantra one binds [dominates] living beings. Vidyá Tantrics accept Paramátmá as their object of supreme adoration, and in order to become one with Him, they channelize all the powers they have acquired towards Him.
items.statement: Vidyá Tantra channelizes spiritual power inward toward union with Paramátmá, whereas Avidyá Tantra squanders occult power for external mundane domination.
items.title: Tantra and Supernatural Power

items.quote: One of the characteristics of Tantra is this, that the different gods and goddesses originate from one idea or other. Those ideas were conceived in order to arouse and develop the finer sensibilities of the human mind. Thus a person conceived of a certain idea, and to make concrete that abstract idea, an image was invented. But such an idea, whether good or bad, is not an integral idea, it is a non-integral idea.
items.statement: Tantric and Puranic deities are externalizations of specific non-integral psychic ideas rather than the integral Supreme Consciousness.
items.title: Tantric Goddesses

items.qualifiers: can only be relaxed under exceptional centralized approval
items.quote: (2) Ácárya/ás who have a minimum of five hundred initiates and are adept in the difficult Visheśa Yoga will be eligible for purodhá training.
items.statement: Purodhá training requires an ácárya to have initiated at least five hundred persons and attained mastery in Visheśa Yoga.
items.title: Táttvika, Ácárya/á, and Purodhá

items.quote: It has been prescribed to spell the mantras in one’s mother tongue, because to read out words of oath in some other language without understanding their meaning is nothing but a farce.
items.statement: The ritual mantras for the Játakarma ceremony must be recited in the vernacular mother tongue so that participants fully understand their social oath of child welfare.
items.title: Táttvika Diipiká (Caturtha Parva)

items.qualifiers: applies strictly to children under age five
items.quote: It is meaningless to impart diikśá under five years of age, since at this stage the nerve cells of a human child are undeveloped. Consequently, at age of five, there is no disposition or propensity for intricate types of spiritual practices.
items.statement: Spiritual initiation (diikśá) should not be imparted prior to age five because the nerve cells and sense of responsibility are insufficiently developed.
items.title: Táttvika Diipiká (Paiṋcama Parva)

items.quote: “Shamanam” means bringing the external enemies under control, and “damanam” means bringing the internal enemies under control.
items.statement: In Sanskrit terminology, shamanam refers to subjugating external enemies, whereas damanam designates conquering the mind's internal enemies.
items.title: Ten Wonts of Dharma

items.quote: Every vibration in this universe has colour and sound. Every vibration also represents a particular idea, and hence each idea has a vibrational sound and vibrational colour. Many vibrational waves are too long or too short to be perceived by human beings - we cannot hear their sound or see their colour – but they do exist. We can speak of them as causal matrices in the realm of vibrational colour; and consider them as the biija mantras [acoustic roots] of the ideas with which they are concerned.
items.statement: Every vibration in the universe possesses a corresponding vibrational colour and vibrational sound, which constitute its causal matrix or acoustic root (biija mantra).
items.title: The Acoustic Roots of the Indo-Aryan Alphabet

items.qualifiers: occurs during prolonged historical pause phases
items.quote: Under such circumstances, service from a greater personality is required. And just to give a proper medicinal dose to that society – that society will become just like a stagnant pool of water – Parama Puruśa sayeth in this shloka that “I come.”
items.statement: When collective social impurities accumulate during structural pause phases beyond the problem-solving capacity of sadvipras, Parama Puruśa descends as Mahásambhúti.
items.title: The Advent of Mahásambhúti

items.quote: As long as ahaḿ remains smaller than citta, the psychic faculty is called mánaśa (crude mind-stuff). But when ahaḿ surpasses citta in size as a result of increased clash the enlarged portion of the mind is called maniiśá (intellect). And when mahat becomes larger than ahaḿ due to extreme clash, that enlarged portion is called bodhi (intuition).
items.statement: Mind consists of three functional stages: crude mind (citta), intellect (maniiśá when ahaḿ exceeds citta), and intuition (bodhi when mahat exceeds ahaḿ).
items.title: The Ascent of the Mind

items.qualifiers: time cannot exist without space and observer
items.quote: Time or Kála is the mental measurement of the dynamism in action. Where there is no action there is neither mind nor time.
items.statement: Time (kála) is the mental measurement of dynamism in action, and therefore constitutes a relative truth dependent on space and person.
items.title: The Base and the Relative Truth (Ádhára and Ápekśika Satya)

items.qualifiers: practised within regular family and social life
items.quote: The practice whereby we develop detachment from finite objects, i.e. the discipline whereby the mind is not influenced by the attractions of worldly objects is Vaerágya Sádhaná.
items.statement: True vaerágya is not escapist ascetic renunciation, but the mental discipline of non-attachment achieved by viewing all finite entities as expressions of Infinite Brahma.
items.title: The Base of Life

items.qualifiers: when not engaged in necessary physical work
items.quote: Whenever there is no important job to do, do not waste your time in idle thinking, because idle thinking means mental deterioration, mental degradation, psychic degeneration. So utilize each and every moment of your life in doing something good, in thinking something good. When you are not physically doing something good, then mentally do something good. And the best mental work, the best mental engagement, is kiirtaniiyah sadá harih – “Do the kiirtana of Parama Puruśa.”
items.statement: Because the mind cannot remain idle without degrading, all spare mental capacity should be occupied with spiritual ideation or kiirtana of the Supreme.
items.title: The Best Mental Engagement

items.qualifiers: serves as the final guiding factor for salvation
items.quote: And the resultant of the jiṋána sádhaná and the karma sádhaná is bhakti. So bhakti is not a sádhaná, bhakti is not a practice. It is the resultant of two practices – jiṋána and karma.
items.statement: Bhakti (devotion) is not an independent practice, but the subtle culmination and resultant of jiṋána sádhaná and karma sádhaná.
items.title: The Best Process

items.quote: Actually, tiirtha means that stance from where if you go a step deeper, a step inner, you will be in the land of bliss, and if you go a step cruder you will be within the realm of crude materiality, the crude world.
items.statement: A real tiirtha is the internal mental threshold from which one can turn inward toward spiritual bliss, making external physical pilgrimage sites unnecessary.
items.title: The Best Tiirtha

items.quote: Now, the mind is blind. With the help of the viveka [conscience] it is able to see and visualize. So the mind is Dhritarastra [the blind king of the Mahábhárata], and its forces – that is, the ten agents, the bahihkarańa – can work in ten directions simultaneously. So the mind has ten by ten or one hundred external expressions. Or in other words, Dhritarastra has one hundred sons.
items.statement: In the allegorical interpretation of the Mahábhárata, King Dhritarastra represents the blind mind whose one hundred sons are the ten external organs operating across ten directions.
items.title: The Biological Machine

items.quote: Parama Puruśa cannot do two things, and there lies His imperfection. He cannot create a second Parama Puruśa . He always remains a singular Entity. He loves, but while loving He wants that entity to also become Parama Puruśa, like Him. But as soon as that entity becomes Parama Puruśa, that entity becomes one with the original Parama Puruśa . So Parama Puruśa always remains One. He cannot create a second Parama Puruśa . And the second thing he cannot do is: He cannot hate anybody.
items.statement: Parama Puruṣa is incapable of creating a second Parama Puruṣa or hating any entity.
items.title: The Birthright of All

items.qualifiers: governed by crudity versus subtlety of thoughts and actions
items.quote: Now, when one’s goal goes from crude to cruder, the distance, i.e., the length of the radius, increases. The person has drifted away from the centre because of his base thoughts, base longings and base actions. And when the thoughts and actions go from subtle to subtler, the length of the radius decreases, and a day comes, a sweet moment comes, when the person becomes one with the Nucleus. That is what is called mokśa.
items.statement: A person drifts further from the Supreme Nucleus as thoughts and actions become cruder, whereas subtler thoughts decrease this radius until attaining mokṣa.
items.title: The Birthright of the Microcosm

items.quote: There are three main systems of cropping which will ensure the maximum utilization of land – mixed cropping, supplementary cropping and crop rotation.
items.statement: The maximum utilization of agricultural land relies on three primary cropping systems: mixed cropping, supplementary cropping, and crop rotation.
items.title: The Blending of Crops

items.quote: In supplementary cropping there is one main crop and a minor crop to support it. This system is different from mixed cropping where all crops are major.
items.statement: In mixed cropping, all co-cultivated crops are major crops, whereas in supplementary cropping, a minor crop supports a single main crop.
items.title: The Blending of Crops

items.quote: The meaning of the word bhakti is “attraction to the Supreme”. When the attraction is to something limited, it is called ásakti, and when the attraction is to the Supreme, it is devotion, bhakti. There is no compromise, no meeting point, between ásakti and bhakti, between attraction to the Supreme and attraction to the objects of the world. In ásakti, the feeling is that I get the object. In bhakti, the feeling is that I merge myself in Him.
items.statement: Āsakti is attraction toward limited mundane objects seeking acquisition, while bhakti is attraction toward the Supreme seeking self-mergence.
items.title: The Bliss of the Devotee

items.qualifiers: nāsāpāna is conditioned on having an empty stomach
items.quote: (Method of doing vyápaka shaoca: At first wash your genital organs; then hands up to elbows and legs up to knees; then, taking a mouthful of water, splash water on the eyes and face at least twelve times. Finally wash the ears and the neck. Do násápána (flushing the nostrils with water) also (only if your stomach is empty).)
items.statement: Vyāpaka shaoca must be performed by washing genital organs, hands to elbows, legs to knees, splashing water on eyes and face twelve times with a mouthful of water, and washing ears and neck, with nāsāpāna performed only on an empty stomach.
items.title: The Body

items.qualifiers: in the context of Aśt́áuṋga Yoga
items.quote: The Paiṋcakośas shall have to be perfected, but how is it possible? They can be consummated only through the practice of Yama and Niyama. The Annamaya Kośa is perfected through Ásanas (physical postures). Yama and Niyama Sádhana perfect the Kámamaya Kośa. The Manomaya Kośa is perfected through Pránáyáma. Through Pratyáhára the Atimánasa Kośa is perfected. The Vijiṋánmaya Kośa is perfected through Dhárańá and the Hirańmaya Kośa through Dhyána.
items.statement: Each of the five mental sheaths (pañcakoṣa) is perfected through specific limbs of Aṣṭāṅga Yoga.
items.title: The Call of the Supreme [in printed editions titled Invocation of the Supreme, pending correction]

items.qualifiers: relative factor requiring action and a measuring mind
items.quote: Time is not an eternal factor. Because what is time? It is mental reckoning of the motivity of action. This mental reckoning of the motivity of action [means that] where there is no action, there cannot be any time.
items.statement: Time is defined as the mental reckoning of the motivity of action.
items.title: The Causal Matrix

items.quote: For yojanát in Sanskrit there are two verbs. ( 12 ) One is yuj and the other is yuiṋj. Yuj means to come in close contact but maintaining one’s individuality. It is [just like] a mixture of sand and sugar. There is close contact between the sand and sugar, but they maintain their individual identities. And then there is yuiṋj. Yuiṋj means [not just] to come in contact, but to become one with each other. One is addition and the other is unification. The root verb yuj means “to add” and the root verb yuiṋj means “to unify”. Here, yojanát means unification.
items.statement: In Sanskrit roots of association, 'yuj' signifies maintaining separate individual identity during contact, whereas 'yuñj' signifies total unification.
items.title: The Causal Matrix

items.quote: What is the system of thought-process? What is thought? Some portion of the ectoplasmic stuff takes a particular form, and that form is a crudified form of ectoplasm; when projected internally, it takes form. Similarly this quinquelemental universe is a projected crudified form of Cosmic ectoplasm.
items.statement: The quinquelemental universe is a projected, crudified form of Cosmic ectoplasm within the mind of the Supreme Entity.
items.title: The Causal Matrix

items.quote: You are to do kiirtana . During kiirtana what happens? The mind gets lifted, exalted, and as a result you will enjoy a particular nature of peace. And if you start your sadhana just after doing kiirtana, you will enjoy bliss. So kiirtana is a necessity, is an indispensable necessity for proper sadhana.
items.statement: Kiirtana elevates and exalts the mind to a state of composure necessary to achieve one-pointedness in sādhanā.
items.title: The Chance to Be One with Him

items.qualifiers: based on the predominance of subtle or crude forces
items.quote: According to the predominance of subtle or crude forces we may divide the motor and sensory organs into three groups. The subtle sattvaguńa (sentient quality) is predominant in the vocal organ and tamoguńa (static quality) in the region of the genitals. Vocal organ and hands are sattvaguńii because speech expresses internal ideas externally and the hands give form to subtle inner feeling, or create arts and crafts. The feet are rajogúnii(mutative) due to their kinetic or locomotive characteristics, and the anus and the genitals are tamogúnii (static). According to the five functional distinctions of speech, action, movement, excretion and procreation we determine the individual characteristic of the motor organs. There are functional distinctions among the sensory organs also: the ear receives sounds, the subtlest of the tanmátras, and so it imbibes the greatest amount of sattvagúna. The nose is tamogúnii in the highest degree. The ear and the skin are sattvagunii and the tongue and nose tamoguńii.
items.statement: Sensory and motor organs are categorized into sentient, mutative, and static qualities based on their functional characteristics.
items.title: The Chariot and the Charioteer

items.quote: Remember, restraint or control over the senses or organs does not mean their annihilation. The meaning of saḿyama (restraint) is not extermination or murder. It means the judicious use or application of one’s impulses.
items.statement: Restraint (saṁyama) over the senses does not mean extermination or destruction, but the judicious and controlled application of impulses.
items.title: The Chariot and the Charioteer

items.quote: Nature dislikes disobedience or the act of breaking the law. As long as legal statutes exist, they must be obeyed. If they are found to be harmful or stand in the way of the progress of society, or if they hold back the forward march of humanity like a serpent entwined around the legs of a person, these statutes should be ground into the dust and new laws should be enacted and obeyed.
items.statement: Legal statutes must be obeyed as long as they exist, and if they obstruct social progress, they should be destroyed and replaced by new enacted laws.
items.title: The Civil Disobedience Movement

items.quote: Now why does He come in contact with the quinquelemental factors? Why does He come within the jurisdictions of the temporal-spatial-personal factors, these three fundamentally-related factors? What is the cause? There are two reasons. One thing is, the human intellect may get satisfaction after coming in psychic contact with the Impersonal Entity, but the human heart is not satisfied with that Impersonal Entity. The human heart wants something closer, something more sentimental, something more pleasing. And that’s why just to satisfy, just to give pleasure to, His progeny, He comes within the scope of these relative factors. Parama Puruśa becomes Táraka Brahma . And the second reason is that in this created world, in this universe, each and every progress is a progress through clashes and cohesion. And human beings must have sufficient intellectual stamina to move forward, fighting against all those pebbles of obstacles. When the human intellect fails to do something new in helping society to move forward, Parama Puruśa finds no alternative but to bring Himself within the scope of the temporal-spatial-personal factors just to guide the depraved and degenerate human society.
items.statement: Parama Puruṣa embodies as Tāraka Brahma to provide a tangible personal relationship for the human heart and to guide society when human intellect fails amid degeneration.
items.title: The Coming of Táraka Brahma

items.quote: Doing what a human being should not do is pápa, and not doing what a human being should do is pratyaváya. Pátaka includes both pápa and pratyaváya. You should not steal, and, if you do, you commit pápa. You should assist a helpless person, and, if you do not, you commit pratyaváya.
items.statement: Pāpa is committing prohibited actions, pratyavāya is failing to perform obligatory actions, and pātaka encompasses both.
items.title: The Complications of Doing Evil

items.qualifiers: regardless of wealth, social position, or rank
items.quote: When he or she is to impart any duty to anyone, he should be strict, strong and exact, like a diamond. He or she should never consider social position, wealth, rank, etc. Only those who are established in Yama and Niyama [moral code] and practise sádhaná can be given any responsibility.
items.statement: Responsibilities and leadership positions in society should be granted exclusively to individuals who strictly practice sādhanā and are established in Yama and Niyama.
items.title: The Conduct of an Ácárya

items.qualifiers: methods of redemption match the severity of the offense
items.quote: The sins committed by a pátakii are not of very serious nature. The redemption of a pátakii is possible if one, forgetting whatever has been done, takes to the path of spirituality. The second form of a pátakii is atipátakii. This is one who has done permanent physical or mental damage to a particular person. Then the third type is mahápátakii. The sins committed by a mahápátakii are of recurring nature. The best course for an atipátakii is to sacrifice his individual pleasure and involve himself in the welfare of humanity. But of course the mahápátakii has to sacrifice his life for the welfare of mankind. In addition to that, he will have to do something which will be of permanent benefit for human beings.
items.statement: Sinners are classified into pātakī, atipātakī (inflicting permanent damage), and mahāpātakī (committing recurring damage), with redemption requiring progressively greater personal sacrifice for humanity.
items.title: The Consequences of Free Will and Mind

items.quote: The principles of Prout depend upon the following fundamental factors: No individual should be allowed to accumulate any physical wealth without the clear permission or approval of the collective body. There should be maximum utilization and rational distribution of all mundane, supramundane and spiritual potentialities of the universe. There should be maximum utilization of physical, metaphysical and spiritual potentialities of unit and collective bodies of human society. There should be a proper adjustment amongst these physical, metaphysical, mundane, supramundane and spiritual utilizations. The method of utilization should vary in accordance with changes in time, space and person, and the utilization should be of progressive nature.
items.statement: Prout establishes five fundamental principles governing the accumulation, utilization, distribution, and temporal adaptation of universal resources and human potentialities.
items.title: The Cosmic Brotherhood

items.quote: Táńd́ava – which was not invented by me, but by Sadáshiva some seven thousand years ago – is an all-corporal exercise, an exercise for the entire body, including the brain. (There are intellectual exercises for the brain, but hardly any physical exercise. In fact, táńd́ava is the only physical exercise for the brain.) And among all dances it is the best. But it is not for women.
items.statement: Tāṇḍava is an all-corporal physical exercise invented by Sadāshiva that exercises the whole body including the brain, but is not for women.
items.title: The Cosmic Father Has a Special Responsibility

items.quote: Non-qualified liberation, or mokśa, is, however, only possible if the mental body, starting from the crudest mental subjectivity of the physical body, can, by any force, retrace against the singular positive force emanating due to the thought-projection of the Macrocosm. This force against the singular positive force must be a negative one. Hence the path of non-qualified spiritual practice which can reach final mokśa is always the path of negativity. The theoretical negative force with its fundamental negativity, which tends towards the final merger into Puruśa for attaining mokśa, is called kulakuńd́alinii – the “coiled serpentine”.
items.statement: Attaining non-qualified liberation (mokṣa) requires the fundamental negative force of kulakuṇḍalinī in the mūlādhāra to retrace against the positive thought-projection of the Macrocosm.
items.title: The Creation of the Universe

items.qualifiers: comprehensive across physical, psychic, and spiritual domains
items.quote: The fact is that a guru – if one is to be accepted as a real guru – shall have to remove darkness from all the strata of the physical world, all the strata of the psychic world, and also all the strata of the spiritual world.
items.statement: A true guru must be capable of removing darkness across all three strata of human existence: physical, psychic, and spiritual.
items.title: The Criteria of a Guru

items.qualifiers: prerequisite to be a spiritual guru
items.quote: Kaolas are those who by dint of sádhaná have successfully elevated their microcosmic stance and established it in the Macrocosmic one; but a Mahákaola is one who is a kaola, certainly, but at the same time possesses the capacity to help others as well to get to that exalted kaola position. In the past Lord Shiva was one such Mahákaola. Lord Krśńa was another. To be a guru one must be a Mahákaola.
items.statement: A Mahākaola is an elevated spiritual master who is established in the Macrocosmic stance and possesses the capacity to elevate others to that state.
items.title: The Criteria of a Guru

items.quote: When the mind moves along a particular track or follows a particular discipline in a methodical way, this is called “devotion” or bhakti; but when it does not follow a particular method, when it moves haphazardly, swept away by whim, it is called “emotion”. This is the fundamental difference between devotion and emotion.
items.statement: Devotion (bhakti) is mental flow moving along a methodical spiritual discipline, whereas emotion moves haphazardly on whim.
items.title: The Cult of Spirituality – the Cult of Pinnacled Order

items.quote: So in the first stage of sádhaná, as a result of the constant superimposition of Cosmic ideation, Bhavánii Shakti is changed into Bhaeravii Shakti. Then all the objects of the world are seen as expressions of Brahma.
items.statement: Through the continuous superimposition of Cosmic ideation in sādhanā, Bhavānī Shakti is transformed into Bhairavī Shakti, eliminating the perception of differentiation.
items.title: The Devotee and the Lord

items.quote: The question of fasting (upavása) arises in this context. The Saḿskrta prefix upa means near. Upavása means sitting near. So upavása by connotation means sitting near Parama Puruśa as opposed to being extroversial. On the day of fasting people abstain from eating solid food. It is easier to concentrate the mind on those days than on other days. The meaning of the word anashana is “not taking food”.
items.statement: Upavāsa denotes sitting near Parama Puruṣa by withdrawing the mind from extroversial thoughts, whereas anaśana means physical fasting.
items.title: The Devotee and the Lord [to be retitled “The Lord of the Devotee”]

items.quote: During meditation you should think that the entity on whom you are meditating is looking at you as His object. He is not your object. He sees whatever you are doing. This should be the psychology. He can never be your object. During meditation you should remember that the Supreme Entity looks on you, sees you as His object. He is not your object, you are His object.
items.statement: During meditation, an aspirant should realize that Parama Puruṣa is the Supreme Subject witnessing the aspirant as His object, rather than treating Parama Puruṣa as an object.
items.title: The Devotee and the Object of Adoration

items.quote: What is átmajiṋána? Átmajiṋána means “self-realization” – not “self-knowledge” [in the ordinary sense]. Suppose you know of a flower. Here there are three – the knower, you; the known, the flower; and the knowledge, the link between you and the flower. But in the case of self-realization, the knower, the known, and the knowledge are all one.
items.statement: Ātmajñāna (self-realization) is the complete non-dual state where the knower, the known, and knowledge merge into one single entity.
items.title: The Dialogues of Shiva and Párvatii – 2

items.qualifiers: structural distinction of mind in evolution
items.quote: The fundamental difference between the mind of a developed organism having citta, ahaḿtattva and mahattattva, and the mind of a human having mahattattva, aham and citta, is that the former is guided by instinct because the scope of the citta is bigger than that of the other two parts, while the latter is guided by intellect and intuition, because in it the scope of the mahat and the aham is bigger than that of the citta.
items.statement: Lower minds are guided by instinct because citta dominates mahat and ahaṁ, whereas human minds are guided by intellect and intuition because mahat and ahaṁ dominate citta.
items.title: The Difference Between Developed and Undeveloped Mind

items.quote: According to Ánanda Márga philosophy, this doomsday or pralaya will never occur. On the one hand, the flow of creation will continue and on the other, there will be jadasphota [gradual or instantaneous disintegration]. There will never be a complete thermal death. of the universe.
items.statement: Complete universal dissolution (pralaya) will never occur because the flow of creation and jaḍasphoṭa occur simultaneously.
items.title: The Divine Drama

items.quote: Saḿskrta is not the Vaedika language. After the death of the Vaedika language Prákrta was born. The synthetic language which was made by rectifying the Prákrta language was known as Saḿskrta. “Saḿskrta” means “reformed” – the reformation of the Prákrta language.
items.statement: Sanskrit was an artificial, reformed language derived from Prākrta rather than being identical to the older spoken Vaedika language.
items.title: The Education System of the Mahábhárata Age

items.qualifiers: Systaltic nature of movement and belligerent forces in the microcosm
items.quote: That is why I say that there cannot be any actual progress in the physical and psychic planes; there can only be progress in the stratum of spirituality.
items.statement: Real progress cannot occur in the physical and psychic planes; genuine progress occurs exclusively in the spiritual stratum.
items.title: The Essence of Spiritual Progress

items.quote: Thus there are three Tántrik phases in spiritual progress: pashvácár, viirácárá, and divyácáŕa.
items.statement: Spiritual progress in Tantra Sadhana proceeds through three sequential phases: pashvácára, viirácára, and divyácára.
items.title: The Essence of Spiritual Progress

items.quote: He looked deeply into human psychology and found that human beings do not really want happiness – they want absolute peace: peace is better than happiness.
items.statement: Human beings do not intrinsically seek ordinary happiness, but rather absolute direct direct peace.
items.title: The Essential Dharma

items.qualifiers: Universal condition for human societal survival
items.quote: An analytic perspective brings divisions, and divisive tendencies create impediments to peace. The only way out now to save human beings from destroying tranquillity is to adopt the path of synthesis; there is no other way than this.
items.statement: A purely analytic perspective drives national and sectarian divisions, whereas permanent human peace requires adopting the path of synthesis.
items.title: The Ever-Expanding Domain of the Microcosm

items.quote: The Mayan civilization is a transplanted Indian civilization. It migrated to Central America during the rule of the Pallavas of South India.
items.statement: The historical Mayan civilization originated as a transplant of Indian civilization during the reign of the Pallavas of South India.
items.title: The Evolution of Human Civilization

items.qualifiers: Expressed as the speaker's firm conviction
items.quote: I replied that my firm conviction is that atom bombs do not have the power to annihilate the human race because they are merely a product of the human mind. They do not have the power to destroy the minds of those who created them.
items.statement: Atom bombs lack the inherent power to annihilate the human race because they are mere products of the human mind.
items.title: The Evolution of Human Civilization

items.quote: You know, a language has an average longevity of 1000 years.
items.statement: A natural language possesses an average longevity of approximately 1000 years before transforming.
items.title: The Evolution of Indian Languages

items.quote: Now, when Saḿskrta died she left behind seven daughters: 1) Mágadhii Prákrta, 2) Shaurasenii Prákrta, 3) Paeshachii 73 Prákrta, 4) Páshchátya Prákrta, 5) Saendhávii Prákrta, 6) Málavii Prákrta and 7) Maháráśt́rii Prákrta.
items.statement: Upon dying, Sanskrit left behind seven daughter languages known as Prakrtas.
items.title: The Evolution of Indian Languages

items.quote: The philosophies that human beings follow can be divided into four categories: (1) dogma-centred philosophy, (2) matter-centred philosophy, (3) self-centred philosophy and (4) God-centred philosophy.
items.statement: Human philosophies fall into four distinct categories: dogma-centred, matter-centred, self-centred, and God-centred.
items.title: The Excellence of God-Centred Philosophy

items.quote: The greatest blunder of communism was that it attacked God-centred philosophy. This is the immediate cause of the death of communism.
items.statement: The immediate catalyst for the downfall of communism was its attack on God-centred philosophy.
items.title: The Excellence of God-Centred Philosophy

items.quote: The idea, the spirit of “prapatti” is that whatever happens in this Universe of ours is nothing but an expression of Cosmic desire or Cosmic will. Neither can there be any volcanic eruption nor can any blade of grass move without his order.
items.statement: Prapatti is the philosophical stance that all occurrences in the universe are exclusively expressions of Cosmic will, without which nothing happens.
items.title: The Excellence of a Bhakta

items.quote: All worldly knowledge and other mundane knowledge and so-called wisdom has little value. Such knowledge is known as “prápta vákya”, that is, vákya coming from, coming through, the media of different worldly persons, worldly expressions.
items.statement: Prápta vákya represents mutable knowledge derived from mundane human media, whereas ápta vákya is immutable guidance coming directly from Parama Puruśa.
items.title: The Excellence of a Bhakta

items.quote: Where the object of adoration is matter, as in the case of materialism, the mind will certainly become matter, and when the mind takes the form of matter a vacuum is created in its place. The object of Átman is mind, so when a vacuum is created in the psychic sphere the Átman or unit consciousness will take the form of this vacuum that was mind. Similarly, when spirit or Átman takes the form of mind a vacuum is created in the Átmic sphere and the cognitive principle takes the form of this vacuum in the Átmic sphere. Thus the very existence of human beings is converted into matter. This is the final effect of materialism.
items.statement: Meditation on crude matter causes the mind, unit consciousness, and cognitive stance to sequentially take the form of vacuums, ultimately reducing human existence to matter.
items.title: The Existential Value of Ideology

items.quote: So diversity is the law of nature and identicality can never be. But diversity is not the same as disparity. Disparity encourages exploitation based on differences, while diversity recognizes multiplicity which reflects underlying unity.
items.statement: Diversity represents natural multiplicity reflecting an underlying unity, whereas disparity is an unnatural concept used to justify exploitation.
items.title: The Existential Value of Ideology

items.quote: When the internal clash becomes so intense that the structure can no longer maintain it’s structural solidarity it is called jad́asphota. Jad́asphota converts all the fundamental factors into the ethereal factor, from which they again move within the flow of Saiṋcara evolving once more to their solid base where they again get the scope to become a living structure.
items.statement: Jad́asphota is the structural explosion that occurs when internal matter reaches extreme condensation and crudity, disintegrating solid matter back into the ethereal factor.
items.title: The Expansion of the Microcosm

items.quote: When He remains associated with the collective manifestation of the universe as its witnessing force that is His prota yoga, and when He remains associated with the individual microcosm as its witness, that is His ota yoga.
items.statement: Parama Puruśa relates to the collective manifestation of the cosmos via prota yoga and to individual unit microcosms via ota yoga.
items.title: The Expansion of the Microcosm

items.quote: In the mechanical sphere, knowing, or the functional side of knowledge, occurs with the perception of special types of reflections and refractions, but in the psychic sphere, it occurs as a result of the subjectivization of objectivity or objectivities.
items.statement: Mechanical knowing operates through physical reflection and refraction, whereas psychic knowledge consists of the subjectivization of external objective realities.
items.title: The Faculty of Knowledge – 1

items.quote: The exact mental reproduction of what has been previously perceived is called smrti or memory.
items.statement: Memory (smrti) is the exact mental reproduction and re-creation of previously perceived vibrations and impressions.
items.title: The Faculty of Knowledge – 2

items.quote: Remember that psychic disease and brain disease are not the same thing; they are quite different. Brain disease occurs due to some disorder in a part of the brain, or due to a congenital defect, or perhaps due to hereditary causes which hamper the proper formation of the brain. Mental disease is different. It arises due to a disorder in the objectivated mind, in the first stage in the process of subjectivization.
items.statement: Brain disease stems from physical organic, congenital, or hereditary disorders in the brain, whereas psychic disease arises from defective control in the objectivated mind.
items.title: The Faculty of Knowledge – 3

items.qualifiers: Method for reaching unity with the Supreme Subjectivity
items.quote: Ultimately, the best way to meditate on Parama Puruśa, or remember Him, is to bear in mind that, in actions big or small, significant or insignificant, in wakeful state or in sleep, in dream or in reality, the Supreme Subjectivity is maintaining a constant and close watch on me.
items.statement: To meditate effectively on Parama Puruśa, an aspirant should hold the ideation that the Supreme Subject is constantly witnessing all their actions across all states of existence.
items.title: The Faculty of Knowledge – 5

items.quote: For the renunciate there is only the Universal Family to serve, but the family man must always maintain a balance between his small family and his large Family. He cannot neglect either one.
items.statement: While family persons must split their service between their small domestic family and the Universal Family, renunciates are dedicated wholly to serving the Universal Family alone.
items.title: The Family Man and the Renunciant

items.quote: When the code of discipline is imposed with the spirit of welfare, with the spirit of development, it is called “anushásanam” in Saḿskrta.
items.statement: Anushásanam is a code of discipline that is imposed specifically with the benevolent spirit of welfare and development.
items.title: The Fear of Him

items.quote: So who is Dhritarastra? He who controls the ráśt́ra, he who controls the physical body: that is, the mind. Dhrtaráśt́ra uváca means “The mind says” – “The question arose in the mind, in the human mind.”
items.statement: In the allegorical framework of the Giita, the blind King Dhritarastra represents the mind controlling the physical structure, while Sanjaya represents the viveka or discriminating conscience.
items.title: The Field of Dharma

items.quote: Viveka is of five types, and their collective name is viveka paiṋcaka.
items.statement: Conscience (viveka) is categorized into a five-fold framework known as viveka paiṋcaka: nityánitya, dvaetádvaeta, átmánátma, paiṋcakośa, and mahávákya viveka.
items.title: The Five Kinds of Conscience (Viveka)

items.quote: Though the mind is very powerful it has one serious shortcoming. It cannot think of two objects concurrently.
items.statement: The human mind cannot cognize or concentrate upon two distinct objects simultaneously; perceived concurrent thoughts are due to rapid sequential switching.
items.title: The Form of Sádhaná

items.qualifiers: Comparative psychology of humans and animals
items.quote: In the case of animals or other creatures, the approach is physico-psychic, no doubt, but it is never psycho-physical. In the case of man, it is both physico-psychic and psycho-physical.
items.statement: While animals are capable only of a physico-psychic approach, human beings possess both physico-psychic and psycho-physical approaches.
items.title: The Four Kinds of Approach

items.quote: This path of movement is divided into four stages: yatamána, vyatireka, ekendriya and vashiikára.
items.statement: The psychic progression of spiritual sadhana advances through four stages: yatamána (sincere effort), vyatireka (intermittent control), ekendriya (complete control of single faculties), and vashiikára (complete psychic mastery).
items.title: The Four Stages of Human Progress

items.quote: Itihása is that part of itikathá whose study leads to human welfare. It has immense educative value. A study of the entire history may not be beneficial for the reader, but that little portion of history which we call itihása is definitely beneficial for human welfare.
items.statement: Itikathá is a general chronological record of historical events, whereas itihása is that specific portion of benevolent history whose study promotes human welfare and the attainment of the four vargas.
items.title: The Four Vargas and Devotion

items.quote: According to the Vedas, practical life is guided by theory. But the efficacy of a theory should first be tested in the practical sphere. Movement on the basis of an untested theory may or may not be fruitful. The theory of Tantra has been evolved on the basis of practical experience on the path.
items.statement: In the Vedic tradition practical life is directed by untested theoretical speculation, whereas Tantra formulates its theories directly from practical application and experimental experience.
items.title: The Fundamental Difference between Veda and Tantra

items.quote: In Sanskrit, the ordinary meaning of Vák is expression of vocal cord, but in philosophical language, Vák means all the expressions of efferent nerves.
items.statement: In philosophical terminology, Vák denotes the complete operational expression of the efferent nerves across all strata of life.
items.title: The Fundamental Principles of Life

items.quote: If you are to ask for anything, you should only say, “Oh God, guide my brain, guide my mind, onto the path of bliss. Give me shubha-buddhi. I want only this much from You and nothing else.” There must not be any other prayer.
items.statement: Spiritual aspirants should refrain from non-cardinal, material petitions and pray solely for benevolent intellect (shubha-buddhi).
items.title: The Futility of Non-Cardinal Prayers

items.quote: The entire social structure is dependent on these six factors. Bhati is meaningless without them. The weakness of one among them may jeopardize the very existence of Bhati.
items.statement: The sustainable existence and progress of human society depends on six indispensable factors of Bhati: spiritual ideology, spiritual cult (sadhana), socio-economic theory, fraternal social outlook, scripture, and a preceptor.
items.title: The Future of Civilization

items.quote: That day I told you that “a” is the acoustic root of the generating faculty, “u” is the acoustic root of the retaining faculty, and “ma” is the acoustic root of the destroying faculty. Therefore He has three functions. He becomes G-O-D, that is, “Generator’s” first letter G; “Operator’s” first letter O; and “Destroyer’s” first letter D: “God”.
items.statement: Prańava represents the dynamic acoustic momentum composed of 'a' (creation), 'u' (preservation/operation), and 'ma' (withdrawal/destruction).
items.title: The Glory of Prańava

items.qualifiers: Cosmological genesis of mind and matter
items.quote: That is, matter is the creation of the Supreme Mind, matter is the creation of the Cosmic Mind, but the unit mind is the creation of matter.
items.statement: Matter is the direct creation of the Cosmic Mind, whereas the unit mind (microcosm) is the creation of powdered-down matter through internal clash and cohesion.
items.title: The Grandeur of the Supreme Entity

items.quote: So through prema one can attain liberation (mukti). But to attain salvation (mokśa), Parábhakti, exclusive devotion to Parama Puruśa is required. Parábhakti liberates spiritual aspirants from the bondage of I-feeling permanently.
items.statement: Prema (love for the Supreme) enables the attainment of mukti (liberation), but parábhakti (exclusive devotion) is required to permanently dissolve the I-feeling and attain mokśa (salvation).
items.title: The Highest Category of Devotion

items.quote: According to some persons, this universe is infinite, but this is not true. As this universe also is a created manifestation of the Supreme Consciousness, due to the influence of the static principle of Prakrti it is bound to have a particular shape and form. And since it is under the static principle, it must be under bondage and limitations. Hence the universe is certainly finite, although it is very vast; it is not infinite or ananta.
items.statement: The universe is finite in volume and bounded by the static principle of Prakrti, rather than infinite.
items.title: The Hub of Universal Activities

items.quote: Direct guidance is without any application of force. You want someone to go with you and they go. “Guiding” means making some effort to bring someone along the path of your choice. “Goading” means compelling someone to move and act according to your desire. That is, it means to push or to move by the application of force.
items.statement: There are distinct definitions for direct guidance, guiding, and goading based on the application of effort and force.
items.title: The Human Body Is a Biological Machine

items.quote: In the múládhára cakra there are four propensities – dharma [psycho-spiritual longing], artha [psychic longing], káma [physical longing] and mokśa [spiritual longing]. So spiritual longing is a fundamental human urge.
items.statement: The human mind possesses four propensities at the múládhára cakra comprising psycho-spiritual, psychic, physical, and spiritual longings.
items.title: The Human Body Is a Biological Machine

items.quote: The human psyche is guided by these four aspects. Socio-economic theory and cult have to adjust with them.
items.statement: The human psyche operates through four distinct aspects: urge, passion, propensity, and sentiment.
items.title: The Human Body Is a Biological Machine

items.quote: The experience of pleasure through the mind can be divided into five varieties: Anukulavedaniiyam Pratikulavedaniiyam Avedaniiyam Nirapekśavedaniiyam Aplutavedaniiyam
items.statement: The experience of pleasure through the mind is classified into five specific varieties of feelings.
items.title: The Human Search for Real Progress

items.quote: Only one form of feeling is expressed in the spiritual realm and this is Aplutavedaniiyam. This expression is either non-lateral or multilateral. Being non-lateral, it does not allow the formation of reactive momenta, and being multi-lateral, it is immune from the effect of reactive momenta.
items.statement: True progress is only possible in the spiritual realm because it operates through pointed psychic existence devoid of negative speed and reactive momenta.
items.title: The Human Search for Real Progress

items.quote: When the vibrations of pain or pleasure in the physical realm are consumed in the physico-psychic vibrations, the feeling of pain or pleasure will not be so acute, although the physical sphere will remain as large as before. In other words, this process will save the mind from reaction.
items.statement: To avoid reactive momenta and the extreme impacts of physical and intellectual changes, cruder waves must be consumed by subtler waves.
items.title: The Human Search for Real Progress

items.qualifiers: Theoretical equivalence versus practical operational difference
items.quote: When the three principles of prakrti – sentient, mutative and static – are in perfect equilibrium and equipoise, Prakrti is said to be lying dormant in her primordial state there is no manifestation of creation. To described this state the term Prakrti is used. But when the three principles lose their equilibrium and equipoise, the attributive expression manifests. In this state, when prakrti is committed to start the creation, (of course within the limited sphere of the infinite body of Puruśa, the Supreme Cognitive Principle). She is called Máyá, (the Supreme Creative Principle).
items.statement: Prakrti denotes the primordial state when the three gunas are in perfect equilibrium, whereas Máyá denotes the operative state when the gunas lose equilibrium to commence creation.
items.title: The Influence of Máyá on the Human Mind

items.quote: This battle of sádhaná can be carried out in one of three ways - Dakśińácára sádhaná, Vámácára sádhaná or Madhyamácára sádhaná.
items.statement: Tantric spiritual battle against Máyá is categorized into Dakśińácára, Vámácára, and Madhyamácára sádhaná.
items.title: The Influence of Máyá on the Human Mind

items.quote: The seven Vedic notes, the seven Tantric notes and two ideational notes – this constituted the sixteen notes which was known as the ́system of sixteen sounds’ ( śoŕasha dhvanikalá ) in Indo-Aryan science of phonetics.
items.statement: The Indo-Aryan science of phonetics comprised a sixteen-note system composed of seven Vedic notes, seven Tantric notes, and two ideational notes.
items.title: The Inner Science of Surasaptaka – Excerpt B

items.quote: Where the expressions of life are diverted to crude objectivities it is called krśt́i, which is a part of Saḿskrti. Crude manifestations of expressions are called krśt́i. THe sum total of both crude and subtle manifestations of expressions is Saḿskrti. Krśt́i may differ from one group of people to other but the Saḿskrti of human beings is one.
items.statement: Culture represents the sum total of human life expressions and is universal, while krśt́i denotes only the crude manifestations of those expressions.
items.title: The Interplay of Culture and Civilization

items.quote: Cultural expressions and civilization are not synonymous. Where there is control and rationality in the different expressions of life, there is civilization. To take a concrete example, eating is a cultural expression of life. Those who ration ally think that over-eating is bad, think restraint from it may be called civilized. The cultural expressions in people are many. People who cannot control the different expressions may be called culturally advanced but not civilized.
items.statement: Cultural advancement reflects the diversity and quantity of life expressions, whereas civilization specifically denotes the exercise of rationality, reasoning, and restraint over those expressions.
items.title: The Interplay of Culture and Civilization

items.quote: Vidyá and Avidyá have contrary concomitants. Neither of them has equilibrated movements. People with calm and collected intellect, Sádhakas with developed intuition, who could very well understand such things due to their judgment, have made the above declaration with regard to Vidyá and Avidyá i.e. salvation is not possible through the cultivation of only one of these two principles. For the attainment of salvation, there must be balance between Vidyá and Avidyá to move forward. Although the movement towards Brahma must be introvertive (Vidyá), one should not give up Avidyá completely in relation to the practical world. This also has got to be made compatible with one’s own spiritual way of life by ascribing normal and divine bearing to it.
items.statement: Neither the exclusive pursuit of Vidyá nor Avidyá leads to salvation; spiritual progress requires balancing Vidyá with the divine ascription to practical worldly actions.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 1

items.quote: People generally use four words, Satya, Tothya, Samyak and Rta synonymously or in an identical sense. But in reality there is a great difference in their meanings. The English equivalents of Tathya, Samyak and Rta are “Fact”, “Correct”, and “Truth” respectively. But in other languages “Satya” (Truth) has no equivalent. The Philosophical meaning of the word “Satya”, is unchangeable, i.e., that which has no distortion, that which is beyond distinctions of time, space, and person.
items.statement: In philosophy and language, the concepts of Satya, Tathya, Samyak, and Rta carry precise technical distinctions, with Satya specifically denoting the unchangeable Entity beyond time, space, and person.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 2
