items.quote: The region below the navel is dominated by Tamoguńa (Static principle), the region from navel to throat, by Rajoguńa (Mutative influence) and the region from throat to Trikuti (the junction of the two eyebrows, where the seat of the mind is located,) by Sattvaguńa (Sentient influence). Normally, a particular region in the body becomes more active in accordance with the Vrtti or epithymetic influence or the inter- and intra-ectoplasmic occupation of an individual.
items.statement: The human body is divided into three attributional regions governed by the three gunas, each associated with specific symbolic colors and qualities.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 3

items.quote: Of the five internal Vayus, viz., Práńa, Apána, Samána, Ud́ana and Vyána, the Práńa, situated between the navel and the throat controls the functions of lungs, heart etc.; the Apána, situated below the navel (i.e., between the navel and the anus) controls the excretion of stool, urine etc.; the Samáná, situated within the navel, maintains the equilibrium between Práńa and Apána; the Udána, situated in the throat, controls the vocal cord (power of speech) and the Vyána, permeating the entire body, controls the circulation of the blood, vital secretions etc., and, with the help of the nerve fibres brings the sensory and motor organs into contact with the knowable i.e. the objects to mentally dealt with. The vibration necessary for the faculty of contemplation is also supplied by Vyána Váyu.
items.statement: The five internal vital airs (váyus) in the human body perform specific physiological and contemplative functions based on their somatic locations.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 4

items.quote: Turiiya Brahma (Nrsiḿha or Puruśottama) is concerned with the Causal Body in four kinds of associations or dissociations: Ota Yoga or the state of pervasive or intimate association. Anujiṋatá Yoga or the state of cosmotheistic bearing. Anujiṋá Yoga or the Cognitive meditational approach to infinity. Avikalpa Yoga or Absolute identity with the infinite.
items.statement: Turiiya Brahma associates or dissociates with the Causal Body through four specific yogic states.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 5

items.quote: In other words the yoga or link that constitutes the witness-ship of the unit entities is called Ota Yoga and that which constitutes the pervasive witness-ship of the collective whole is called Prota Yoga.
items.statement: Ota Yoga constitutes the witnessing link of unit entities, while Prota Yoga constitutes the pervasive witnessing link of the collective whole.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 5

items.quote: In the human mind Avidyámáyá (Extroversive Force) manifests herself in two ways: Vikśepátmaka (extroversive or centrifugal) and Ávaranátmaka (obstructive). Philosophically we call them Vikśepa Force and Ávarańii (covering) Force, respectively. Due to the remoteness of the original object to be known, a lack of valid knowledge results, that is, due to the remoteness of Brahmabháva, a lack of spiritual knowledge results, and with the increase of remoteness even the semblance of knowledge gradually vanishes. These are all the actions of this Vikśepa or Centrifugal Force. And in spite of the opposite condition, proximity, the lack of valid knowledge that occurs due to the darkness of ignorance is the act of the Ávarańii or the Obstructive Force. The reason why I call this an Ávarańii Force is that it works as a cover or lid over the original object.
items.statement: Avidyá operates through two distinct forces: Vikśepa shakti, which causes remoteness from spiritual ideation, and Ávarańii shakti, which obscures valid knowledge like a covering.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 6: Avidyá

items.quote: Where the two forces, Vidyá and Avidyá, are in equilibrium, none of the satellite forces like vikśepa, samvit, ávarańii or hládinii, are in evidence. In such a balanced state the microcosm undergoes neither regeneration nor degeneration. Such a condition is indeed rare. Yet in common terms I can say that such a condition does exist in most of the jiivas or units. The equilibrium of forces that causes this non-progressive and non-regressive condition is called tatastha shakti or the coastal Force.
items.statement: The coastal force (tatastha shakti) represents the equilibrium between Vidyá and Avidyá where neither progress nor regress occurs.
items.title: The Intuitional Science of the Vedas – 6: Avidyá

items.qualifiers: Conditional upon the intactness of the temporal seed of respiration
items.quote: Actually, the unit structure dies thousands of times every day, after every exhalation. In the scriptures this sort of microcosmic death is called the khańd́a pralaya [partial annihilation] of the unit entity. When the temporal factor is evident and the seed of or potential for further inhalation and exhalation is intact, this cannot be considered death.
items.statement: The human respiratory cycle involves miniature cycles of life and death, where post-exhalation pause constitutes partial annihilation (khańd́a pralaya).
items.title: The Kśatriya Age

items.quote: These warlike people gave great importance to increasing their numbers so that they could fight against their enemies. That is why the courageous but uncultured kśatriyas of ancient times invented linga, or phallus, worship as a symbol for the increase of their numerical strength. This mentality of the kśatriyas can be found in the Mayan civilization of America and the Dravidian civilization of India as well as in particular types of Tantric ritual. No matter how phallus-and-vulva worship be philosophically explained today, it essentially expresses the ancient kśatriya desire to increase their population.
items.statement: Early kśatriya society originated phallus (linga) and vulva worship primarily as a primitive symbol and ritual desire to increase their numerical population for warfare.
items.title: The Kśatriya Age

items.qualifiers: Absence of pronunciation or literature reduces the status to a dialect (Upabháś)
items.quote: According to PROUT there are eight constituent factors of a full-fledged language – case endings, verb endings, pronouns, vocabulary, pronunciation, written or unwritten literature including folk literature, psycho-acoustic notes and inferential acoustic notes, and syntax.
items.statement: According to PROUT, a full-fledged language is composed of eight essential constituent factors.
items.title: The Language Issue

items.quote: The characteristic of a unit mind is that its goal is multi-purposive whereas its expression is unilateral, confined to a particular space, time and individuality. The goal of the Cosmic mind, however, is uni-purposive and Its expression multilateral, manifested in all time, space and individuality. This is the major difference between the microcosm and Macrocosm.
items.statement: The unit mind is multi-purposive in goal but unilateral in expression, whereas the Cosmic Mind is uni-purposive in goal but multilateral in expression across all time, space, and individuality.
items.title: The Macrocosm and the Microcosm – 1

items.quote: This process of mutual conversion is called homomorphic evolution (svarupa parináma). Some people use the term svarúpa parińáma in a different sense, but I am not in favour of that.
items.statement: Svarúpa parińáma is the mutual conversion of the three gunas within the balanced triangle of forces, whereas sadrsha parińáma is the successive flow of curved vibrations (kalá) moving toward crudification.
items.title: The Macrocosm and the Microcosm – 2

items.quote: The seed point represents will force, náda represents cognitive force, and kalá represents actional force.
items.statement: The evolutionary flow from the triangle of forces proceeds through biija bindu representing will force, náda representing cognitive force, and kalá representing actional force.
items.title: The Macrocosm and the Microcosm – 2

items.quote: Though the Avidyá force is expressed in various ways, its expression in the human mind can be divided into five categories: avidyá, asmitá, rága, dveśa, and abhinivesha.
items.statement: The expression of the Avidyá force in the human mind is categorized into five distinct psychic afflictions.
items.title: The Macrocosmic Stance and Human Life

items.quote: Those fifty main propensities function both internally and externally. One may donate something to someone both internally and externally. Likewise, one can steal both mentally and physically. Hence every propensity is functioning in two ways, and fifty times two equals one hundred. Furthermore, each propensity functions in ten directions [north, south, east, west, northeast, northwest, southeast, southwest, up and down]. One hundred times ten equals one thousand. Hence there are one thousand functioning propensities. These one thousand vrttis are controlled by the mind from the pineal gland, which is why [its corresponding cakra] is called sahasrára [sahasra means “thousand”].
items.statement: A total of one thousand functional propensities are controlled from the pineal gland because each of the fifty basic vrttis acts internally and externally across ten directions.
items.title: The Meaning of “Krśńa” in Rája Yoga

items.quote: According to the then Indian system books were classified in four divisions – kávya, puráńa, itikathá and itihása. The subject matter of kavya might not be real, but the way of expression is lucid and beautiful.
items.statement: Traditional Indian literature is categorized into four distinct classes: kávya, puráńa, itikathá, and itihása.
items.title: The Meaning of the Name

items.quote: Viśa cikitsá is native to India, and its first reference is found in the Mahábhárata period. Later on this viśa cikitsá was encouraged not by Aryans, but rather by non-Aryans, and South India, especially Malabar, saw it expand a lot. These people attribute the origin of viśa cikitsá to Lord Krśńa, i.e., viśa cikitsá was originated by Krśńa. And vaedyaka shástra was originated by Lord Sadáshiva.
items.statement: Elementary homoeopathy originated in ancient India as viśa cikitsá founded on the principle 'Samah samam shamayati' and attributed to Lord Krśńa.
items.title: The Medical Science of the Age

items.quote: This sort of treatment by hypnotic spell, people say, was started by Dr. Mesmer of France, and so this system is known as “mesmerism.” But prior to Dr. Mesmer, this system was known to Indians. In India it was named “rákśasii vidyá.” In ancient India (by ancient India I mean the non-Aryans, the natives of India) there was a non-Aryan lady doctor, Kárkatii Rákśasii. This Rákśasii was very famous for her mesmeric treatment.
items.statement: Treatment by hypnotic suggestion, termed rákśasii vidyá, was practised in ancient non-Aryan India prior to Dr. Mesmer.
items.title: The Medical Science of the Age

items.quote: Meditation should be performed knowing fully well the location of different glands and sub-glands and also the different cells in the human brain. And people should not only know the location of these glands and sub-glands, they should also be acquainted with their respective systems of hormone secretion, otherwise their meditation will not produce any fruit.
items.statement: Meditation must be performed with scientific knowledge of the location of glands, sub-glands, brain cells, and their hormonal secretions to be effective.
items.title: The Mind Grows in Magnitude

items.quote: A single microvitum is insufficient to form one carbon atom, but when billions of microvita get solidified, a carbon atom is formed – generally or naturally of heterogeneous nature, and under special circumstances of homogeneous nature.
items.statement: Microvitum is not of carbonic origin; rather, billions of solidified microvita form a single carbon atom.
items.title: The Neo-Ethics of Multi-Lateral Salvation

items.qualifiers: Social value is denied to uncorrected criminals while human value is preserved
items.quote: Human beings form the society, and hence human value must lay the foundation for the social value. In other words, those who show respect to human value will be entitled to social value. It was mentioned earlier that human value means nothing but to treat the joys and sorrows, hopes and aspirations of human beings sympathetically, and see them merged in Cosmic Consciousness and established in divine majesty.
items.statement: For sadvipras, human value must lay the foundation for social value, and society must never deny human value even to criminals.
items.title: The Neohumanism of Sadvipras

items.quote: Similarly, the influence of the concentric force, the vidyá shakti, has two effects. One is samvit shakti, another is hládinii shakti.
items.statement: The concentric force (vidyā shakti) exerts two effects: samvit shakti, which is physico-psychic and awakens the urge for intuitional practice, and hlādinii shakti, which directs the unit being toward supreme beatitude.
items.title: The Noumenal Progenitor

items.qualifiers: pratisaḿvedii defined in ontological and cognitive terms
items.quote: When an object, due to its objective existence, [[is substantiated]] as the counterpart of [[another action or as the counterpart of an existence, that object]] is called [[prati]]saḿvedii. For instance, when the sound wave is reflected on an object we hear the echo of the original sound. The object [[on which the]] original wave is reflected is called [[pratisaḿvedii]] [reflecting plate].
items.statement: An object that is substantiated as the counterpart of an action or existence upon which an original wave is reflected is termed a pratisaḿvedii.
items.title: The Omni-Reflective Cognitive Consciousness

items.quote: Thus, on the path of synthesis citta will have to be merged in ahaḿtattva. In the subsequent stage all the faculties of ahaḿtattva will have to be merged into mahatattva, the existential I. And in the fourth stage the faculties of mahatattva will have to be merged in jiivátmá or unit consciousness. The pratisaḿvedii of jiivatma is Parama Puruśa.
items.statement: In the spiritual path of synthesis, unit consciousness ascends hierarchically: sensory expressions are withdrawn into citta, citta is merged into ahaḿtattva, ahaḿtattva into mahattattva, mahattattva into the unit consciousness (jiivátmá), whose ultimate reflecting plate is Parama Puruśa.
items.title: The Omni-Reflective Cognitive Consciousness

items.qualifiers: Specific linguistic and contextual meaning in Vedic discourse
items.quote: The word kalilam has a number of meanings in the Vedic language. But the general or popular meaning of the word is ádhára – a structure, a base. What sort of structure? A structure with which I am associated through inference. For instance, suppose a very bright light is emanating from an object. Light may be emitted from any object. But the very object which is radiating light and which you are trying to perceive – that very light-radiating object is known as kalila.
items.statement: In Vedic terminology, 'kalila' popularly signifies a base or structure with which one is associated through inference, such as an object from which light radiates.
items.title: The Omnipotent and Omnipresent Consciousness

items.qualifiers: Etymological and acoustic analysis of the word 'sarva'
items.quote: Therefore, “sa” means “origination from sattva guńa”, “ra” means “moved by energy”, and “va” means “dharma”. “Sa”, “ra” and “va” are in every entity. Therefore, “Sarvát sarva ucyate”. Every object or entity is moved by these biija mantras. Therefore “sarva” means “every object”, “all objects”.
items.statement: The word 'sarva' is formed from acoustic roots representing cosmological principles: 'sa' for origination from sattva guṇa, 'ra' for movement by energy (kriyā shakti), and 'va' for inherent characteristic (dharma).
items.title: The Omniscience of the Causal Matrix

items.qualifiers: Distinction between cosmological descent and spiritual ascent
items.quote: If we call this process anuloma vyávasthá (descending order of metamorphosis) the process of sádhaná should be described as pratilom vyávasthá (ascending order of evolution.
items.statement: The cosmic metamorphosis moving from subtle to crude is termed 'anuloma vyāvasthā' (descending order), whereas spiritual sādhanā is 'pratiloma vyāvasthā' (ascending order of evolution) returning from crude to subtle.
items.title: The Only Way to Salvation

items.qualifiers: Comprehensive definition of āstitvika prāṇinatā across three strata
items.quote: The sum total of our existential potentialities emanating from unit consciousness, interacting through motor and sensory organs in our physical stratum, interplaying through the ectoplasmic projections in our psychic stratum, and flowing one-pointedly through the psycho-spiritual approach in our spiritual stratum constitute our existential stamina (ástitvika práńinatá).
items.statement: Existential stamina (āstitvika prāṇinatā) is defined as the sum total of an entity's potentialities emanating from unit consciousness, operating through physical organs, psychic ectoplasmic projections, and psycho-spiritual flow.
items.title: The Origin of Existential Stamina

items.qualifiers: Refutation of four conventional drives in favor of jiivātman
items.quote: So the origin or source of our existential being is rooted in the “I” of “I know”, and that supreme identity is indeed our soul, our unit consciousness – jiivátman.
items.statement: The ultimate source of existential stamina is the unit consciousness (jiivātman) rather than sentiment, logic, desideratum, or actional faculty.
items.title: The Origin of Existential Stamina

items.qualifiers: Definition of gopii and gopii bhāva
items.quote: When a human being does something to please Parama Puruśa, this is called gopii bháva. The Saḿskrta word gopii means one who is in the very habit of pleasing Parama Puruśa.
items.statement: Gopii bhāva refers to the attitude of performing all actions purely for the pleasure and satisfaction of Parama Puruśa rather than for personal satisfaction.
items.title: The Path of Salvation

items.quote: And this pulsation, that is movement through speed and pause, is an essential factor for each and every animate or inanimate object. Wherever there is existential factor there must be this pulsation. An entity acquires strength and stamina, during the pause phase, and emanates vibration during the speed period.
items.statement: Human beings move within a system characterized by systaltic pulsation, wherein stamina and strength are gathered during the pause phase, while vibrations are emanated during the speed phase.
items.title: The Path of Salvation

items.qualifiers: Buddha's eightfold path contextualized within cosmocentric movement
items.quote: Those factors will help the spiritual aspirant in lessening the length of the radius. The first is Samyak Darshan or proper philosophy.
items.statement: Lord Buddha's eight-fold factors (Aśṭāṅga Mārga) serve as practical methods to reduce the radius of centrifugal movement and strengthen centripetal Vidyā Shakti toward the Cosmic Nucleus.
items.title: The Path of Salvation

items.qualifiers: Four-stage framework of spiritual relationship and realization
items.quote: In this stage, the Supreme Entity is not only the Lord, the Lord of all Lords, and He is not only the Supreme progenitor, in the third phase He is also the Guru, and in this fourth phase the relationship is just like a piece of paper; the unit consciousness of the spiritual aspirant is one side of the paper and the Cosmic Consciousness of Parama Puruśa is the other side of the paper; they are inseparable, one cannot be removed from the other.
items.statement: The spiritual path toward beatitude progresses across four stages characterized by evolving relationships with the Supreme: first as the Lord of Lords, second as the Supreme Progenitor, third as the Supreme Guru, and fourth as an inseparable singular reality like two sides of one sheet of paper.
items.title: The Path unto the Abode of Beatitude

items.qualifiers: Philosophical distinction between potential/formless action and finalized action
items.quote: When the actional expressions take a definite form, a definite shape or a definite size, that shape is known as “kriyá”. And before that, when there are only actional expressions but no definite form, or shape, or size, it is called “karma”.
items.statement: Karma denotes actional expressions prior to taking a definite form or size, whereas kriyā refers to actional expressions that have assumed a definite form, shape, or finalized state.
items.title: The People's God

items.qualifiers: Distinguishing the historical biography of Shiva from later mythological legends
items.quote: Yes, Shiva did have a wife – Gaorii, or Párvatii. And another wife was Káliká, or Kálii. Kálii was born in a non-Aryan community which was ethnically Austrico-Mongolo-Negroid.
items.statement: The historical Shiva lived approximately 7,000 years ago and had three human wives: Pārvatii (an Aryan girl from the Himalayas), Kālikā (from the indigenous Austrico-Mongolo-Negroid community), and Gaṅgā (a Mongolian girl from Tibet), none of whom are identical to multi-armed Puranic deities or rivers.
items.title: The Pervasive Influence

items.qualifiers: Evolutionary phases of Buddhist philosophical cults in India and northern regions
items.quote: Due to the influence of Duhkhaváda, Buddhism became estranged from the practical world. But during the days of Vajrayána and Kalacakrayána, which were propounded about 1600 or 1700 years ago, the Buddhists made a departure from their old doctrine and preached a new philosophy which was known as Atisukhaváda.
items.statement: Centuries after Gautama Buddha, northern Mahāyāna Buddhism evolved into Mantrayāna and Tantrayāna, the latter subdividing into Kālacakrayāna and Vajrayāna, shifting Buddhist philosophy from Duḥkhavāda (pessimism) to Atisukhavāda (hedonistic pleasure-seeking).
items.title: The Pervasive Influence of Shiva (Discourse 4)

items.qualifiers: Classical psycho-spiritual stages of impulse control and self-mastery
items.quote: Now, this movement is a phased path and there are four main phases. They are known as yatamána, vyatireka, ekendriya and vashiikára.
items.statement: The four progressive phases of human spiritual struggle against bondages are: yatamāna (initial struggle against internal and external enemies), vyatireka (control over specific propensities while yielding to others), ekendriya (control over specific sensory/motor organs while failing in others), and vashīkāra (complete mastery over all fifty propensities and organs).
items.title: The Phases of Human Approach

items.qualifiers: Acoustic mechanics of the Tantric biija 'phat́'
items.quote: So in this Tantric system, if one wanted to transform his or her work or thought into quick action, then the phat́ mantra was uttered before performing the action.
items.statement: In ancient Tantra, the acoustic root 'phaṭ' was uttered before performing an action to quickly translate thought into immediate action.
items.title: The Phat́ Mantra

items.qualifiers: Contrast between relative physical/mental change and absolute spiritual progress
items.quote: Hence we may say that in the physical stratum, progress means a never-ending process of metamorphosis. If there is any weakness in the mind of an individual or in the mind of a collective body, weakness for any particular status quo, weakness for any particular framework, then there cannot even be any relative progress in the physical stratum.
items.statement: In the physical and psychic strata, progress is strictly relative and consists of a continuous process of metamorphosing the status quo, whereas true, absolute progress occurs exclusively in the spiritual realm.
items.title: What Is the Philosophical Interpretation of Progress?

items.qualifiers: Causal diagnosis underlying social and psychic unrest
items.quote: Yet the strange thing is that this lacuna in the physical sphere, and the consequent disparity, is the noumenal cause of all phenomenal troubles. Due to this noumenal cause, peace in the psychic sphere is being disturbed again and again.
items.statement: The unresolved lacuna and material disparity in the crude physical sphere is the noumenal cause of all phenomenal troubles, which continuously disturbs psychic peace in human society.
items.title: The Physical, Psychic and Spiritual Strata

items.qualifiers: Core functional and ethical definition of sadvipra
items.quote: Those spiritual revolutionaries who work to achieve such progressive changes for human elevation on a well-thought, pre-planned basis, whether in the physical, metaphysical or spiritual sphere, by adhering to the principles of Yama and Niyama, are sadvipras.
items.statement: Sadvipras are morally and spiritually equipped spiritual revolutionaries adhering to the ten principles of Yama and Niyama who actively intervene in the social cycle to prevent any class from becoming exploiters.
items.title: The Place of Sadvipras in the Samája Cakra

items.qualifiers: Historical evaluation of Madālasā's pedagogical contribution
items.quote: According to historical records, Madálasá’s children were the first to embrace missionary life and take the vow of sannyásii-hood in order to serve humanity.
items.statement: Queen Madālasā educated her sons to serve humanity as renunciant spiritual missionaries, making them the first historical figures to embrace missionary sannyāsa for collective service rather than personal comfort.
items.title: The Place of Women in the Spiritual World

items.qualifiers: Geophysical impact on neurological and psycho-spiritual faculties
items.quote: And if the magnetic order is disrupted, then certain remarkable changes, certain remarkable metamorphoses in the electromagnetic vibrations of this Earth and also of the entire solar system, will occur. As a result of this type of change in the electromagnetic vibrations, human thought waves will certainly be affected.
items.statement: Shifts in the Earth's geographical and magnetic poles alter electromagnetic vibrations and environmental balance, which in turn neurologically reshapes human thought waves and accelerates introversive, spiritual development.
items.title: The Poles Shift Their Respective Positions

items.qualifiers: Aesthetic and philosophical classification of literary works
items.quote: Literature which is based on a feeling of benevolence, and which without severing its relationship with us completely, is marching so far ahead of our time that we are not really in step with it, is called tat́astha sáhitya, ( 2 ) rather than yuga sáhitya [“epochal literature”].
items.statement: Literature is categorized into epochal literature (yuga sāhitya), which addresses the immediate psychological demands of an era in popular language, and coastal literature (taṭastha sāhitya), which links relative temporal realities to eternal transcendental truth.
items.title: The Practice of Art and Literature

items.qualifiers: Historical and material context of early Vedic culture
items.quote: In that age, during the Vedic rituals pertaining to the rites of yajiṋopaviita [the wearing of sacred threads as religious symbols], the practice of using threads was not in vogue, because cotton ( kárpás ) was then unknown to people. To serve the purpose of yajiṋopaviita , they would use a wild animal’s skin or sheepskin with little gossamer on the left shoulder.
items.statement: During the Ṛgvedic period, cotton (kārpāsa) was unknown, and thread was made from gossamer or pashm (ūrṇa), which was why skins with wool were used across the shoulder rather than cotton threads for yajñopaviita rites.
items.title: The Practice of Songs – Sore Throat and Its Remedy

items.qualifiers: Seven-point verse containing six explicit requisites for success in Tantra
items.quote: Phaliśyatiiti vishvásah siddherprathamalakśańam; Dvitiiyaḿ shraddhayá yuktaḿ trtiiyaḿ gurupújanam; Caturtho samatábhávo paiṋcamendriyanigrahah; Śaśt́haiṋca pramitáháro saptamaḿ naeva vidyate.
items.statement: According to Shiva, success in any mission requires six fundamental factors: firm faith/determination (vishvāsa), reverence for the goal (shraddhā), guru pūjā (constant remembrance of the preceptor), equanimity of mind (samatābhāva), control of senses (indriyanigraha), and balanced/measured sentient diet (pramitāhāra).
items.title: The Primary Causes of Success

items.qualifiers: Refutation of time as the primordial causa prima
items.quote: Time is only a relative factor, which is entirely dependent on the mutual relationship of place and person. Time is but the mind’s measurement of the motivity of action. When there is no motivity of action, or when there is motivity of action but no mind to measure it, there is no time.
items.statement: Time is not an absolute entity because it is merely the mind's subjective measurement of the motivity of action and depends entirely on relative space and person factors.
items.title: The Primordial Cause of Creation [in early editions titled Kśiire Sarpirivárpitam]

items.qualifiers: Deconstruction of Tantric anthropomorphic imagery into non-integral abstract ideas
items.quote: One of the characteristics of Tantra is this, that the different gods and goddesses originate from one idea or other. Those ideas were conceived in order to arouse and develop the finer sensibilities of the human mind. Thus a person conceived of a certain idea, and to make concrete that abstract idea, an image was invented. But such an idea, whether good or bad, is not an integral idea, it is a non-integral idea.
items.statement: Tantric deities originated not as absolute realities but as external concrete symbols representing non-integral, abstract concepts and psychological states conceived to cultivate specific mental sensibilities.
items.title: The Psychology behind the Origin of Tantric Gods and Goddesses

items.qualifiers: Philosophical definition of Tāraka Brahma's dual manifestation
items.quote: What is samyak birth? When the Nucleus of the universe gets a quinquelemental base, that alone is sambhavámi. In your philosophy, that is known as Táraka Brahma. By accepting the physical base, that Entity roams in the world of bháva [idea], and at the same time It remains connected with the nirguńa [unqualified], nirákára [formless] and bhávátiita [transcendental] Entity, beyond the periphery of mind.
items.statement: Táraka Brahma represents the supreme nucleus acquiring a quinquelemental physical base (sambhavámi), functioning simultaneously in the realm of idea (bhāva) while remaining linked to the formless, transcendental non-attributional entity.
items.title: The Purpose Behind the Advent

items.qualifiers: Explanatory mechanism of occult and pseudo-paranormal phenomena
items.quote: In a disembodied state the mind cannot work, because ectoplasmic structure can never function in that state. The stuff of which the mind is composed cannot function once it is detached from the body, because the mind-stuff functions only when the brain is active and the nerve cells are active. Physical death brings about dissociation of the nerve cells, hence the ectoplasmic structure stops functioning.
items.statement: A disembodied mind lacks an active physical brain and cannot function on its own; apparent haunting phenomena occur when a living individual with strong ectoplasmic capacity connects their own ectoplasm to activate that disembodied mind's saṁskāras.
items.title: The Real Culprit

items.qualifiers: Triadic essential components of human dharma
items.quote: What is Bhágavata Dharma? It is vistára (psychic expansion), rasa (flow) and sevá (service). Bhágavata Dharma differentiates humans from animals.
items.statement: Bhāgavata Dharma is the unique innate spiritual characteristic that differentiates human beings from animals, defined by three essentialities: vistāra (psychic expansion), rasa (cosmic flow), and sevā (selfless service to all creation).
items.title: The Requirements for Sádhaná

items.qualifiers: Ethical and socioeconomic analysis of capitalism
items.quote: The aspiration to become rich by exploiting others is always a kind of psychic ailment. Capitalists argue, “We amass wealth through our intellect and labour. Let others also amass wealth in the same way if they have the intellect or capacity to work. Who will stop them?” They do not want to accept that the number of consumable commodities in the world is limited, but all need their basic necessities.
items.statement: The urge to accumulate excessive physical wealth by exploiting others is a psychic ailment; because material resources are finite while human collective needs are universal, individual physical rights cannot be allowed to violate collective welfare.
items.title: The Responsibility of Society

items.qualifiers: Historical social flexibility of the varna system during the Mahābhārata era
items.quote: His worldly father, Vasudeva, was a kśatriya by profession. His guardian, Nanda, was a gopa (vaeshya); and his uncle, Maharsi Garga, was a vipra, because he adopted a life of scriptural study, contemplation and meditation. There was no rigidity in the caste system.
items.statement: During the Mahābhārata era, social varnas were functional and non-rigid: Lord Kṛṣṇa's father Vasudeva was a kṣatriya military commander, his foster father Nanda was a vaeshya (gopa), and his uncle Maharśi Garga was a vipra.
items.title: The Role of Lord Krśńa

items.qualifiers: Differentiates two distinct modes of samādhi
items.quote: The basic difference between these two kinds of samádhi is that in the samádhi of inferential bliss, the sádhaka enjoy bliss through the medium of the tanmátras, whereas in the samádhi of non-inferential bliss the sádhakas derive bliss directly from the cosmic mind.
items.statement: In the samādhi of inferential bliss (sārūpya samādhi), bliss is experienced through the medium of tanmātras (inferences), whereas in the samādhi of non-inferential bliss, vibrations are induced directly in the mind by the Cosmic Mind without sensory or inferential media.
items.title: The Samádhi of Inferential and Non-Inferential Bliss

items.quote: What is action? Action is the relative change of position or place of an object. When an object is transferred from one place to another, or when an object acquires a new position temporarily or permanently leaving its former position, we call it an action.
items.statement: Action is defined as the relative change of position or place of an object.
items.title: The Science of Action

items.qualifiers: Distinction between original and reactive karma
items.quote: An action which is done independently is called pratyayaḿulaka karma (original action). Suppose one has a desire to go to Calcutta and then actually goes there. This is an original action because to go or not to go to Calcutta depends entirely on one’s will. But an action which one is obliged to perform mechanically under pressure of circumstances is called saḿskáraḿulaka karma (reaction to the original action). In these actions it is the indirect will and not the direct will which functions.
items.statement: Original action (pratyayamúlaka karma) is performed independently by direct will, whereas reactive action (saḿskáramúlaka karma) is performed mechanically under circumstances driven by the indirect will.
items.title: The Science of Action

items.qualifiers: Categorization of karmas based on experience
items.quote: The action which creates a pleasurable sensation in the mind is called shukla karma (white action), and the vibration which creates a painful sensation is called kŕśńa karma (black action). The action which creates both pleasurable and painful experiences is called shuklakŕśna karma (black and white action), and the action which creates neither pleasurable nor painful experiences is called ashuklakŕśna karma (neither black nor white). Worldly actions are either shukla, kŕśna, or shuklakrśńa. Only an action or reaction related to samádhi, that is, spiritual sádhana, can be called ashuklakŕśna, for spiritual actions take one beyond the state of pleasure and pain.
items.statement: Actions are classified into white, black, black-and-white, and neither black nor white (spiritual actions/samádhi) based on whether they produce pleasurable, painful, both, or transcendent experiences.
items.title: The Science of Action

items.quote: Human beings possess one unique characteristic which is lacking in animals – the capacity to follow Bhágavata Dharma.
items.statement: The unique distinguishing characteristic of human beings compared to non-human creatures is the capacity to follow Bhágavata Dharma.
items.title: The Secret of Dharma Lies Hidden in the Mind

items.quote: Shraddhá comes from shrat, meaning satyam, and dhá from the root verb dha. When one ascribes everything to one’s goal, or one’s object, or to the Supreme Subjectivity appearing as one’s object, and moves, or rather directs one’s everything towards Him, then that movement is shraddhá. First ascribing that supreme veracity to the object (actually it is the Supreme Subjectivity taken as an object) and then directing one’s everything towards Him, is that mental movement which is called shraddhá.
items.statement: Shraddhá is defined as first ascribing supreme veracity to the Supreme Subjectivity and then directing one's entire existence towards Him.
items.title: The Seven Secrets of Success

items.quote: Here the word pramitáhára has been used, not parimitáhára. Parimita means “controlled”, not taking too much, not taking too little. But in this shloka, pramitáhára has been used, which means that the food should be controlled or balanced, and at the same time substantial or nutritious.
items.statement: Pramitáhára differs from parimitáhára in that it requires food to be balanced/controlled and simultaneously substantial and nutritious.
items.title: The Seven Secrets of Success

items.qualifiers: Etymological derivation from Sanskrit roots of walking
items.quote: What is the meaning of “samáj”? Samánam ejati is samáj. “To walk” – sah calati. “To walk while eating” – sah carati. “To walk while looking” – sah gacchati. “To follow” – sa anugacchati. “To walk while looking from side to side” – sa at́ati. “To walk while writing” – sa pargat́ati. “To walk calmly” – sa ejati. Samanam ejati samája. Samáj or “society” means a group of people who are moving happily and peacefully.
items.statement: Samája is derived from 'Samánam ejati', meaning a group of people moving together happily and peacefully.
items.title: The Significance of Language

items.qualifiers: Philosophical definition distinguishing from mere memorization
items.quote: What is jiṋána? You read a book and retain in memory what is there in the book. That is not jiṋána. The real meaning of jiṋána is the subjectivization of objectivity.
items.statement: Real jiṋána (knowledge) is defined as the subjectivization of objectivity.
items.title: The Significance of the Word “Bhagaván”

items.quote: Bhaga stands for six different attributes collected together – a synthesis of six attributes. One of these attributes is aeshvarya, which means “occult power”.
items.statement: Bhaga is synthesized as six attributes: aeshvarya (occult power), pratápa (commanding authority), yasha (reputation), shrii (charm/energy), jiṋána (true knowledge), and vaerágya (renunciation).
items.title: The Significance of the Word “Bhagaván”

items.qualifiers: Etymological and philosophical distinction of root verbs
items.quote: When the word “yoga” is derived from the root verb yuj it means “addition”, no doubt, but here the added components retain their original identity, just as when sand and sugar are added together the individual grains can still be identified. The root verb yunj , however, refers to a type of addition where the original components lose their respective identities, as in the case of a mixture of sugar and water which creates a syrup in which the sugar can no longer be separately identified.
items.statement: Yoga derived from the root 'yuj' denotes addition where components retain identity, whereas when derived from 'yunj' it signifies unification where original identities are lost.
items.title: The Significance of The Word “Yuga”

items.quote: He is connected with the universe both individually and collectively. His individual relationship is known as “ota-yoga” and His collective relationship is known as “prota-yoga”. That is why we say, “otah protah yogábhyáḿ saḿyuktah puruśottamah”.
items.statement: Parama Puruśa's relationship with the universe is twofold: individual contact is ota-yoga, and collective contact is prota-yoga.
items.title: The Singular Entity

items.qualifiers: Excludes fear complex; limited to physical and socioeconomic strata
items.quote: Inferiority and superiority complexes – not fear complex which is altogether different – arise due to a defective social order. Some people have to live like slaves in the society and thus suffer from a strong inferiority complex – their heads remain forever bowed – while others inherit vast wealth as well as family pride from their ancestors and keep their heads held so high that at times it appears as if it will fall backwards. These complexes are due to a defective social order. The complex is in the crude physical world and in the socio-economic strata, not in the stratum of spirituality.
items.statement: Superiority and inferiority complexes are caused entirely by a defective social and socioeconomic order, having no place in spirituality or the existential sphere.
items.title: The Social Order and Superiority and Inferiority Complexes

items.qualifiers: Sequential experiential stages of acoustic perception in Saguńa realm
items.quote: When those inner senses develop, then in the first phase sádhakas [spiritual aspirants] can hear the sound, that inner sound, that inner voice, that divine sound. In the first phase it is like the sound of crickets.
items.statement: As inner senses develop in sádhaná, internal sound progresses through five phases (crickets, ankle bells, flutes, ocean, bells) before reaching pure oṋḿkára.
items.title: The Sound of God

items.qualifiers: Distinction in ideation and acoustic scope
items.quote: Kiirtana and bhajana are not the same. Kiirtana’s greatness exceeds that of bhajana ; it is incomparable. The difference between the two is firstly that bhajana is not heard at as great a distance as kiirtana , and secondly that people sing bhajans so that they can experience happiness, not so much to give happiness to others. Conversely, the ideation behind kiirtana is that others might also enjoy the same happiness listening to the praises of God that I get by singing the praises of God.
items.statement: Bhajana is sung at closer range primarily for personal satisfaction, whereas kiirtana is sung loudly and outwardly so that others may enjoy the happiness of hearing the Lord's praises.
items.title: The Source of Internal Stamina

items.qualifiers: Applies to the fifth fundamental principle of PROUT
items.quote: Time and space are changing and PROUT will also have to adjust with that change. The principles of PROUT will not change, rather the application of PROUT will adjust with the changing circumstances. Human beings will have to move forward by recognizing and adjusting with changes in time and space. Adjustment and flexibility are essentials for human progress.
items.statement: Under Prout's fifth principle, practical applications and policies must change flexibly with time, place, and person, while fundamental principles remain constant.
items.title: The Speciality of the Fifth Fundamental Principle of Prout

items.qualifiers: Philosophical critique of mental suspension vs redirection
items.quote: A yogi can never remain without his or her Lord. The psychic propensities of a yogii must not be suspended. Rather all the propensities must be goaded unto the Lord. So there is no question of suspension but there is the question of diversion. The flow must be there and we should enjoy the divine flow or Rasa.
items.statement: Patanjali's definition of yoga as cittavrttinirodhah is rejected because the mind's essential nature is movement, requiring diversion of psychic propensities toward the Supreme rather than absolute suspension.
items.title: The Spirit of Yoga

items.quote: So you see, in the intellectual stratum liberation is possible but liberation of permanent nature is not possible. Do you follow? Liberation of permanent nature is only possible in spiritual sphere.
items.statement: Permanent liberation (salvation) is impossible in the physical and intellectual spheres due to relative factors and endless questions, and can only be attained in the spiritual sphere.
items.title: The Stance of Salvation and How to Attain It

items.quote: Where there is only acoustic rhythm, it is called Japakriyá and when that acoustic rhythm maintains parallelism with mental rhythm it is called Prańidhána.
items.statement: In japakriyá there is only acoustic rhythm, whereas práńidhána maintains acoustic rhythm in direct parallelism with mental rhythm.
items.title: The Stance of Salvation and How to Attain It

items.qualifiers: Scope encompasses both animate and inanimate down to sub-atomic levels
items.quote: Neohumanism includes within its scope not only human beings and animate creatures, such as plants and animals, but all inanimate entities as well, for the scope of Neohumanism extends down to the smallest particles of sub-atomic matter.
items.statement: Neohumanism extends not only extensively across all animate beings, but intensively into the sub-atomic inanimate realm where unit existence is recognized as pure Consciousness.
items.title: The Status of Inanimation in the Philosophy of Neohumanism

items.qualifiers: Division of the fifty human mental vrttis
items.quote: The mind’s connection, the mind’s ties, with matter are represented by forty-nine propensities, and the mind’s connection with the spirit is represented by one propensity. Those forty-nine propensities are mundane propensities, and they can function only with the help of interior or exterior organs. And the singular propensity that connects the mind with the spirit is paráshakti. It is beyond the campus of the organs.
items.statement: The human mind operates through fifty propensities: forty-nine connect the mind with mundane matter through organs, while one singular subtle propensity (pará) connects the mind with the spirit.
items.title: The Subtlest Propensity

items.qualifiers: Transition from aesthetic science to supra-aesthetic science (Mohana Vijiṋána)
items.quote: What happens when he or she is lost? He or she feels “I take the ideation of Parama Puruśa not for my sake, not for me. I love Parama Puruśa so that he may get pleasure because of my love, I wish to give Him pleasure. I may or may not get it.” When this stage is attained, this is called Rágátmiká Bhakti.
items.statement: Rágánugá bhakti represents the stage of aesthetic science where one enjoys serving God for one's own pleasure, whereas Rágátmiká bhakti enters supra-aesthetic science where one loves Parama Puruśa solely to give Him pleasure.
items.title: The Supreme Aesthetic Science and the Cult of Devotion

items.qualifiers: Cosmological evolutionary sequence of unit mind
items.quote: The human mind is a creation of physical factors. Ectoplasm is a creation of physical factors. The human mind is a creation of the human body. The quinquelemental universe is a creation of the Cosmic Mind, of the Macrocosm, but the microcosm, the unit mind, is a creation of the quinquelemental factors. The human mind did not come directly from the Macrocosm; it came from matter. And matter is a creation of the Macrocosm.
items.statement: The unit human mind and ectoplasm did not originate directly from the Macrocosm, but emerged from the physical quinquelemental factors animated by vital force.
items.title: The Supreme Cognition

items.qualifiers: Epistemological and ontological distinction between mind and soul
items.quote: To know is the faculty of the mind. To witness is the faculty of the átman. Clear? The mind knows, and the átman witnesses that the mind has known. The mind is knowing.
items.statement: The function of knowing belongs to the mind, whereas witnessing that the mind knows is the exclusive faculty of the átman.
items.title: The Supreme Cognition

items.qualifiers: Philosophical concept of Puruśa as witnessing catalytic entity
items.quote: Puruśa is that which lives in the pura of the body ( deha pure ). Secondly, Purasi shete yah sah Puruśah . Purasi means – “in the front”. Purasi hitam karoti yah sah purohitah – one who comes forward to bring about your welfare. Similarly, one who lies quiescent before you is Puruśa . In whatever direction you go, you find Him before you. There is no way to ignore or bypass Him. Thus Puruśa akartá .
items.statement: Puruśa is an akartá (non-doer) acting like a catalytic agent whose indispensable presence enables all actions without It undergoing change or spatial displacement.
items.title: The Supreme Entity – the Non-Doer

items.qualifiers: Stages of acoustic and speech expression through the cakras
items.quote: At svádhiśt́hána cakra we visualise the next form of material speech called pashyanti shakti. Pashyanti shakti permits people to visualise an idea according to their inherent saḿskáras. That is, people mentally visualise what they are going to articulate. At anáhata cakra, madhyamá shakti transforms pashyanti shakti into mental language, which seeks to find expression through dance, gestures or speech. This inner urge to vocalise the mental language is externalized through dyotamáná shakti, which operates between anáhata cakra and vishuddha cakra. Finally, with the help of vaekharii shakti, dyotamáná shakti takes the form of language.
items.statement: Vocal expression evolves upward through five stages: paráshakti (múládhára), pashyanti shakti (svádhiśt́hána), madhyamá shakti (anáhata), dyotamáná shakti, and vaekharii shakti (vishuddha) which interacts with ether as shrutigocará shakti.
items.title: The Supreme Question – 1

items.quote: If someone desires to offer gifts in response to an invitation, the best gifts are flowers, but even flowers are not essential. If someone has an intense desire to offer a special present, it should be done either in the absence of the other invited guests or on some other day, otherwise it will be considered an antisocial act.
items.statement: If a guest offers a special present in response to an invitation, it must be given either privately away from other guests or on a different day, otherwise it is considered antisocial.
items.title: The System of Invitation

items.qualifiers: Second characteristic of the ten dharmalakśańas
items.quote: When the time comes for you to take revenge, you should not express any reaction yourself. In this way you will break the continuity of the chain. This point at which the cycle of action and reaction stops, due to your initiative, is called forgiveness. This is the second characteristic of dharma.
items.statement: Forgiveness (kśamá) is defined as the deliberate point at which an individual stops the otherwise endless cycle of action and reaction by choosing not to retaliate.
items.title: The Ten Characteristics of Dharma

items.qualifiers: Framework explaining social and individual transgression
items.quote: Now, let us come to the three causes of sin. If sin and crime are considered together there are three reasons for them. The first cause is shortage of physical and psychic pabula. The second one is non-utilization of over-accumulated physical and psychic pabula. The third one is stagnancy in the psychic and physical strata.
items.statement: Sin and crime stem from three root causes: shortage of physical and psychic pabula, non-utilization of over-accumulated pabula, and stagnancy in physical and psychic strata.
items.title: The Three Causes of Sin

items.qualifiers: Distinction between commercial give-and-take and unilateral service
items.quote: Sevá means “selfless service”. Service is there where there is no desire to get anything in return. When there is a desire to take while giving, it is not service, but business. Any kind of business is attached to give-and-take.
items.statement: Sevá is strictly defined as selfless service where there is solely giving with no desire to take anything in return, distinguishing it from commercial business transactions.
items.title: The Three Factors for Spiritual Elevation

items.qualifiers: Tripartite spiritual typology of human beings
items.quote: So among humans, there are these three species – pashu, viira and deva.
items.statement: Human beings are categorized into three species based on internal development: pashu (animal in human form), viira (fighting heroic human), and deva (god in human form), practiced via pashvácára, viirácára/Ciinácára, and divyácára.
items.title: The Three Species of Human Being

items.quote: When sand and sugar are mixed together, that physical mixture is unity. They are united: sand and sugar are united. But when water comes in contact with sugar, it is a case of unification. We get sarvat [syrup]. In sarvat, we will not find those separate entities of sugar and water. So your union with the Supreme Father will not be a case of unity, but a case of unification.
items.statement: Unity involves a physical mixture where separate identities remain (like sand and sugar), whereas unification involves dissolving into a single entity without separate components (like sugar dissolved in water).
items.title: The Three Vital Factors

items.quote: Pariprashna means to know what to do and how to do. That is, the person is prepared to do something. He is prepared to do sádhaná, and for that purpose he wants to know how to do, what to do. This special type of question is called pariprashna.
items.statement: Pariprashna refers specifically to practical questions asked by a spiritual aspirant who is ready to act and practice, seeking to know what to do and how to do it, distinct from ordinary intellectual debate.
items.title: The Three Vital Factors

items.qualifiers: occurs every three to four thousand years at acute staticity
items.quote: At a certain stage in the movement of human society along its path, the behaviour, manners, customs, intellect and wisdom of the people cease to develop – they become static; and society loses its capacity to move forward. This is the critical juncture in history when the society feels the need for an extraordinarily powerful personality, a Mahásambhúti. At this juncture the advent of such a mighty personality is inevitable.
items.statement: When human society reaches acute staticity where intellect and customs cease to progress, the advent of an extraordinarily powerful personality (Mahásambhúti) becomes inevitable to infuse dynamism and accelerate social movement.
items.title: The Transitional Period

items.quote: I have already explained that when one channelises one’s attractions towards Iishvara, it is “bhakti” and when they are channelized towards any other object it is “ásakti”. Similarly, if one’s attachment is channelized towards any supra-psychic or spiritual object it may be called “prema” or “love”. But love in the physical and psychic spheres is called “káma” and not “prema”.
items.statement: Channelizing attractions toward the spiritual or supra-psychic (Iishvara) constitutes bhakti or prema, whereas channelizing desire toward physical and psychic objects is termed ásakti or káma.
items.title: The True Nature of Bhakti

items.quote: Not only that, the ájiiva, or occupation, of every person is different. These occupations are also of two types, crude and subtle – that is, physical and mental. For example, a person may be a doctor or a lawyer. This is the person’s crude occupation. Like crude occupations, mental occupations are different. Mental occupations, mental ájiivas, are known in the shástras [scriptures] as ábhogas.
items.statement: Occupations (ájiiva) are categorized as crude physical occupations (like profession) or subtle mental occupations, which scriptures call ábhogas.
items.title: The Ultimate Aim of All

items.quote: Why Hari? In Sanskrit hr means “to steal”. So He is Hari, because Harati pápánii ityarthe Hari [“One who steals sins is called Hari”]. He steals. He steals what? He steals your sins.
items.statement: Parama Puruśa is termed 'Hari' (derived from the root 'hr', meaning to steal) because He secretly steals the sins of surrendered spiritual aspirants without their permission.
items.title: The Universal Expression of Parama Puruśa

items.quote: Both the kśatriyas and the vipras like to enjoy material wealth, though their methods of accumulating material objects are different. The vaeshyas, however, are more interested in possessing material objects than enjoying them. Looking at their possessions, or thinking about them, gives them a certain peace of mind. So in the Vaeshya Age the practical value of material goods is less than at any other time.
items.statement: Kśatriyas and vipras seek to enjoy material objects, whereas vaeshyas derive satisfaction primarily from possessing and accumulating material objects rather than enjoying them.
items.title: The Vaeshya Age

items.qualifiers: when ownership is forcibly collectivized without individual control
items.quote: Furthermore, if large amounts of capital are placed under collective management, a small error on the part of the managers will lead to gross misutilization. This is the main reason why the system of collective farming, or the commune system, has failed in socialistic countries. If the ownership of wealth is taken away from individuals and placed in the hands of the state – in other words, if the vaeshya system is abolished by force – managers will not have the same control over that wealth as individual owners would.
items.statement: Entrusting capital to collective management, governments, or communes inevitably leads to misutilization or failure because managers lack the personal control and stakes of individual owners.
items.title: The Vaeshya Age

items.qualifiers: accounts for roughly eighty per cent of cases
items.quote: In order to eradicate this sinful occupation in India, it will be necessary to eliminate the vaeshya social system, because in eighty per cent of cases the cause of prostitution is economic injustice.
items.statement: Prostitution in society is primarily caused by economic injustice and the dynamics of the vaeshya social system, which cannot be cured solely by legal bans.
items.title: The Vaeshya Age

items.quote: The witnessed entities have a trifarious existence – doer, doing and done, a trifarious existence – and above those three is the Witnessing Entity.
items.statement: Every action within the arena of relativities requires three factors (doer, doing, done), while essence of philosophy requires a fourth factor beyond relativities: the witnessing factor (Witnessing Entity).
items.title: The Value of Dance

items.quote: The most important difference is that kśatriyas try to enslave matter directly by fighting with it, whereas vipras, using their intellects, try to enslave the kśatriyas (who can then triumph over matter).
items.statement: Kśatriyas attempt to dominate matter directly through physical struggle, whereas vipras dominate matter indirectly by using intellect to control and enslave the kśatriyas.
items.title: The Vipra Age

items.quote: Phallus worship had been invented by the primitive, uncultured kśatriyas as a symbol of increasing their population. The cultured vipras now interpreted it in a new way. They contended that the linga was a symbol for Parama Puruśa [Supreme Consciousness] and the piit́ha [vulva] a symbol for Prakrti [Supreme Operative Principle].
items.statement: Phallus worship was originally invented by primitive kśatriyas as a symbol to increase numerical population, and was only later reinterpreted philosophically by cultured vipras as liuṋga and piit́ha.
items.title: The Vipra Age

items.quote: In Sanskrit, the word shilpana means an activity done with one’s hands that requires artistic skill (in a word, handicraft). Suppose, a certain carpenter made a bedstead. It was done with his or her hands. Hence we shall say that the bedstead is a handicraft and the carpenter an artist. But the song sung by a singer is in no way a work done by hand. So the word saḿgiita shilpii is a misnomer. Be that as it may, those who play a musical instrument have scope to display the dexterity of their hands. Hence you can call an instrumentalist an artist.
items.statement: The Sanskrit term 'shilpana' strictly refers to manual handicraft requiring dexterity, making 'saḿgiita shilpii' a misnomer for vocal singers though applicable to instrumentalists.
items.title: The Virtuoso of Saḿgiita

items.quote: Chátra does not mean “students”; chátra means “jurisdiction”. People living within the jurisdiction of a particular teacher used to receive and to follow guidance from that teacher, hence they were called his or her chátras . These days students and professors in colleges differ in their opinions, hence the students are not chátras in the real sense of the term.
items.statement: The term 'chátra' historically designated individuals living within the jurisdiction of a particular teacher whose guidance they followed, rather than modern college students with differing opinions.
items.title: The Vital Energy of Students

items.qualifiers: Except when killing born enemies where no sin applies
items.quote: Actions, done unknowingly and independent of others, are not included in one’s account; one is not culpable. Only those actions that have the backing of the conscious mind are included in one’s account.
items.statement: Actions done unconsciously or without mental intention accrue no karmic sin, whereas actions performed with the backing of the conscious mind create mental distortion and karmic consequences.
items.title: The Witness-ship of Parama Puruśa Is of Supreme Importance

items.quote: The idea that the disembodied mind experiences the auspicious consequences of its good actions is indeed a fantasy. This fantasy world is called heaven. It means that if one has performed a good action, then one will reap the consequences of that auspicious action after death. But the mind can experience its good consequences, if and only if, it has a body. One experiences joy and agony, pleasure and pain only if one has a brain, nerve cells and nerve fibres. If there is no physical body, how can there be any experience?
items.statement: The notion of a disembodied mind experiencing heaven or hell is a fantasy, because pleasure and pain require a physical brain, nerve cells, and nerve fibres.
items.title: The Witness-ship of Parama Puruśa Is of Supreme Importance

items.quote: When a very big entity comes within the scope of measurement, we say it is vishála. And when a very big entity does not come within the scope of measurement, we say it is brhat. Brhat and vishála. Our country of India is vishála, not brhat. Now, in the entire universe the only brhat entity is Parama Puruśa, the Supreme Puruśa, and there is no other brhat entity.
items.statement: In Sanskrit, 'vishála' denotes an entity that is very large but falls within measurable limits, whereas 'brhat' applies strictly to an immeasurable entity, which is true only of Parama Puruśa.
items.title: There Is Oil in the Sesame

items.qualifiers: perceptually treated as present due to sensory limitations in detecting microscopic time gaps
items.quote: Actually there is no such thing as the present tense. When I say something, you do not then hear it. You hear it after a small gap. What is the gap? The time taken by the air to carry the sound to your ear. And when you hear, it is past for [me]. So when I say it, just when I am saying it, it is future for you, because you hear after a short gap, and when you hear it is past for [me].
items.statement: The present tense does not physically exist because sensory perception requires a finite time gap for sound or light waves to reach and be processed by the human organs.
items.title: There Should Be Subjective Approach through Objective Adjustment

items.quote: Kurukśetra thus stands for the manifested world around us, the saḿsára, where you exist in your physical body (which is your dharmakśetra).
items.statement: Kurukśetra represents the manifested active world (saḿsára) compelling dynamic action ('kuru' meaning 'do'), while dharmakśetra denotes the physical human body through which spiritual practice is realized.
items.title: This Very World Is Kurukśetra

items.quote: When the form of an object is materialized in the mind through the instrumentality of the sense organs it is anubhúti. When this relationship with the objects becomes deeper resulting in the citta completely identifying itself with them it is called “realization” or upalabdhi (upa means “near”, and labdhi means “to get”). When this proximity with objects becomes still and deeper, when the mind-stuff becomes almost completely identical with them, the expression of the individual “I” feeling then becomes very indistinct. In that state, the sense of individuality almost disappears – the seeable and the seer become almost one, but not completely. This state is called labdhi or substantial attainment.
items.statement: Mental perception develops through three distinct stages of proximity: anubhúti (feeling), upalabdhi (realization), and labdhi (substantial attainment where the seer and seen almost merge).
items.title: This World and the Next

items.quote: There are three cardinal socio-political principles which should never be violated. First, people should not be retrenched from their occupations unless alternative employment has been arranged for them. Secondly, people should not be forcibly converted from one religion to another. Thirdly, no mother tongue should be suppressed.
items.statement: Society and leadership must strictly uphold three cardinal socio-political principles: no retrenchment without alternative livelihood, no forced religious conversions, and no suppression of mother tongues.
items.title: Three Cardinal Socio-Political Principles

items.quote: It has been said that this procedure, this method should be based on “Prańipátena, pariprashnena and sevaya”. That is to say, in order to succeed in the field of karma, one should be fully conversant with prańipátena, pariprashnena and sevayá.
items.statement: Success in the field of action (karma) on the spiritual path requires adherence to three methods: total surrender (prańipáta), practical guidance questions (pariprashna), and selfless service to the oppressed as manifestations of Brahma (sevá).
items.title: Three Fundamental Factors to Succeed in Sádhaná Márga

items.quote: This jiivabháva, or kulakuńd́alinii shakti, is called “Rádhá” in Tantric scriptures, while the central controlling power in the sahasrára, from where all the manifold activities of humans are controlled, is called “Krśńa”. When the kulakuńd́alinii reaches the sahasrára, the person attains mokśa [non-qualified liberation]. This is the significance of “Krśńa” in yoga.
items.statement: In yoga and Tantric terminology, the latent microcosmic force (kulakuńd́alinii) is called 'Rádhá', while the supreme controlling nucleus at the sahasrára cakra is called 'Krśńa'.
items.title: Three Interpretations of the Word “Krśńa”

items.quote: However, a full-fledged civilization, with the four symbols of advancement – agriculture, the wheel, dress and script – start ed only about 7,000 years ago. Human beings had grasped the rudimentals of these inventions by this time. Pictorial letters were invented less than 7,000 years ago, and philosophy was discovered only about 4,000 years ago.
items.statement: Full-fledged human civilization characterized by agriculture, the wheel, dress, and script began roughly 7,000 years ago, whereas spiritual occupations (Atmic/Dharmic jiivika) began 15,000 years ago.
items.title: Three Types of Occupation

items.qualifiers: Creation is liilá to unit humans but kriid́á to Parama Puruśa
items.quote: There is a subtle difference between liilá and kriid́a. When the cause of an effect is easily discernible it is called kriid́a, but when the cause is unknown and only the effect is easily discernible it is called liilá. This creation is the liilá of Parama Puruśa because human beings do not know why He has created it.
items.statement: When the cause of an observed effect is discernible it is called 'kriid́á', whereas when the effect is visible but its fundamental cause remains unknown to the limited unit mind, it is called 'liilá'.
items.title: To Know Him Is to Be Free from All Fetters

items.quote: In reality, a kind of sentiment created either directly or indirectly on the basis of one or more factors such as country, language, religion, etc., plays a vital role in forming a nation. The factors themselves are quite insignificant. It is the sentiment and nothing else that creates a nation.
items.statement: A nation is not fundamentally created by physical factors such as geography, language, race, or religion, but by a shared collective sentiment formed directly or indirectly around such factors.
items.title: To the Patriots

items.quote: When, as a result of anti-British sentiment, the Indian nation was formed in the nineteenth century, the then leaders of India should have started a struggle for economic independence instead of launching a political movement. All Indians could have fought together unitedly, there being no Hindu, Muslim, Punjabi or Marathi feelings in this economic struggle, and as a result an anti-exploitation sentiment could have been developed in India.
items.statement: Partition of India occurred because the independence leadership pursued purely political power and sectarian fears instead of an economic struggle against exploitation that would have united all communities.
items.title: To the Patriots

items.quote: But, on analysis, you will discover that behind the vices there is one fundamental vice. And that primary vice is falsehood. Here falsehood is the fundamental sin from which other sins originate.
items.statement: Falsehood is the primary noumenal vice from which all other phenomenal crimes and vices originate.
items.title: Towards the Noumenal Entity

items.qualifiers: Recognized by Páńini towards the end of the Vedic Age
items.quote: So when a transaction would be effected through an exchange of commodities, the root verb krii (with the conjugation kriińiite) continued to be used. But when a transaction would be effected through the medium of sea shells – the system known today in English as “buying” (“to purchase” can mean to get something through barter, but “to buy” can only mean to get something with money) – though the same root verb was used, it was conjugated as kriińáte. Thus, towards the end of the Vedic Age the root verb krii became ubhayapadii, conjugated in both the above ways.
items.statement: In ancient Sanskrit, the root verb 'krii' was conjugated as 'kriińiite' for barter transactions and as 'kriińáte' for purchases made using sea-shell currency, making 'krii' an ubhayapadii verb.
items.title: Trade and Barter in Ancient Bengal – Excerpt B

items.quote: What are psychic pabula? The word “psychic” means mental and “pabula” implies “mental objects” or “mental foods”. Communism and capitalism are essentially materialist philosophies. Both encourage a psychology of material attachment, which in turn encourages the pursuit of money, name, fame, etc. People living under either of these two systems develop the psychic pabula which run after crude physicalities. All these objective tendencies are the inevitable outcome of the continuous extroversial movement of psychic urges, insatiably driving themselves from one object to another. While running after such material attachments, the mind constantly creates objects in its objective chambers or citta bhumi. All these mental objects are mental food, and they are called psychic pabula.
items.statement: Psychic pabula are mental objects or mental foods created in the objective chambers of the mind (citta bhumi) as an outcome of the extroversial movement of psychic urges.
items.title: The Transformation of Psychic Pabula into Psycho-spiritual Pabulum

items.quote: That which is obtained through some medium is called “prápti” and that which is obtained directly from Parama Puruśa is termed “ápti”. Knowledge acquired from the study of books is called “prápta vákya” and the knowledge which we acquire directly in our minds is called, “ápta vákya”. We cannot retain prápti for long because it is transitory by nature.
items.statement: Transitory attainment derived through external sources or mediums is called 'prápti', whereas eternal spiritual attainment and grace received directly from Parama Puruśa is termed 'ápti'.
items.title: Treading the Broad Path of Spirituality

items.quote: A triangle with one vertex up superimposed on another triangle with one vertex down, with the rising sun having a swastika inside. These are symbols of energy, knowledge, advancement and permanent victory, respectively.
items.statement: The Ananda Marga emblem (Pratiika) consists of an upward triangle, a downward triangle, a rising sun, and a swastika, symbolizing energy, knowledge, advancement, and permanent victory respectively.
items.title: Treasures of Ananda Marga

items.quote: That very entity or that very personality which liberates one by persuading one to follow the code of discipline and the code of dos and don’ts is known as Shástra. Shásanát tárayet yastu. Shásana means to persuade one to follow the path of blessedness.
items.statement: Shástra is defined as that entity or personality that liberates an individual by guiding them to follow a code of discipline and righteous conduct.
items.title: Trio in Spiritual Progress

items.quote: A devotee can only be for the Infinite Entity. If the object of ideation be finite, the term “devotion” should not be used; “addiction” is the proper language. Where the object is infinite, then the psychic movement is called “devotion”.
items.statement: Genuine devotion requires an infinite object of ideation, whereas directing the identical psychic attachment toward a finite object (such as wealth, name, or fame) constitutes addiction.
items.title: Two Hundred Mirrors

items.qualifiers: asserted as a principle of equal spiritual rights derived from Cosmic Fatherhood
items.quote: If the boys are the sons of Parama Puruśa, then the girls are His daughters, and they are entitled to equal rights. Just as a father takes his son on his lap and dotes over him, similarly, he takes his daughter on his lap and showers his love on her. He certainly does not hold any idea in his mind that he will not love her because she is a girl. So those who say that women are not entitled to spiritual salvation are clearly opportunists. They are social exploiters, they are wicked, they are bad.
items.statement: Denying women spiritual salvation is a form of psycho-economic and social exploitation based on opportunistic double standards.
items.title: Two Wings – Excerpt C

items.qualifiers: specifically identifies the mechanism through subconscious damage
items.quote: In Sanskrit, repression is called avadamana. Repression directly affects the subconscious mind. Gradually the psychic structure is severely damaged, and finally the mind is totally changed. The result is that people are inflicted with a defeatist psychology and an inferiority complex.
items.statement: Psychic repression (avadamana) damages the subconscious mind, leading to defeatist psychology and inferiority complexes.
items.title: Two Wings – Excerpt H

items.qualifiers: refinement is the touchstone of civilization
items.quote: What is civilization? The subtle sense of refinement that we come across in the different expressions of life is called civilization.
items.statement: Civilization is defined as the subtle sense of refinement evident across different expressions of life and grounded in discriminative judgement.
items.title: Two Wings – Excerpt G

items.qualifiers: directed to Renaissance movements as an imperative for social progress
items.quote: Society should have a cooperative leadership, not a subordinated leadership; there should be a coordinated, cooperative leadership, leadership between males and females. Renaissance people will have to start a movement immediately to fight against all these disparities; otherwise if fifty percent of the population, that is the ladies, remain downtrodden, how can there be all-round progress of human society?
items.statement: Society requires coordinated cooperative leadership between males and females rather than subordinated leadership to achieve all-round progress.
items.title: Two Wings – Excerpt J

items.quote: Whenever any action goes from the level of conception to the level of objective expression, then the first stage of that objective expression is called bodhana. When this bodhana is done by calling the people ceremoniously with the help of musical instruments then it is called udbodhana.
items.statement: In the science of language and grammar, bodhana represents the initial objective expression of a concept, and udbodhana is bodhana performed ceremoniously with musical instruments.
items.title: Ui to Uluka (Discourse 9)

items.quote: In the case where these instructions [deshaná], what-is-to-be-done and what-is-not-to-be-done, are articulated in detail and what action is to be taken according to those instructions is also articulated, then it is called upadesha (advice). When what-is-to-be-done and what-is-not-to-be-done is carefully articulated and according to that orders are given, then it is called nirdesha (nir – dish + ghaiṋ = nirdesha – direction). When that something is made compulsory, either to do or not to do, regardless of whether something is said about whether it is proper to do or not to do, then it is ádesha (order; á – dish + ghaiṋ = ádesha).
items.statement: Advice (upadesha) details what to do and what not to do, direction (nirdesha) provides orders based on those instructions, and order (adesha) makes action compulsory regardless of propriety explanations.
items.title: Ui to Uluka (Discourse 9)

items.qualifiers: introduced to end a million-year era of non-marriage and lack of paternal responsibility
items.quote: The women of that day stood at Shiva’s door and said: “O Sadáshiva, save us from this beastly, distressful condition. There is no man or woman strong enough today to lay down rules in this matter and to put them into practice with a firm hand.” Shiva’s heart melted; he understood their pain. He introduced the custom of marriage and firmly fixed the rights and responsibilities of the father. For the first time human beings felt the contact of a peaceful environment in social life.
