items.statement: Lord Shiva was the first to formalize and enforce the institution of marriage, establishing paternal responsibility to protect women and stabilize social life.
items.title: Úk/Uk to Úd́ha (Discourse 10)

items.quote: When the sudhárasa [bliss-causing hormones] emitted by the glands and sub-glands situated above the ájiṋá cakra are consumed in the ájiṋá cakra, the result is that the ájiṋá cakra is strongly affected by the high secretion of hormones brought about by sádhaná [spiritual practices] in that upper region, and consequently the irises of the eyes move upwards and a state of trance ensues. A pleasant drowsiness of tandrá [somnolence] mixed with nidrá [sleepiness] overcomes the eyes, and the person is immersed in a type of slumber of a subtle loka [realm].
items.statement: When sudharasa (bliss-causing hormones) secreted above the ajna cakra is consumed within the ajna cakra during sadhana, upward movement of the irises and a hypnotic trance state (yoga nidra) ensue.
items.title: Under the Shelter of the Guru

items.qualifiers: structural distinction between ideational and physical brain control points
items.quote: That which I call the sahasrára cakra is an ideational point – without any realistic existence based on the nerve cells – but this is not the case with the Guru cakra. So human beings must take recourse to the Guru Cakra – they must take shelter under it: Nányapanthá vidyate-ayanáyá [“There is no other way than this”].
items.statement: The sahasrara cakra is an ideational point without biological nerve-cell existence, whereas the Guru cakra possesses a realistic physiological controlling point in the brain.
items.title: Under the Shelter of the Guru

items.qualifiers: conditioned on the cause-and-effect relativities of time, space, and person
items.quote: Anything big but having boundary lines is known as vishála in Sanskrit; and anything big having no boundary lines is known as virát́a in Sanskrit. Parama Puruśa is virát́a, but this universe is vishála, not virát́a. So space is not infinite. It is a causal entity, and what is the cause? What is the causal matrix? The Supreme Mind.
items.statement: Space and time are not infinite or causal matrices because they are mental measurements created by the static principle within the Cosmic Mind.
items.title: Unit Spirit and Cosmic Spirit

items.qualifiers: relative perception due to sensory-transmission delays
items.quote: In the true spirit of kála [time], there is no vartamána, there is nothing vartamána. I am speaking. When I am speaking, you are not hearing. You will be hearing after some time. Let the air go from this place to that place, then you will hear. When I am speaking, what happens? It is past for me, it is future for you. So in the true spirit of kála, there is nothing present – there is either past or future.
items.statement: In the objective reality of kála (time), there is no present tense, only past and future, while the concept of the present is a mental assimilation of the immediate past and close future.
items.title: Unit Spirit and Cosmic Spirit

items.qualifiers: absolute philosophical and psychological limitations of Supreme Consciousness
items.quote: Once I told you that Parama Puruśa is omnipotent no doubt, all-powerful no doubt. But He cannot do two things. You may do those things, but Parama Puruśa cannot do them. And what are those two things? One thing is, He cannot create a second Parama Puruśa – this is one defect. And the second defect is, He cannot hate you. He cannot hate anybody.
items.statement: Parama Puruśa is omnipotent but cannot do two things: create a second Parama Puruśa, and hate anyone.
items.title: Unit Spirit and Cosmic Spirit

items.quote: They do not want to understand that matter is absolutely dependent on time, space, and person for its existence. Matter comes out of energy and energy comes out of Idea. And Parama Puruśa is the metempirical entity. They do not want to recognize the Supreme Causal Factor from whom countless vibrations are emanating and in whom all entities finally dissolve. In reality whatever we normally accept as a fundamental material cause of this colourful creation – whether the molecule, atom, electron or etheron – is only the expression of energy. Moreover, energy itself is not an original entity, but a particular manifestation of the static influence of Prakrti the emanent principle of Parama Puruśa.
items.statement: Physical matter is not an ultimate reality but an expression of energy, which in turn is a manifestation of the static principle of Prakrti originating from Idea.
items.title: Unity in Diversity

items.quote: Similarly, no race can claim the absolute purity of its blood. Hitler’s clam about the purity of Aryan blood was to mislead the people. In Europe alone there are so many races such as the Nordic, Mediterranean, Alpine and Greek races. In India there are Austrics, Austrico-Negroids, Dravidians, Mongolo-Negroids, and the like. Therefore, no race is absolutely free from blending. Everywhere there is universal blending. Nowhere in the world will you find a single original race and language. Human society is a singular entity.
items.statement: No language or racial lineage is pure or original; all existing languages and races are products of universal blending and constitute a singular human patrimony.
items.title: Universality in Race, Language, Religion and Culture

items.qualifiers: etymological definition contrasting subjective ideation with mere fasting
items.quote: “Upa” is a Saḿskrta prefix. In Saḿskrta there are twenty recognized prefixes, and one of these prefixes is “upa”. “Upa” means “proximity”. And “Vása” means “to live”, “to reside”. The word “upavása” means then, “to live near the Lord”.
items.statement: Upavasa means to reside in close proximity to the Lord mentally, distinct from mere physical fasting without food (anashana).
items.title: Upavása

items.qualifiers: moral classification distinguishing commission and omission
items.quote: There are two types of pápa or sin: pápa, which occurs when one does something one should not do, and pratyávaya, which occurs when one does not do something which should be done. For example, one should nurse a sick person. If one does not do that one is committing pratyáváya. Pratyáváya is more harmful than pápa.
items.statement: Sins of commission (papa) occur when doing what should not be done, whereas sins of omission (pratyavaya) occur when omitting what should be done, the latter being more harmful.
items.title: Vaedhii Bhakti and Shuddhá Bhakti

items.qualifiers: exemplified by actions disguised as virtuous or holy roles
items.quote: Mahápátaka is a sinful action for which there can be no atonement and which has a recurring effect.
items.statement: Mahapataka is an un-atonable sinful action that sets a recurring harmful precedent for society.
items.title: Vaedhii Bhakti and Shuddhá Bhakti

items.qualifiers: acoustic science framework of acoustic roots
items.quote: The latent or dormant condition of a word is called pará . At the first stage of expression, one visualizes that word with one’s inner eye. Then it takes the name of pashyanti (the feminine gender of pashyat with the suffix shatr ). Thereafter, the stage of continuous effort that goes on from the navel to the vocal cord regions to transform the visualized word from mental image into an expressible state or language is called madhyamá. The stage that follows this madhyamá, when it goes on pushing … stirring the uvula continuously, is known as dyotamáná . Afterwards, when, with the help of the uvula, it is transformed into an audible sound, it is called vaekharii .
items.statement: Sound manifestation transitions through five acoustic stages: para (latent seed), pashyanti (inner visualized form), madhyama (navel-to-throat processing), dyotamana (uvular activation), and vaekhari (audible vocalized sound).
items.title: Vaekharii Power

items.qualifiers: explains why psycho-economic and socio-economic exploitation often go unnoticed by victims
items.quote: Exploitation in the psychic stratum is mostly perpetrated or perpetuated in the first phase through dogma. These dogma are also the harbingers of economic exploitation or social exploitation. Sometimes the exploitation carried on in the spiritual stratum is also perpetrated through some kind of dogma. In the spiritual stratum, as in the physical stratum, the exploiters, together with dogma, create inferiority complexes or superiority complexes in the minds of the people, and later perpetrate economic or social exploitation.
items.statement: Psychic and spiritual exploitation are initiated through dogmas that inject inferiority or superiority complexes, paving the way for eventual economic and social subjugation.
items.title: Various Forms of Exploitation

items.qualifiers: based on the principle that land is common property of all humanity
items.quote: The preservation and utilization of land should be the responsibility of the local government, which in turn should carry out its duty through producers’ cooperatives composed of actual farmers. The disadvantages of private ownership will not manifest if the land is collectively owned in a cooperative system.
items.statement: Arable land should not be owned by individuals or non-producing business entities, but held collectively as common property utilized through producers' cooperatives under local government.
items.title: Various Occupations

items.qualifiers: business enterprises may only handle luxury and non-essential items
items.quote: It is undesirable for business people to have the right to distribute food grains. Only consumers’ cooperatives should have this right. As long as the production and distribution of crops is controlled by vaeshyas rather than by cooperatives, it is absolutely impossible to stop hoarding, speculation, black marketing and adulteration in food markets.
items.statement: The production and distribution of essential commodities such as food, clothing, and medicines must be restricted to cooperatives and autonomous bodies rather than profit-seeking business enterprises.
items.title: Various Occupations

items.quote: Thus the psycho-spiritual path is divided into four stages: yatamána, vyatireka, ekendriya and vashiikára. When the mind hovers between the crude and the subtle it is the yatamana stage. When, after vacillating between petty gains and losses one wishes to want to snap the bondage of gains and losses for good and plunge into the world of psychic bliss, it is the second stage, vyatireka. When bliss comes like a flood of light on a moonlit night, it is ekendriya. And when one strives hard to establish oneself in the absolute word by suspending all the mundane longings through psycho-spiritual endeavour it is vashiikára.
items.statement: The psycho-spiritual progression is divided into four successive stages: yatamana (vacillating effort), vyatireka (turning to psychic bliss), ekendriya (experiencing flood-like bliss), and vashiikara (complete control over mundane longings).
items.title: Vashiikára – 1

items.qualifiers: attributed to Shaevatantra concepts of dharma
items.quote: Eśa dharma catuśpádah . That is, dharma is a four-legged entity ( vistára , i.e., expansion , rasa , i.e., flow , sevá , i.e., service and mokśa or turiiya ). We are familiar with three of these but not with the fourth. The effort to become familiar with that fourth leg is called dharma. Dharma is an all-round effort to become familiar with the state of turiiya .
items.statement: Dharma is described in Shaevatantra as a four-legged entity comprising expansion (vistara), flow (rasa), service (seva), and liberation (moksa or turiya).
items.title: Vasu and Vásudeva

items.qualifiers: literary and philosophical taxonomy of Sanskrit compositions
items.quote: The fourth category of literature is itihása. Itihásati ityarthá itihása. The word itihása is derived from iti + has + ghaiṋ. Itihása is that part of itikathá which carries some educative value. The entire history or itikathá is not all itihása; itihása, which has no English synonym, is only that particular part of itikathá which has educative value.
items.statement: Itikatha is a mere chronological record of events (history), whereas itihasa is specifically that portion of historical record that provides moral, ethical, and spiritual education across the four vargas.
items.title: Verse, Mythology, History and Itihása

items.quote: In Ananda Marga Sadhana, the method of withdrawing the mind from degrading tendencies, and absorbing oneself in the colour of the Great, is called Pratyáhára Yoga (the yoga of withdrawal) or Varńárghyadána (the offering of colours). All people have a particular attraction for one or another object or activity and as soon as they become attracted to an object, then their minds become coloured with the colour of that object. You can withdraw your mind from the colour of that object and dye yourself in His colour by offering Him the captivating colour of the object that has attracted you: this is the real Pratyáhára Yoga.
items.statement: Pratyahara Yoga (or Varnarghyadana) is the method of withdrawing the mind from crude attachments by consciously offering the specific colours of attractive mental objects to the Supreme.
items.title: Vibration, Form and Colour

items.qualifiers: contrasted with Buddhist and Astika schools
items.quote: The Charvaka school of philosophy believes in caturbhúta [four fundamental factors] only. This is also known as dehátmaváda [the doctrine that the body is everything]. This philosophy accepts caturbhúta , namely, earth, water, fire and air, that is, kśiti, apa, teja and marut [respectively]. According to Charvaka, caetanya [consciousness] came into existence by the combination of the four bhútas [fundamental factors], just as mixing lime and catechu produces a red colour.
items.statement: Charvaka philosophy recognizes only four fundamental material factors (caturbhuta) and direct perception (pratyaksa) as valid proof, denying ether, consciousness as an independent entity, rebirth, and karmic reaction.
items.title: Views of Other Faiths

items.quote: There are four sections in Buddhist Máyáváda [the Buddhist doctrine of illusion]: 1) pratyakśa váhya vastuváda [the doctrine of direct perception of external matter], or saotántrika darshana; 2) ánumeya váhya vastuváda [the doctrine of inferred perception of external matter], or vaebháśika darshana; 3) sarva shúnyaváda [the doctrine of nihilism], or mádhyamika darshana; and 4) kśańika vijiṋánaváda [the doctrine of transience], or Baoddha yogácára .
items.statement: Buddhist Mayavada comprises four distinct philosophical branches: Sautantrika (direct perception of external matter), Vaebhasika (inferred perception of external matter), Madhyamika (sarva shunyavada), and Baoddha Yogacara (ksanika vijnanavada).
items.title: Views of Other Faiths

items.qualifiers: refutation of dualist claims of eternal distinctness
items.quote: Thus in the final stage of spiritual elevation dualism cannot survive. Even if someone says that he or she loves to eat sugar, still dualism cannot survive. That is why one should never think, “Parama Puruśa is so vast and I am only an ordinary human being.” This is almost blasphemy. A drop of water in the ocean is small, no doubt, but it resides within the depths of the mighty ocean. Similarly, a human being may be but an ordinary mortal, but he or she has the capacity to become one with Parama Puruśa. When one draws close to Parama Puruśa, one merges in Him whether one likes it or not.
items.statement: In the ultimate culmination of spiritual realization, dualism cannot survive because prolonged ideational proximity inevitably dissolves the individual point into oneness with the Supreme.
items.title: Vraja Krśńa and Dvaetaváda (Discourse 17)

items.qualifiers: thematic distinction of Krsna's two missions
items.quote: Lord Krśńa’s role is divided into two main parts – one is Shrii Krśńa, Vraja Krśńa; and the other is Krśńa the king of Mathura. The natures and jurisdictions of the duties of the two aspects were different, hence the roles also were different. People in general could not become as easily intimate or familiar with the king Krśńa – Párthasárathi Krśńa – as they could be with Krśńa of Vrindavana. Vraja Krśńa was a sweet personality, and that sweetness was mixed with spirituality; whereas Krśńa the king was a tough personality, but that toughness was also mixed with spirituality.
items.statement: Krsna's life embodies two distinct divine roles: Vraja Krsna, characterized by sweetness and spiritual intimacy, and Parthasarathi Krsna, characterized by toughness, righteous battle, and social reconstruction.
items.title: Vraja Krśńa and Párthasárathi Krśńa – 1 (Discourse 1)

items.qualifiers: core epistemological and spiritual distinction between the two roles
items.quote: The one wished to lead humanity to the highest realization through aparokśa anubhúti, while the other wished to lead humanity to that highest state of human excellence first through parokśa anubhúti and only then through aparokśa anubhúti. The difference is very vast indeed. The resoluteness, the firmness, that is found in Párthasárathi Krśńa is conspicuously absent in Vraja Krśńa. Similarly, virtues that are found in Vraja Krśńa are totally absent in Párthasárathi Krśńa.
items.statement: Vraja Krsna guides humanity to the highest realization directly through devotion and direct experience (aparoksa anubhuti), whereas Parthasarathi Krsna leads humanity first through struggle, intellect, and indirect experience (paroksa anubhuti) before reaching direct realization.
items.title: Vraja Krśńa and Párthasárathi Krśńa – 2 (Discourse 2)

items.qualifiers: philosophical definition of Radha as a psychological stance
items.quote: When the jiivabháva [microcosmic bearing] becomes pinnacled and advances towards Parama Puruśa to the complete exclusion of all other thoughts, becomes “I don’t want anything of this world, I want only Parama Puruśa, the Supreme Entity,” it is termed “Rádhá”. This is the expression of the single-minded devotion of the microcosmic mind.
items.statement: Radha bhava represents the pinnacled, one-pointed state of the microcosmic mind that rejects all transient worldly pursuits to seek only Parama Purusa.
items.title: Vraja Krśńa and Sáḿkhya Philosophy (Discourse 7)

items.quote: The fundamental difference between Vishiśt́ádvaetaváda and Vishuddha Advaetaváda is that Vishiśt́ádvaetaváda is qualified, or attributional. The difference lies in the fact that in Vishiśt́ádvaetaváda, the world has not been discarded as Máyá, and Parama Puruśa has been accepted as the nucleus of the universe.
items.statement: Vishistadvaetavada differs fundamentally from Vishuddha Advaetavada by not dismissing the world as Maya and by recognizing Parama Purusa as the active Cosmic Nucleus.
items.title: Vraja Krśńa and Vishiśt́ádvaetaváda (Discourse 15)

items.quote: Puruśa and Prakrti are avinábhávii. Puruśatattva remains as the fundamental substance, as well as the witnessing entity, while Prakrtitattva is responsible for creating the countless number of entities. Tvameko dvitvamápannah Shivashaktivibhágasah – “You are one, called Brahma or Parama Puruśa. Your one side is Puruśa, or Citishakti, and the other is Máyá, or Prakrti.” Essentially, He is one, like a sheet of paper.
items.statement: Purusa and Prakrti are avinabhavii (inseparably connected like two sides of a single sheet of paper), making the Mayavada claim of an unreal creative principle ontologically absurd.
items.title: Vraja Krśńa and Vishuddha Advaetaváda – 3 (Discourse 12)

items.quote: The rágánugá bhakta says, “Why do I love the Lord, my Vrajagopála, my Parama Puruśa? Because my love for Him gives Him joy and from this I get joy.” This is rágánugá bhakti. Rágátmiká is somewhat different from rágánugá. The rágátmiká bhakta says: “I love Parama Puruśa because I want to give Him ánandam. I don’t care whether or not I get ánandam. My only desire is to give Him joy through my love.
items.statement: In aesthetic science, raganuga bhakti involves both giving and receiving joy from Parama Purusa, whereas ragatmika bhakti seeks exclusively to give joy to Parama Purusa without concern for personal joy.
items.title: Vrajagopála and Aesthetic Science (Discourse 25)

items.quote: There is mutual attraction everywhere. A tiny ant attracts a large entity, and the large entity attracts the tiny ant. When in a sentimental flow of devotion a person thinks, “I am attracting the vast universe, including Parama Puruśa, and I am also being attracted,” this conscious feeling of mutual attraction is termed bhakti in psychological parlance.
items.statement: In psychological terms, bhakti is the conscious feeling of mutual sentimental attraction between the finite microcosm and the infinite Macrocosm.
items.title: Vrajagopála and Bhaktitattva (Discourse 21)

items.qualifiers: core psychological principle of mental ideation
items.quote: The human mind can be compared to these ayogaváhá letters because it, too, cannot exist alone but always remains attached to some object or other. Suppose you are walking along a road without looking at the houses, animals, traffic, etc. Does this mean that your mind is disassociated from all objects? Not at all. You may be thinking that if you don’t hurry up the ration shop will be closed. So the ration shop is your mental object. You are unable to keep your mind in a state of objectlessness.
items.statement: The human mind cannot remain objectless and functions like ayogavaha letters, requiring continuous attachment to physical, psychic, or spiritual objects.
items.title: Vyatireka – 1

items.qualifiers: It is not always the case that kalá is transformed into káśt́há
items.quote: It is called vyatireka because when kalá is getting transformed into káśt́há (it is not always the case that kalá shall be transformed into káśt́há ), sometimes káśt́há becomes smaller than the kalá , while at other times, under the pressure of káśt́há , the subsequent kalá becomes larger than its normal state. That is why the state of vyatireka is very perplexing.
items.statement: Vyatireka is the stage of spiritual and psychological development where control is gained over certain thoughts or propensities but not over others, as systaltic flow (kalá) transforms into linear flow (káśt́há).
items.title: Vyatireka – the Stage of Control

items.qualifiers: Obstacles appear more from within than without
items.quote: In the stage of vyatireka the obstacles appear more from within than from without. These obstacles are psychic in nature. For example, when in the course of sadhana one attains the state of yatamána , then obstacles appear from all sides. Family members create obstructions. The environ-ment creates obstructions. But in the stage of vyatireka there is hardly any external obstruction. The disorder is internal.
items.statement: In the stage of yatamána obstacles are primarily external, whereas in the stage of vyatireka obstacles are primarily internal and psychic.
items.title: Vyatireka – the Stage of Control

items.qualifiers: Fertility is safe if subterranean water is above 20-25 feet, but drops below 50 feet cause barrenness
items.quote: Well irrigation causes the level of the water-table to drop, while the continuous use of well irrigation dries up the subterranean flow of water. Initially the effects of continuous well irrigation may not be easy to perceive, but eventually a fertile region will be transformed into a desert. In fact, if the subterranean water level stays at above twenty to twenty-five feet, the surface vegetation will not be affected, but if it drops below fifty feet, the surface of the earth will become a barren wasteland.
items.statement: Intensive deep tube well irrigation causes severe ecological damage, including falling water tables, desertification, and soil salinity from harmful minerals.
items.title: Water Conservation

items.quote: Why do droughts occur? What are the most important causes of drought? There are three main causes. The first is the wanton destruction of plants or indiscriminate deforestation, the second is low pressure systems over oceans and big seas, and the third is sudden changes in the angular movement of the sun and other celestial bodies like comets, nebulae and galaxies.
items.statement: Droughts are triggered by three primary causes: deforestation, oceanic low-pressure systems, and sudden changes in the angular movement of celestial bodies.
items.title: Water Conservation

items.quote: In Tantra, there is hardly one percent theory; ninety-nine percent is practice. And you also know that a good theory may not help a person, it is practice that counts.
items.statement: Tantra is distinguished from theoretical systems by giving primacy to practice, where ninety-nine percent is practice and theory succeeds practice.
items.title: What Are You?

items.qualifiers: Only for Parama Puruśa versus both
items.quote: And that is why you may use the word namaste only for Parama Puruśa, but namaskára for both Parama Puruśa and the jiiva [unit being].
items.statement: The term 'namaste' is reserved exclusively for Parama Puruśa, whereas 'namaskára' can be used for both Parama Puruśa and unit beings (jiivas).
items.title: What Are You?

items.qualifiers: Sorrow is not a personal entity
items.quote: Where did this universe come from – what is the source of its emanation? Sorrow is not a personal entity; hence out of sorrow nothing can be created. But Ánandam or the Infinite Happiness is a personal Entity. Parama Puruśa in His eternal stance is ánandasvarúpa, the embodiment of bliss.
items.statement: Sorrow cannot be the source of creation because it is not a personal entity, whereas Ánandam is a personal Entity that manifests the universe.
items.title: What Are the Noble Truths?

items.qualifiers: Only until one receives Iśt́a mantra sádhaná
items.quote: Gáyattrii can be used till a person gets Iśt́a mantra sádhaná. Once a person gets the Iśt́a mantra sádhaná, he or she would not need gáyattrii.
items.statement: The Gáyatrii mantra serves as an aid only until one is initiated into Iśt́a mantra sádhaná, after which it is no longer required.
items.title: What Do You Want?

items.quote: The word dharma signifies “property”. The English word for it is “nature”, “characteristic” or “property”. The nature of fire is to burn or produce heat. It is the characteristic or property of fire and is also termed the nature of fire. Similarly, the dharma or nature of a human being is to seek the Cosmic Entity.
items.statement: Dharma signifies the innate property or fundamental characteristic of an entity; for human beings, it is the quest for and realization of the Cosmic Entity.
items.title: What Is Dharma?

items.quote: The microscopic fraction of a wave radiated from an object and received by the indriyas is called tanmátra or inference.
items.statement: Tanmátra is the microscopic fraction of a wave radiated from an object and received by sensory and motor organs.
items.title: What Is Dharma?

items.qualifiers: Absence of logic and intellectual debate
items.quote: What is dogma? Where there is no logic, where there is no support of intellectuality, where there is no debate and free discussion, but there is only a severe imposition forcing people to accept something, there is dogma.
items.statement: Dogma is an imposed belief system that lacks logical foundation, intellectual support, and free discussion.
items.title: What Is Dogma?

items.qualifiers: Measured in mental terms of pleasure and pain, not identical physical events
items.quote: It is important to clarify here that the actual form of suffering is not predetermined. It cannot be said what might be the actual reaction of a particular action. For example, it is not preordained that if one commits theft his things of the same value will be stolen as a reaction. The suffering is measured in terms of mental suffering to the extent which was inflicted on others by stealing their property. Thus the measure of experiencing the result of an action is mental and is in terms of pleasure and pain, and the actual form of experience has relatively no importance.
items.statement: Reactions to actions (karmaphala) are not preordained in specific physical forms, but rather as equivalent magnitudes of mental pleasure or pain.
items.title: What Is My Relation with the Universe and the Cosmic Entity?

items.qualifiers: Mind requires a physical brain to function or experience reaction
items.quote: After death the mind is incapable of any action due to the lack of its physical base, the brain, and has to be reborn for experiencing reactions of its previous actions. Hence the concept of hell or heaven where human beings are supposed to proceed after death is entirely incorrect.
items.statement: Rebirth is inescapable because the non-functional mind after physical death requires a physical brain to express and exhaust its potential reactions (saḿskáras), thereby disproving the existence of independent ghosts.
items.title: What Is My Relation with the Universe and the Cosmic Entity?

items.qualifiers: Neither absolute truth nor pure falsehood
items.quote: Hence the universe has to be considered as neither true nor false; it is something between the two; it is relative truth.
items.statement: The crude universe exists as a thought-projection (kalpaná) in the Cosmic Mind (Saguńa Brahma), making it relative truth (satyápekśikam) rather than absolute reality or pure illusion.
items.title: What Is This World?

items.qualifiers: State of bondage versus state of emancipation
items.quote: Before Saguńa Brahma became free from bondage, It was called Prajápati, and after It attained emancipation by sádhaná and became muktapuruśa, It was called Hirańyagarbha.
items.statement: Prior to attaining emancipation through sádhaná, Saguńa Brahma was designated Prajápati; upon attaining emancipation as a muktapuruśa, It is called Hirańyagarbha.
items.title: What Is This World?

items.qualifiers: Spiritual yoga derives specifically from yunj
items.quote: The root verb is “Yunj,” not “Yuj”, and the word Yoga is also derived from that root “Yunj”. Here “Yunj” verb means to unify, not to add, but to unify. Yuj means to add and Yunj means to unify. Suppose there is sugar and there is water. Sugar plus water, what will happen? Sugar will unify with water. You won’t find sugar in a separate form after this unification.
items.statement: Spiritual yoga derives from the Sanskrit root 'yunj' meaning unification, distinct from the root 'yuj' which means mere arithmetical addition.
items.title: What Is Yoga?

items.quote: In the human mind there are 50 propensities controlling 20 directional movements or propensities. So in all, there are 50 x 20. How many? 50 x 20 = 1000. So human expressions – human intellectual or human psychic expressions are 1000 in number. Those 1000 propensities are controlled by the pineal gland in the human body.
items.statement: The human mind possesses fifty propensities functioning across twenty directional expressions, generating one thousand psychic expressions governed by the pineal gland.
items.title: What Is Yoga?

items.qualifiers: Higher than mukti; permanent release from creation
items.quote: Freedom from the bondage of Prakrti is the merger with the Non-Qualified Supreme Entity or attainment of the supreme rank, and that is termed mokśa. Merger with the Non-Qualified Brahma relieves one from the influences of the Supreme Prakrti and She, not being able to influence That, will be incapable of dragging one into the creation.
items.statement: Mukti is merger into Saguńa Brahma which may re-enter the cycle of creation, whereas mokśa (kaevalya mukti) is permanent non-qualified merger into Nirguńa Brahma beyond all Prakrtic influence.
items.title: What Is the Aim of Humanity?

items.qualifiers: Prakrti is weaker than Puruśa in Nirguńa Brahma
items.quote: Puruśa in Nirguńa Brahma is not qualified in spite of the presence of Prakrti, fully awake. That Prakrti is weaker than Puruśa in Nirguńa Brahma can be the only reason for this. She is less powerful and so is unable to qualify Puruśa. This is how Prakrti and Puruśa have existed in Brahma for eternity. Puruśa, therefore, is by nature more powerful than Prakrti and is the transcendental entity and Prakrti is the innate principle.
items.statement: Puruśa and Prakrti are co-eternal and non-causal, but Puruśa is inherently more powerful, rendering Prakrti unable to qualify Him in the state of Nirguńa Brahma.
items.title: What Is the Cosmic Entity?

items.quote: “Accident” is a misnomer. No effect can take place without a cause. When a person receives an opportunity to do sádhaná, it is to be understood that the person is being allowed today to do sádhaná due to the good and virtuous deeds he or she performed in various past lives. The opportunity is the effect of the factors that lie behind it.
items.statement: Accident is a conceptual misnomer arising from ignorance of an event's causal factors, as no effect can occur in the universe without a cause.
items.title: What Is the Primary Cause of the Universe and Who Is the Only Object of Ideation?

items.qualifiers: When attempting to reform individuals with strong negative influence
items.quote: It is the duty of every human being to avoid wicked people. You may ask, “Can wicked people ever become virtuous?” Of course they can, but remember that only those people having greater psychic power than them should try to transform them. So what should you do? Instead of going alone, you should take five or ten friends with you so that your collective psychic strength will be greater than theirs.
items.statement: To effectively reform or interact with wicked people (durjanas), an individual must not go alone but must mobilize a collective whose combined psychic power exceeds that of the wrongdoers.
items.title: What Should Human Beings Do?

items.qualifiers: Spiritual anatomical location between pituitary and pineal glands
items.quote: It should be understood that this váráńasii does not refer to a particular city of Uttar Pradesh in India but to a point situated between the ájiṋá and sahasrára cakras, that is, between the pituitary and pineal glands. Spiritual aspirants, through the practice of sádhaná and with the help of the Divine Spirit, become established in that point, attaining great mental power and omniscience.
items.statement: Philosophically and spiritually, Váráńasii or Káshi does not denote the geographical city, but rather a luminous internal plexus located between the ájiṋá and sahasrára cakras.
items.title: Where Is Varanasi?

items.quote: The aspects of Bhágavata Dharma that make human beings unique are four in number: 1) Vistára or expansion, 2) rasa or flow, 3) sevá or service, 4) tadstithi or ensconcement in the Supreme.
items.statement: Bhágavata Dharma comprises four essential pillars: vistára (expansion), rasa (flow), sevá (service), and tadsthiti (ensconcement in the Supreme).
items.title: Where There Is Dharma There Is Iśt́a, and Where There Is Iśt́a There Is Victory

items.quote: Kuńt́há means “contraction.” For example, people are contracted in the cold; they are contracted out of fear or shame. So vaekuńt́ha is used in the sense of contraction having passed, that is, where the mind does not undergo any kind of contraction, where it is liberated, free, absorbed in the love of the Paramátmá . Where there is no kuńt́há it is vaekuńt́ha . Vaekuńt́ha does not mean a distant place.
items.statement: Vaekuńt́ha philosophically designates a psychic state free from contraction (kuńt́há) and absorbed in love of the Divine, rather than an external geographic heaven.
items.title: “Wherever My Devotees Sing”

items.quote: The part of the mind in which the “I” resides is called “guhá”. Here “guhá” does not mean a mountain cave but that innermost cavity within the human mind where the seer “I” lies hidden. And this seeing or witnessing entity of the small “I” is the very root of dharma. Who lies hidden in that innermost cavity of the existential “I” feeling? Parama Puruśa, of course.
items.statement: In spiritual scripture, 'guhá' refers not to a physical mountain cave, but to the innermost cavity of the existential 'I' feeling in the human mind where Parama Puruśa resides.
items.title: Which Is the Right Path?

items.qualifiers: Buddhitattva is an objective mental idea dependent on átman
items.quote: The individual entity of “I”, therefore, is not unit consciousness; it is buddhitattva, which is only a part of his or her mind.
items.statement: The human feeling of 'I' is not the unit consciousness (átman) itself, but buddhitattva, an abstract mental projection created by the qualifying influence of sentient Prakrti.
items.title: Who Am I and What Am I?

items.qualifiers: Derived from root verb gup meaning to give pleasure
items.quote: In Saḿskrta, the root verb “gup” means “to give pleasure to”, and the man who has developed this type of love for the Supreme is called “gopa.” “Gopayate yah sah gopae” – the one who gives pleasure to Lord Krśńa is “gopa.”
items.statement: A 'gopa' is defined through the Sanskrit root 'gup' as an advanced devotee whose exclusive desire is to impart joy to Parama Puruśa without seeking reciprocal pleasure.
items.title: Who Is Gopa?

items.quote: That muktidátá is known as Táraka Brahma in Saḿskrta (táraka = trae + ńak, the liberating faculty). The word táraka is prefixed only to His name and not to the name of Saguńa Brahma or Nirguńa Brahma or any other entity or entities.
items.statement: Táraka Brahma is the specific entity possessing the liberating faculty that bridges the unexpressed Supreme Consciousness and the expressed universe.
items.title: Who Is the Liberating Entity of Human Society

items.qualifiers: Subjugation of all 14 extroversial tendencies (six enemies and eight fetters)
items.quote: Brahmacarya means to introvert the extroversial tendencies of the mind and to devote it completely to Brahma. To understand the meaning of Brahmacarya clearly one should know what is meant by the extroversial tendencies of the mind and how these should be introverted.
items.statement: Brahmacarya is the practice of introverting extroversial mental propensities and keeping the mind continuously absorbed in Brahma, rather than merely observing physical celibacy.
items.title: Why Are People Afraid of Intuitional Practice?

items.quote: If human suffering originates at a particular point in time and then goes away for the time being, that momentary relief is called tráńa. But that suffering may come back again. You feel hungry, you eat something, and you feel relieved for the moment. But it is sure that you will feel hungry again after some time. If, on the other hand, there is suffering and it goes away never to come again, that is called paritráńa.
items.statement: Tráńa represents temporary relief from suffering that may recur, whereas paritráńa represents permanent liberation from suffering that never returns.
items.title: Why Does Supreme Consciousness Descend?

items.qualifiers: Specific to Dáyabhága vs Mitákśará legal systems
items.quote: The rest of India is governed by the Mitákśará law of inheritance, which is based on the Manu Saḿhitá ( 3 ) [as interpreted] by Vyasadeva. Bengal is governed by the Dáyabhága system ( 4 ) which is based on the interpretation of the Manu Saḿhitá by Jiimútaváhana. In northern India, sons are entitled to ancestral property even during the lifetime of their fathers. In fact, the children, even when they are in their mothers’ wombs, acquire the right to property. When they are grown up, they can get their share by filing lawsuits against their fathers. But this is not permissible in Dáyabhága laws. As long as the fathers are alive, they [fathers] are the sole owners of the ancestral property.
items.statement: Bengal's historical Dáyabhága inheritance system based on Jiimútaváhana empowered fathers with complete ownership of ancestral property during their lifetime, distinct from northern India's Mitákśará system where sons acquired ownership rights at birth.
items.title: Women of Bengal – Excerpt A

items.qualifiers: Application of force vs tremendous force
items.quote: [Accelerating the movement of the social cycle by the application of force is called “evolution”.]
items.statement: Accelerating the social cycle through the application of force is defined as evolution (krántih), whereas using tremendous force constitutes revolution (viplavah).
items.title: Word-for-Word Sútra Translations

items.qualifiers: Microscopic fractions created by vibrational clash
items.quote: [Tanmátras (microscopic fractions of bhútas, or fundamental factors) represent the bhútas, are carried by the bhútas, and are created by vibrations from the clash within the bhútas.]
items.statement: Tanmátras are microscopic fractions of fundamental factors created by clash vibrations and serving as the media through which matter is recognized.
items.title: Word-for-Word Sútra Translations

items.quote: Ordinarily Yajiṋa is of four kinds: Bhúta Yajiṋa, Nr Yajiṋa, Pitr Yajiṋa and Adhyátma Yajiṋa. Of these four Yajiṋas, the first three, namely Bhúta, Nr, and Pitr Yajiṋas, are psycho-physical, that is, both mental and physical, but Adhyátma Yajiṋa is one hundred percent internal.
items.statement: Yajiṋa (action) is categorized into four classes: Bhúta Yajiṋa, Nr Yajiṋa, Pitr Yajiṋa (all psycho-physical), and Adhyátma Yajiṋa (purely internal).
items.title: Yajiṋa and Karmaphala

items.quote: In the course of sádhaná the sádhaka [spiritual practitioner] has to pass through four stages: yatamána, vyatireka, ekendriya and vashiikára.
items.statement: The four progressive stages of spiritual development correspond to successive inward mergers: yatamána (indriyas to citta), vyatireka (citta to aham), ekendriya (aham to mahat), and vashiikára (mahat to Self).
items.title: Yatamána, Vyatireka, Ekendriya and Vashiikára

items.qualifiers: Perpetual endeavor linking finite and infinite
items.quote: What is mysticism? Mysticism is the never-ending endeavour to find out a link between the finite and the Infinite. I do not find any proper synonym in Bengali. I call it mystikváda . Some call it rahasyaváda . But it is not logically sound.
items.statement: Mysticism is defined as the perpetual human endeavor to discover the link between the finite and the Infinite.
items.title: Yatamána – the Stage of Perseverance

items.quote: This is called rágátmika bhakti and is the devotion of the highest category. One should possess this type of devotion. “I will do those actions which will make Parama Puruśa happy, but which may or may not bring joy to me.” Human beings should act in this way.
items.statement: Rágánuga bhakti seeks personal joy by pleasing the Divine, whereas rágátmika bhakti seeks solely to please the Divine regardless of whether it brings pleasure or pain to the practitioner.
items.title: “Ye Yathá Máḿ Prapadyante”

items.quote: It is said that under five circumstances the mind becomes steady – Kśipta, Múŕha, Vikśipta, Ekágra and Nirodha.
items.statement: Mind achieves steadiness under five distinct mental conditions: kśipta, múŕha, vikśipta, ekágra, and nirodha.
items.title: Yoga and Bhakti

items.qualifiers: Fifty primary sounds/colors expanding to one thousand expressions
items.quote: These vibrations, representing some action or some object, are called acoustic expressions. A person when angry speaks in a certain way, but the same person in a normal state speaks in a different way. The voice of the angry man has undergone a clear change from its normal state to an abnormal one. Likewise, each and every propensity has its own vibration, and each vibration has a certain colour and sound. The sounds of the fifty propensities constitute our language. These alphabet sounds – a, á, ka, kha [the first vowels and the first consonants or the Sanskrit alphabet] – are our acoustic expressions.
items.statement: The fifty alphabet sounds (varńamálá) directly represent acoustic roots (biija mantras) corresponding to the internal vibrations and colors of human propensities.
items.title: Yoga and Tantra

items.qualifiers: Mental ideation in meditation reverses conventional subject-object perception
items.quote: Therefore, when you repeat your iśt́a mantra, or when you ideate, you should remember that, in fact, you are the object and Parama Puruśa is the subject. That is, in meditation you do not see Parama Puruśa, but Parama Puruśa sees you.
items.statement: In spiritual practices such as repeating the ishta mantra or ideating, the practitioner should understand themselves as the mental object and Parama Purusa as the Supreme Subjectivity watching them.
items.title: You Are Not Helpless

items.quote: Actions and reactions are inseparably associated. Wherever there is an action, there is a corresponding reaction, because every action gets either reflected or refracted. The wave produced by the action will be either reflected or refracted. Both reflection and refraction are reactions.
items.statement: Every action inevitably generates a corresponding reaction because the mental or physical wave produced by an action is naturally reflected or refracted.
items.title: “You Have the Right to Action Only”

items.qualifiers: Etymological derivation from root kr plus suffix man
items.quote: The word karma is derived from the root verb kr plus the inflection man. You grasp only a particular portion, a partial expression of the eternal flow of time – that is karma.
items.statement: Karma is defined as a partial expression or segment of the eternal flow of time that involves a change of position or motion.
items.title: “You Have the Right to Action Only”

items.quote: The style, the system in which Prakrti [the Operative Principle] operates is known as nature. There is a style of singing, of dancing; there is a style for doing each and every action. The style of the work of the Operative Principle is known as nature. How can the style create? Only the One whose style it is can create.
items.statement: Nature is not an independent creator, but the style or system through which Prakrti operates according to the desire of Parama Purusa.
items.title: You Live According to God's Desire

items.quote: In all the Puranas [mythological scriptures] over 1200 years old, such as the Márkańd́eya Puráńa, the Brhat Nandikeshvara Puráńa, the Devii Puráńa and the Káliká Puráńa, the deity was invariably eight-armed. In those days in Maharashtra also, the custom of worshipping the eight-armed goddess was also popular. The worship of the ten-armed goddess Durgá was first introduced by Kansa Narayana, king of Taherpur of Rajsahi District of Bangladesh.
items.statement: The worship of the ten-armed Durga deity was initially introduced by King Kansa Narayana of Taherpur in the Rajsahi District of Bangladesh, whereas earlier puranic traditions knew only the eight-armed deity.
items.title: You Must Live Glorious Lives

items.quote: When the bondage of the static principle disappears, the aspirant enjoys a particular nature of bliss. There, that is, in that stage, there remains no static bondage, but the bondages of the mutative and sentient principle are there. Then the bondage of the mutative principle disappears. And finally, when the bondage of the sentient principle disappears, man becomes one with his object of ideation.
items.statement: The loosening and elimination of the static, mutative, and sentient principles in occult practice correspond respectively to the spiritual stages of dasha/bhava, bhava samadhi, and mahabhava.
items.title: You Should Do Accordingly

items.quote: By dint of japa kriyá, japa, one attains the attributional stage of samádhi, and by dint of one’s dhyána one attains the non-attributional stance of samádhi, which is the goal of each and every individual of this Universe.
items.statement: Japa kriya leads to qualified (attributional) samadhi, whereas dhyana leads to unqualified (non-attributional / nirvikalpa) samadhi.
items.title: You Should Do Accordingly

items.qualifiers: Unconditional surrender as the sole metric
items.quote: Devotion means unconditional self-surrender. The measure of devotion is the amount of this self-surrender. One who has more of it, is a greater devotee than one who has less of it.
items.statement: Devotion is strictly defined as unconditional self-surrender, measured entirely by the degree of surrender.
items.title: Your Ideal in Life

items.quote: Whatever you consider as the summum bonum of life is sat. And when you direct all your faculties and sentiments towards the attainment of this goal, this is called shrat. And the feeling associated with this is called shraddhá.
items.statement: Shraddha is defined as the directing of all faculties and sentiments toward sat (the summum bonum of life).
items.title: Your Personal Relationship with God

items.qualifiers: In the relative world only mitram exists among mortals; God is bandhu, suhrda, and sakha
items.quote: Atyágo sahano bandhu Sadaevánumatam suhrda Ekaḿ kriyaḿ bhaven mitram Samapráńah sakhá smrtah.
items.statement: Sanskrit distinguishes four types of friend: bandhu (one who cannot tolerate separation), suhrda (one with whom there is never a difference of opinion), mitram (a colleague sharing the same duty), and sakha (two bodies sharing one mental body).
items.title: Your Real Friend

items.quote: The Village, Upabhukti, Bhukti, and the Provincial or State or National, Committees will each contribute 1/8 of its income to the committee immediately higher than it, and the remaining 7/8 will be spent in its own territory on public welfare and the propagation of dharma.
items.statement: Subordinate committees in Ananda Marga must contribute one-eighth of their income to the committee immediately above them and spend the remaining seven-eighths on local public welfare and dharma propagation.
items.title: Your Various Organizations

items.quote: The blind mind, any mind, functions in ten directions; púrva, pashcima, uttara, dakśińa, úrddha, adhah – the six lateral directions, known as “pradisha” in Saḿskrta; and Iishána, Vayu, Agni and Naerta the four corners, called “anudisha” in Saḿskrta. So there are ten directions, six plus four. And the blind mind functions in all ten directions with the help of all ten indriyas. Ten times ten equals one hundred; so the blind mind, Dhrtaráśt́ra, has one hundred sons.
items.statement: In the allegorical interpretation of the Mahabharata, the blind mind Dhritarashtra has one hundred sons representing the mind's operation in ten directions through ten sensory and motor indriyas.
items.title: Yours Is a Never-Ending Fight

items.qualifiers: Internal esoteric mapping of Mahabharata characters
items.quote: The lowermost is kśititattva, i.e., Sahadeva. “Sahadeva” means “abode”, the abode for human habitation. Then the next one up is Nakula. “Kulaḿ násti yasya” – i.e., jalam, apatattva, the aquatic phase. Then Arjuna, i.e., energy kriyá shakti, fire the luminous phase, the luminous structure. Then gaseous, i.e., váyuputra, bhiima: “pavananandana bhiima.” And finally the ethereal level – Yudhiśt́hiira.
items.statement: The five Pandavas allegorically represent the five physical and subtle phases (tattvas) of self-knowledge through which a spiritual seeker progresses: Sahadeva (solid/kshititattva), Nakula (aquatic/apatattva), Arjuna (luminous/tejas), Bhima (gaseous/vayu), and Yudhisthira (ethereal/vyoma).
items.title: Yours Is a Never-Ending Fight

items.qualifiers: Given in a general darshan discourse context
items.quote: He said there are three kinds of laziness—physical, mental, and spiritual. Physical laziness is when we want to do something but we put it off. Spiritual laziness is when we postpone our lessons until 'later.' Mental laziness, Baba said, is a "lack of proper planning."
items.statement: Laziness is classified into three categories: physical (putting off action), spiritual (postponing spiritual lessons), and mental (lack of proper planning).
items.title: 101 Baba Stories

items.qualifiers: First demonstration and instruction given in Patna
items.quote: He said that He reintroduced tandava in 1971 after about 7,000 years ago in Shiva's time. He said the dance is for males only, so the women were feeling left out. "So in order to remove their pain, today I am introducing kaosikii," He said.
items.statement: Kaoshikii was first introduced by Shrii Shrii Anandamurti in 1978 in Patna as a dance suitable for women, after tandava had been reintroduced in 1971.
items.title: 101 Baba Stories

items.qualifiers: Nirvikalpa results in physical rigor within seconds unlike regular death
items.quote: So you should carefully note the difference that in savikalpa samadhi the mind still exists in its most expanded state as one with the Cosmic Mind. In that state of spiritual trance the body is still alive, as the mind still exists. In nirvikalpa samadhi, however, the mind ceases to exist. Hence, the body is no longer alive.
items.statement: Savikalpa samadhi is the absorption of the mind into Saguna Brahma (Cosmic Mind) where expanded mental existence remains, whereas in nirvikalpa samadhi the mind dissolves into Nirguna Brahma and ceases to exist entirely.
items.title: advent_of_a_mystery_compressed

items.qualifiers: Possesses no physical body with five fundamental factors
items.quote: Normally a living being is composed of five fundamental factors — ethereal, aerial, luminous, liquid and solid. But if any entity is composed of only three factors - luminous, aerial, and ethereal - and has no solid or liquid factor, then that entity is called a “luminous body”.
items.statement: A luminous body is an entity composed exclusively of three fundamental factors (ethereal, aerial, and luminous) devoid of liquid and solid factors.
items.title: advent_of_a_mystery_compressed

items.qualifiers: conditional upon keeping the spiritual ideation of the second lesson in mind throughout eating
items.quote: If you take your second lesson before eating and keep the spiritual ideation of the second lesson in your mind till you finish eating the food, you will not feel any negative effects from the it.
items.statement: Practicing Madhuvidya and maintaining its ideation before and while eating shields a spiritual aspirant from the negative mental effects of sentient food prepared or offered with impure thoughts.
items.title: advent_of_a_mystery_compressed

items.qualifiers: applies specifically to a Tantra sadhaka willing to struggle against mental weaknesses
items.quote: The guru places him in a situation where he feels sheer terror, like in a cremation ground, alone in the darkness of the new moon night. Such a place generates tremendous fear in the person, and this releases a great amount of energy. Through a special tantric process the intense energy generated due to fear is sublimated into spiritual force.
items.statement: Tantric sadhana accelerates spiritual progress by having the guru place the aspirant in terrifying situations to sublimate the energy generated by fear into spiritual force.
items.title: advent_of_a_mystery_compressed

items.qualifiers: distinguishing stages of savikalpa samadhi up to ajina chakra from nirvikalpa samadhi beyond it
items.quote: Salokya to sarshthi are the different stages of savikalpa samadhi. The ultimate purpose of yoga is to withdraw one's mind from all mundane objects and to direct all of one's physical, psychic and spiritual propensities towards Parama Purusha.
items.statement: Savikalpa samadhi ranges through the stages from salokya to sarshthi with dualism progressively diminishing, whereas nirvikalpa samadhi is the non-dual state of total mental dissolution where the mind ceases to exist.
items.title: advent_of_a_mystery_compressed

items.qualifiers: categorization based on Baba's philosophical analysis of asteya
items.quote:
Baba also gave a detailed analysis of the meaning of asteya or non-stealing and described four situations that could be categorized as theft:

a) The first is physical or material theft. Under ordinary circumstances, those who steal material objects are thieves. But thieves are not only those who flee with stolen objects or commit armed robbery. Whatever is unjustifiably taken from someone else by using brute force, arms, one's intellect, or one's power and authority, or by any other means is tantamount to theft because these actions are committed with the intention of taking the property of others deceitfully. Baba further pointed out that if a person who renders a service during an emergency, for example medical service, takes advantage of the situation by overcharging the helpless victims of a tragedy, such an action is also tantamount to stealing. And if a trader hoards essential goods in times of scarcity, overcharges customers or indulges in black marketeering, such actions should also be regarded as theft.

b) The second category is psychic theft. In this case, a person does not actually take an object that belongs to others due to fear of the law or of public criticism. However, as he planned to steal it, such action is considered as mental theft and is a violation of the principle of asteya.
items.statement: The principle of asteya (non-stealing) covers four categories: physical/material theft, psychic/mental planning to steal, depriving others of their rightful dues, and mentally planning to deprive others of their dues.
items.title: advent_of_a_mystery_compressed

items.qualifiers: occurs gradually through consistent and regular sadhana
items.quote: At the time of doing sadhana, you are hitting the conscious mind, when in this process the layer of the conscious mind becomes subtle. The effect of this hitting of the mantra goes to the subconscious mind. In this condition, the sadhaka starts hearing or seeing wonderful experiences and starts feeling some kind of peace in the mind. By further regular practice of iista mantra, the subconscious mind also starts getting subtler, and the strokes of the mantra start affecting the unconscious mind. The sadhaka then starts knowing the events of the future. Gradually, as one starts getting established in Iishvara pranidhana, one becomes omniscient
items.statement: Iishvara pranidhana practice progressively penetrates the conscious, subconscious, and unconscious layers of the mind, ultimately leading to omniscience.
items.title: Ananda Katha - Acarya Nagina

items.qualifiers: applies only to sadhakas who have attained absolute perfection and exhausted all samskaras
items.quote: After intense meditation, when sadhakas attain the final goal of sadhana – absolute perfection – if they have also exhausted all their samskaras, they continue to live on the planet with the same bodies, or they obtain new bodies in order to serve creation. The samkalpa to serve creation for a fixed period of time becomes a new samskara for them. They stay on the planet for that fixed time and then depart. Such perfected beings are called ‘nirman citta’
items.statement: A 'nirman citta' person is an absolutely perfected sadhaka who has exhausted all past samskaras but retains a physical body by taking a deliberate samkalpa to serve creation for a fixed period.
items.title: Ananda Katha - Acarya Nagina

items.qualifiers: practiced during guru puja and varnaghyadana at the conclusion of sadhana
items.quote: 'Varna' means 'colour', and every tendency or vrtti of the mental world has its own colour. A person is most attracted to the colour of whatever vrtti dominates the mind at a given moment. Therefore, it is advised to offer the flower of your chosen colour. At the time of guru puja the color of the most dominant propensity at that time will naturally come to the mind of the sadhaka. By offering that colour to the guru one will get rid of that vrtti or propensity.
items.statement: In the practice of varnaghyadana, offering a flower of the color that corresponds to one's dominant mental propensity to the guru rids the sadhaka of that specific propensity.
items.title: Ananda Katha - Acarya Nagina

items.qualifiers: defined in the context of the Buddha's eightfold path and yogic duty
items.quote: Samyak karma'nta means that perfection in action is attained when each work is done well and finished properly. There should be no defect or laxity in its performance. Its beginning, middle and end should all be done meticulously.
items.statement: Samyak karma'nta is the proper and meticulous execution of an action from beginning to end, carried out entirely in the spirit of universal welfare without defect or laxity.
items.title: Anandamurtijii As I Knew Him

items.qualifiers: applies universally to sentient persons undertaking practical action
items.quote: He said that in order to attain success in the practical field of action a sentient person should invariably possess two qualities – absolute sincerity and high degree of competence. Both are admirable qualities. Sincerity is more important that competence. Someone may have abilities and may be competent, but if he or she is insincere in speech and action, he or she will never attain success. And if one has only mediocre talents, but if one is sincere, he or she will finally succeed.
items.statement: In the practical field of action, absolute sincerity is more important than competence for attaining ultimate success.
items.title: Anandamurtijii As I Knew Him

items.quote: The derivative meaning of the word niiti or morality is that which has in it the principle of leading. It is the starting point on the path of sa'dhana', which is the persistent effort to establish spiritual contact or communion with Supreme Entity. But this is not the only significance of morality. Morality is endowed with the distinct faculty of leading human beings towards perfection. If morality fails to provide human beings with sufficient provision to move towards perfection, then it does not deserve to be called morality. Because morality must have an inspirational quality, it cannot afford to lose its dynamic nature by limiting itself to a specific time, place and person.
items.statement: Morality (niiti) is a dynamic living force whose inherent principle is to lead and inspire human beings toward the predetermined limit of perfection and supreme subtlety.
items.title: Anandamurtijii As I Knew Him

items.qualifiers: addressed to a judge presiding over capital cases
items.quote: Before passing sentence, meditate for some time and take second lesson. Then contemplate the case and decide on a sentence. If you meditate and take your second lesson, then you will give the correct judgment. But you should never give capital punishment.
items.statement: Before deciding a legal sentence, a judge should meditate, practice second lesson, and contemplate the case, while strictly avoiding the death penalty to allow criminals scope for rectification.
items.title: Ashutosh Baba

items.qualifiers: a specialized yogic dance highly conducive to spiritual progress
items.quote: Then Baba explained about Rudra tandava, which is where the leg is lifted above the trikuti. It is very rarely seen and very good for a sadhaka’s spiritual progress. Lord Shiva used to practice Rudra tandava, and his avadhutas as well.
items.statement: Rudra tandava is a rare, elevated form of tandava dance practiced by Lord Shiva and his avadhutas in which the leg is raised above the level of the trikuti.
items.title: Ashutosh Baba

items.qualifiers: recounted by Baba regarding the historical use of ostriches
items.quote: He told us how in ancient times soldiers used to fight on ostriches, that they were capable of running faster than horses, nearly eighty kilometres per hour. “Sadly,” he said, “a day will come when this species will disappear from the earth. We should make every effort to save these birds so that future generations will have a chance to see them.”
items.statement: During ancient times, soldiers rode into combat on ostriches, which could run faster than horses at speeds approaching eighty kilometres per hour.
items.title: Ashutosh Baba

items.qualifiers: biological mechanism associated with regular tandava dance
items.quote: He counselled Arun to do a lot of tandava, which releases the male hormones, and gave them his blessing to have a child.
items.statement: The practice of tandava stimulates the release of male hormones.
items.title: Ashutosh Baba

items.qualifiers: fundamental distinction between two cadres of Tantric yogis
items.quote: The difference between kaola and Mahákaola is, the kaola raises his or her coiled serpentine, kulakuńd́alinii, through his or her sádhaná, and establishes the union [of] the fundamental negativity and the fundamental positivity; whereas in the case of the Mahákaola, the Mahákaola has the power to raise the kulakuńd́alinii of others also. A kaola can never raise the kulakuńd́alinii of others; he or she can raise his or her own kulakuńd́alinii. A Mahákaola can, if He so desires, raise the kulakuńd́alinii of others also.
items.statement: A Kaola is a spiritual practitioner who has raised their own kulakundalinii to the pineal gland, whereas a Mahakaola possesses the unique power to raise the kulakundalinii of others as well.
items.title: Baba in Maharlika

items.qualifiers: applies strictly to the Cosmological order of creation
items.quote: If there is any change in the comparative applied force of the centripetal and the centrifugal forces, then the cyclic order will undergo metamorphosis. This is the expression, and in that case it will take a parabolic form, a parabolic movement. The point where the parabolic and the elliptical figures touch each other – that tangential point – is Táraka Brahma as far as the Cosmological order is concerned.
items.statement: The Cosmological manifestation of Taraka Brahma is the tangential point of intersection where an altered elliptical cosmic cycle meets a parabolic movement.
items.title: Baba in Maharlika

items.qualifiers: framework analyzing why social and philosophical principles succeed or fail
items.quote:
The following four circumstances determine whether a set of principles will prove true and be materialized.

(1) Hypocritical psychology. Some principles are "ab initio" insincere and produced with hypocritical mental effort. They are never meant to be put into practice, they are only intended to exploit a situation, or a sentiment of the masses, and meant to befool the masses only.
items.statement: The four circumstances determining whether philosophical principles fail or materialize are hypocritical psychology, purely theoretical psychology detached from physical reality, inefficiency or lack of power to implement, and environmental mismatch.
items.title: Baba in Maharlika

items.quote: On another occasion Bábá talked about Dogma and Sentiment as follows: "Dogma is an established irrational idea" while "Sentiment is an outburst of psychic force."
items.statement: Dogma is an established irrational idea, whereas sentiment is an emotional outburst of psychic force.
items.title: Baba in Maharlika

items.qualifiers: etymological and philosophical reframing of politics/rajniti
items.quote: Rajnitti is raja of nitti, or king of the best principles - that is, those who are established in moral principles are fit for politics. It is not for the corrupt people. You know Ramchandra was known as Purusottama and he was an ideal king, so rajnitti is fit for him.
items.statement: Rajniti is the governance of the best moral principles ('raja of niti'), meaning that statecraft and politics are meant specifically for those established in moral principles.
items.title: Baba Loves All

items.qualifiers: defined by Baba using the analogy of worship atmosphere and concentrated meditation
items.quote: On another day in the same field Baba indicated the general area of the palm trees and said it is a siddha pitha and had a good vibration. I asked, "Baba, what is a siddha pitha?" "Where a person gets the siddhis (occult powers)," Baba replied and then gave the following illustration. "When you worship and use flowers and incense it creates an atmosphere and vibration that others can recognise as good when they enter that place. When a sadhaka sits in meditation in a particular place, that place becomes charged with spiritual vibration and when somebody gets siddhis then that place becomes very powerful and vibrated."
items.statement: A siddha pitha is a location charged with concentrated spiritual vibrations where a spiritual aspirant has attained occult powers (siddhis).
items.title: Baba Loves All

items.qualifiers: philosophical explanation of why evil and free choice exist in creation
items.quote: Suppose Paramapurusa makes a boundary of goodness and keeps all the people inside then all will become good and none will be bad. None can go out of this jurisdiction. But this is also a problem, for to remain in the bondage of goodness, means they cannot know the infinite. Their progress will be stopped. If there is no boundary people can go where they like, towards good or bad. Paramapurusa does not make any bondage of goodness because He does not want to stop the progress of those who desire liberation.
items.statement: Supreme Consciousness does not establish an absolute boundary of goodness because enclosing individuals within a boundary of goodness would restrict them to finite bondage and prevent them from realizing the infinite.
items.title: Baba Loves All

items.qualifiers: etymological derivation based on Sanskrit roots
items.quote: Anushasana is the Samskrta word for discipline. What is the meaning of Anushasana? Hitarthe shasanam iti anushasanam. ‘Hit’ means welfare or benefit. If anyone gives you any advice or rule for your benefit, then you follow it, that will be discipline. A ten year old boy may give some advice to an 80 year old man, but if it is for the older man's benefit, then he should heed it.
items.statement: Discipline (anushasana) means following instructions or advice that are specifically given for one's all-round welfare ('hitarthe shasanam iti anushasanam').
items.title: Baba Loves All

items.qualifiers: Human psychic growth being stopped is the explicit condition under which such restriction is called dogma.
items.quote: This is the specialty of human beings — autonomous thinking. And when this is strangled, impeded or refrained by something internal or external, this impeding entity is a dangerous entity for human progress. When human psychic growth is stopped in this way, this restriction that has impeded human ideas or thinking or human projections can be called dogma.
items.statement: Dogma is defined as internal or external restriction that impedes, strangles, or stops autonomous human thinking, ideas, or psychic projections.
items.title: Baba_s Love for South America

items.qualifiers: Progress is conditional on transcending spatial, temporal, and personal factors.
items.quote: Really speaking, there cannot be any progress in the realm of physicality nor in the psychic arena. You are moving, solving one problem, a few more problems will be created and so on. But human beings cannot remain idle. They will have to move forward. In psychic stratum also, so many psychic knots are unknotted but so many psychic problems are again created. If there is no proper adjustment amongst physical, psychic and spiritual movements, the psychic side of humans will get unbalanced and so many new and newer psychic diseases will get created. This is the present position of the world. There has been enough physical progress, less spiritual progress and the psychic structures of humans have lost their equilibrium, rather their equipoise, and that's why the modern society is suffering from so many psychic ailments. Really speaking there cannot be any true progress in the psychic arena. Progress can be only in the spiritual level, because the spiritual goal, the spiritual desideratum of the humans is beyond the periphery of the fundamental factors -- spatial, temporal and personal.
items.statement: True progress cannot occur in the physical or psychic arenas because they are bounded by relative factors and produce subsequent problems; genuine progress occurs solely on the spiritual level.
items.title: Baba_s Love for South America

items.qualifiers: Occurs when an individual suffers from a superiority complex.
items.quote: Now when you suffer from some complex of superiority, you think that you are a better person than others and the others are worse. As a result of this, you become incapable of accepting external waves in an appropriate manner. In this way, your thoughts are contaminated, are distorted and as a result of this, many other mental processes like memory, become deformed and weakened.
items.statement: Superiority and inferiority complexes distort incoming external thought waves and memory processes, impairing proper discrimination and collective alignment.
items.title: Baba_s Love for South America

items.quote: (1) The Physical Body - made of the five fundamental factors i.e., solid, liquid, luminous, aerial and ethereal (2) The psychic body, which is composed of three parts: existential mind ('I' feeling), doer or planner mind (Doer I) and the objective mind (Done I) (3) The Spiritual body; the soul; the Unit Consciousness; the reflection of Pure Consciousness.
items.statement: Human beings are composed of three distinct bodies: the physical body of five fundamental factors, the psychic body of three functional mental layers, and the spiritual body reflecting Pure Consciousness.
items.title: Baba The Lord

items.qualifiers: Presented as categorical distinctions between Taraka Brahma and ordinary gurus.
items.quote: 1. Taraka Brahma is a born Guru, a born Master, is born liberated. Whereas other Gurus have their own Guru from whom they learn and practice, they are not born Masters. They also practice to get liberated. They are not fully established in Pure Consciousness, in the highest cakra, the Sahasrara, but Taraka Brahma is. HE is always in that state of perfection, in trance, hence people used to think that Lord Shiva was using drugs, but that is not true, HE was in Samadhi, in ecstasy. Taraka Brahma is verily Jagad Guru – the Guru of the Universe. 2. Taraka Brahma leads a family life. He is not an ascetic saint like other Gurus. HE leads a normal life because HE has to set an example for family people, showing that when one is living a family life, one can achieve liberation as well. HE acts as much like an ordinary human being as possible, but HIS every action is superhuman. A very lucky few ever understand who HE is during HIS physical advent. 3. Taraka Brahma touches all aspects of human life like spirituality, philosophy, social problems, economic problems, culture, Arts, literature, music, etc. HE gives solutions for all problems. HE gives guidance for humanity to evolve physically, mentally and spiritually. Whereas other Gurus spend their whole lives covering basic spiritual topics, Taraka Brahma reaches deep into every sphere of human life.
items.statement: Unlike ordinary spiritual gurus who practice to attain realization and may experience fall, Taraka Brahma is born liberated, established permanently in Sahasrara Cakra, leads a family life, addresses all spheres of human existence, and establishes long-lasting Dharma.
items.title: Baba The Lord

items.qualifiers: Possession of occult power (Aeshvarya) alone makes one Iishvara, whereas Bhagavan requires all six qualities.
items.quote: Bhagvan is He who possesses Bhag. In the spiritual world, Bhag consists of six qualities. The combination of these qualities is known as Bhag. These qualities are Aeshvarya, Pratap, Yasha, Shrii, Jinana and Vaeragya. Aeshvarya: Anima, Mahima, Laghima, Iishitva, Vashitva, Prapti, Prakamya and Antaryamitva. They are all called Aeshvarya. It also means an occult power. This one gets through the regular practice of sadhana. One who possesses these qualities is called Iishvara. But Iishvara is not Bhagvan. Bhagvan needs five other qualities also. Pratap: Bhagavan has this quality. This is why He loves us and at the same time punishes us for our evil doings. Love alone will spoil a child. So also punishment or beating. Only He is the true Guru who rules over and loves his disciples.
items.statement: Bhagavan is defined by the possession of six divine qualities: Aeshvarya (eight occult powers), Pratap (ruling and loving balance), Yasha (reputation generating polarization), Shrii (charm, energy, and action), Jinana (true subjective knowledge), and Vaeragya (mental detachment in worldly action).
items.title: Bhagavan Anandamurti - Narada Muni

items.qualifiers: Subject to perceptual defects in the knower, known, or medium until absolute absorption occurs.
items.quote: Therefore, what they had learnt is not real knowledge. The real knowledge is the subjectivisation of external objectivity. In case of knowledge, there is a link between them which is called knowledge. Now, the subjectivisation of external objectivity means absorption of object. There may be a defect in the knower of known. There may be defect in the medium through which we obtain knowledge. A patient of jaundice, due to a defect in the eye, will see everything as yellow color. He will claim a white and call out that with his own eyes. One cannot see an object correctly if light is not properly radiating from it. Such an object will present a distorted shape of itself to the eyes. You then can not see exactly what you should.
items.statement: Real knowledge is the subjectivisation of external objectivity, attained when the knower and the known become unified and the medium dissolves into that unity.
items.title: Bhagavan Anandamurti - Narada Muni

items.qualifiers: Contingent on a minimum threshold of 51% of voters possessing all three criteria.
items.quote: Baba: Democracy can be successful only where the following essential factors are present at least amongst 51 percent of the voters: morality, literacy and socio-economic-political consciousness. Otherwise it is an instrument to befool the public.
items.statement: Democracy can function successfully only when at least 51 percent of voters possess morality, literacy, and socio-economic-political consciousness.
items.title: Bhagavan Anandamurti - Narada Muni

items.qualifiers: Contingent upon the complete exhaustion of original reactive momenta and motivation strictly by universal welfare.
items.quote: Ácarya Nagina in his book ‘Ananda Katha’ has mentioned at one place about ‘Nirman citta.’ “By doing sadhana, when a sadhaka attains his goal of perfection and his Samskaras (reactive momenta) are finished off, and if he, for the welfare of human beings makes use of the same body or assumes another body, such realized soul is called Nirman citta. That very thought of welfare of Creation becomes his new Samskara”.
items.statement: A Nirman Citta is a realized soul whose potential reactive momenta (samskaras) are exhausted through sadhana, but who adopts or maintains a physical body solely for universal welfare.
