items.statement: The notion 'I know' arises from the illusory union of a mental modification (vritti) with the Existence and Consciousness aspects of Atman.
items.title: Self-knowledge - An English translation of Shankaracharyas Atmabodha with notes, comments and introduction (Swami Nikhilananda)

items.qualifiers: must be practised continuously as each thought arises
items.quote: When other thoughts arise, one should not pursue them, but should inquire ‘To whom do they arise?’ It does not matter how many thoughts arise. As each thought arises, one should inquire with diligence, ‘To whom has this thought arisen?’ The answer that would emerge would be ‘To me’. Thereupon if one enquires ‘Who am I?’, the mind will go back to its source; and the thought that arose will become quiescent.
items.statement: To make the mind quiescent through Self-enquiry, one must not pursue arising thoughts but immediately investigate to whom they arise, directing attention back to the source of 'I' in the Heart.
items.title: The Collected Works of Sri Ramana Maharshi

items.qualifiers: breath control is an aid, not the final destroyer of mental tendencies
items.quote: Through the control of breath also, the mind will become quiescent; but it will be quiescent only so long as the breath remains controlled, and when the breath resumes the mind also will again start moving and will wander as impelled by residual impressions. The source is the same for both mind and breath. Thought, indeed, is the nature of the mind. The thought ‘I’ is the first thought of the mind; and that is egoity. It is from that whence egoity originates that breath also originates. Therefore, when the mind becomes quiescent, the breath is controlled, and when the breath is controlled the mind becomes quiescent. But in deep sleep, although the mind becomes quiescent, the breath does not stop. This is because of the will of God, so that the body may be preserved and other people may not be under the impression that it is dead. In the state of waking and in samadhi, when the mind becomes quiescent the breath is controlled. Breath is the gross form of mind. Till the time of death, the mind keeps breath in the body; and when the body dies the mind takes the breath along with it. Therefore, the exercise of breath control is only an aid for rendering the mind quiescent (manonigraha); it will not destroy the mind (manonasa).
items.statement: Breath control leads only to temporary quiescence of the mind (manolaya), whereas Self-enquiry and knowledge alone cause the total destruction of the mind (manonasa).
items.title: The Collected Works of Sri Ramana Maharshi

items.qualifiers: valid regardless of whether one is alone or in family life
items.quote: Sannyasa is only the renunciation of the ‘I-thought’, and not the rejection of the external objects. He who has renounced (the ‘I-thought’) thus, remains the same whether he is alone or in the midst of the extensive samsara (empirical world).
items.statement: Real sannyasa is solely the renunciation of the 'I-thought' within the mind, rather than the mere outward rejection of physical objects or stations of life.
items.title: The Collected Works of Sri Ramana Maharshi

items.qualifiers: explicitly excluded from application to the Guru
items.quote: Keep advaita within the Heart. Do not ever carry it into action. Even if you apply it to all the three worlds, O Son, it is not to be applied to the Guru.
items.statement: The non-dual truth of advaita is to be preserved within the Heart but must never be applied to one's actions or extended to the relationship with the Guru.
items.title: The Collected Works of Sri Ramana Maharshi

items.qualifiers: defined within Patanjali's Yoga aphorisms commentary
items.quote: The waves of thought in the Chitta are called Vrittis (literally "whirlpool") . What is thought? Thought is a force, as is gravitation or repulsion. From the infinite storehouse of force in nature, the instrument called Chitta takes hold of some, absorbs it and sends it out as thought.
items.statement: In the psychological framework of Yoga, Vritti signifies the thought-waves or ripples that rise in the mind-stuff (Chitta) when acted upon by external suggestions.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: posited according to the psychological philosophy of Yoga and reincarnation
items.quote: So with every work we do; by practice it becomes instinct, it becomes automatic; but so far as we know, all the cases which we now regard as automatic are degenerated reason. In the language of the Yogi, instinct is involved reason. Discrimination becomes involved, and gets to be automatic Samskaras. Therefore it is perfectly logical to think that all we call instinct in this world is simply involved reason. As reason cannot come without experience, all instinct is, therefore, the result of past experience.
items.statement: Biological and behavioral instincts are degenerated or involved reason rooted in experiences accumulated across past lives.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: rooted in the conservation of energy principle and ancient Indian cyclical theory
items.quote: The modern scientific man will tell you that you can only get the amount of energy out of a machine which you have previously put into it. Something cannot be produced out of nothing. If a man is an evolution of the mollusc, then the perfect man — the Buddha-man, the Christ-man — was involved in the mollusc. If it is not so, whence come these gigantic personalities? Something cannot come out of nothing. Thus we are in the position of reconciling the scriptures with modern light.
items.statement: Every evolutionary biological and psychological progression fundamentally requires a preceding involution of that same energy and intelligence.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: specifically formulated within Advaita Vedanta philosophy
items.quote: Thus we find that Maya is not a theory for the explanation of the world; it is simply a statement of facts as they exist, that the very basis of our being is contradiction, that everywhere we have to move through this tremendous contradiction, that wherever there is good, there must also be evil, and wherever there is evil, there must be some good, wherever there is life, death must follow as its shadow, and everyone who smiles will have to weep, and vice versa.
items.statement: Advaita Vedanta defines Maya not as an illusion or an abstract theory, but as an empirical statement of the inherent contradictions and conditions constituting existence.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: Germs of all three instruments exist in all human beings in varying degrees of development.
items.quote: So instinct, reason, and inspiration are the three instruments of knowledge. Instinct belongs to animals, reason to man, and inspiration to God-men.
items.statement: In all beings, knowledge is acquired through three successive evolutionary instruments: instinct (developed most in animals), reasoning (developed in humans), and inspiration (belonging to God-men), where each higher instrument fulfills rather than contradicts the former.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: The Sankhyas define it as the equilibrium of three forces, one of which is called Sattva, another Rajas, and the third Tamas. Tamas, the lowest force, is that of attraction; a little higher is Rajas, that of repulsion; and the highest is the balance of these two, Sattva; so that when these two forces, attraction and repulsion, are held in perfect control by the Sattva there is no creation, no movement in the world. As soon as this equilibrium is lost, the balance is disturbed, and one of these forces gets stronger than the other, motion sets in, and creation begins.
items.statement: According to the Sankhya cosmology, nature (Prakriti or Avyakta) consists of the equilibrium of three material forces—Tamas (attraction), Rajas (repulsion), and Sattva (balance)—and creation begins only when this balance is lost.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: Both interpretations are held to be true and complementary for spiritual practice.
items.quote: According to him, "That which is gathered in is Ahara. The knowledge of the sensations, such as sound etc., is gathered in for the enjoyment of the enjoyer (self); the purification of the knowledge which gathers in the perception of the senses is the purifying of the food (Ahara). The word 'purification-of-food' means the acquiring of the knowledge of sensations untouched by the defects of attachment, aversion, and delusion; such is the meaning.
items.statement: In the preparatory stage of Bhakti, Ahara (food/intake) is understood in two distinct ways: by Ramanuja as physical food purified from class defects, wicked handlers, and physical dirt; and by Shankara as sensory impressions gathered by the mind free from attachment, aversion, and delusion.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: Now if a tendency is the result of repeated actions, the tendencies with which we are born must be explained on that ground too. Evidently we could not have got them in this life; therefore we must have to seek for their genesis in the past. Now it is also evident that some of our tendencies are the effects of the self-conscious efforts peculiar to man; and if it is true that we are born with such tendencies, it rigorously follows that their causes were conscious efforts in the past — that is, we must have been on the same mental plane which we call the human plane, before this present life.
items.statement: The Nyaya school establishes the necessity of reincarnation through the causal principle that inborn tendencies (Pravrittis) and unperceived impressions (Adrishta) cannot arise ex nihilo but must be the lingering effects of conscious, self-directed efforts from prior lives.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: conditional based on whether cellular transmission sufficiently explains human experience
items.quote: for the fight between reincarnation and mere cellular transmission is, in reality, the fight between spiritualism and materialism. If cellular transmission is the all-sufficient explanation, materialism is inevitable, and there is no necessity for the theory of a soul. If it is not a sufficient explanation, the theory of an individual soul bringing into this life the experiences of the past is as absolutely true.
items.statement: The conflict between the doctrine of reincarnation and mere cellular transmission represents the fundamental debate between spiritualism and materialism.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: The training by which the current and expression of will are brought under control and become fruitful is called education.
items.statement: Education is the training that brings the current and expression of the will under control so that it becomes fruitful, rather than mere book-learning or accumulated facts.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: applies to conditioned existence; Brahman is beyond this relationship
items.quote: Ishvara is the sum total of individuals, yet He is an Individual, as the human body is a unit, of which each cell is an individual. Samashti or collected equals God; Vyashti or analysed equals the Jiva. The existence of Ishvara, therefore, depends on that of Jiva, as the body on the cell, and vice versa.
items.statement: Ishvara is defined as the sum total of all individuals while simultaneously existing as an Individual entity, coexisting with Jiva.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: On the ethical side there is danger in the development of the power of concentration — the danger of concentrating the mind upon an object and then being unable to detach it at will. This state causes great suffering. Almost all our suffering is caused by our not having the power of detachment.
items.statement: The development of mental and spiritual concentration without the corresponding power to detach the mind at will causes intense suffering.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: Human society is in turn governed by the four castes — the priests, the soldiers, the traders, and the labourers. Each state has its glories as well as its defects.
items.statement: The four castes sequentially govern human society, each bearing distinct societal advantages and cultural defects.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: In the animal kingdom we really see such laws as struggle for existence, survival of the fittest, etc., evidently at work. Therefore Darwin's theory seems true to a certain extent. But in the human kingdom, where there is the manifestation of rationality, we find just the reverse of those laws.
items.statement: The historical causes of species evolution differ between the animal kingdom and the human kingdom.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.qualifiers: so long as the principle is not hurt or destroyed
items.quote: The truth is that so long as the principle, the ideal, of which the outer man is the expression, is not hurt or destroyed, the man lives, and there is hope for that man.
items.statement: National vitality and persistence depend upon keeping the underlying mission and ideal of a race intact.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: Individuality means what cannot be divided. How can you call this state — we are now — individuality? One hour you are thinking one way, and the next hour another way, and two hours after another way. Individuality is that which changes not.
items.statement: True individuality refers to the immutable divine aspect within man rather than the ever-changing mental or bodily state.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: Many of you remember the definition I gave of the soul; that each soul is a circle whose centre is in one point and circumference nowhere. The centre is where the body is, and the activity is manifested there. You are omnipresent; only you have the consciousness of being concentrated in one point. That point has taken up particles of matter, and formed them into a machine to express itself. That through which it expresses itself is called the body. So you are everywhere; when one body or machine fails, you, the centre, move on and take up other particles of matter, finer or grosser, and work through that. This is man. And what is God? God is a circle with its circumference nowhere and centre everywhere.
items.statement: God is defined as a circle having its circumference nowhere and its centre everywhere, in contrast to the individual soul whose centre is in one point and circumference nowhere.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: The Absolute first becomes the mixture of knowledge, then, in the second degree, that of will. If it be said that plants have no consciousness, that they are at best only unconscious wills, the answer is that even the unconscious plant-will is a manifestation of the consciousness, not of the plant, but of the cosmos, the Mahat of the Sankhya Philosophy. The Buddhist analysis of everything into will is imperfect, firstly, because will is itself a compound, and secondly, because consciousness or knowledge which is a compound of the first degree, precedes it. Knowledge is action . First action, then reaction . When the mind perceives, then, as the reaction, it wills . The will is in the mind. So it is absurd to say that will is the last analysis.
items.statement: Will cannot be the ultimate metaphysical basis of manifestation because it is a compound that is preceded by consciousness and knowledge.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: The great point of contrast between Buddhism and Hinduism lies in the fact that Buddhism said, 'Realise all this as illusion', while Hinduism said, 'Realise that within the illusion is the Real.' Of how this was to be done, Hinduism never presumed to enunciate any rigid law. The Buddhist command could only be carried out through monasticism; the Hindu might be fulfilled through any state of life. All alike were roads to the One Real.
items.statement: Buddhism and Hinduism differ fundamentally in their approach to worldly existence: Buddhism commands realizing all as illusion through monasticism, whereas Hinduism teaches finding the Real within the illusion through any station in life.
items.title: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

items.quote: The three great orders of metaphysical thought Dualism, qualified Monism, and absolute Monism —are the stages on the way to supreme truth. They are not contradictory, but rather are complementary, the one to the o'ther. Each is the perspective offered to the mental standpoint of one order of individuals.
items.statement: According to Ramakrishna, Dualism, qualified Monism, and absolute Monism represent complementary progressive stages on the way to supreme truth, each suited to different capacities of individuals.
items.title: The life of Ramakrishna (Rolland, Romain, 1866-1944 etc.)

items.quote: Yama said: The good is one thing; the pleasant, another. Both of these, serving different needs, bind a man. It goes well with him who, of the two, takes the good; but he who chooses the pleasant misses the end. Both the good and the pleasant present themselves to a man. The calm soul examines them well and discriminates. Yea, he prefers the good to the pleasant; but the fool chooses the pleasant out of greed and avarice.
items.statement: The Katha Upanishad distinguishes between the 'good' (sreya) and the 'pleasant' (preya), noting that they bind a person to different ends, and only choosing the good leads to success.
items.title: The Principal Upanishads (Swami Nikhilananda)

items.quote: Turiya is not that which is conscious of the inner (subjective) world, nor that which is conscious of the outer (objective) world, nor that which is conscious of both, nor that which is a mass of consciousness. It is not simple consciousness nor is It unconsciousness. It is unperceived, unrelated, incomprehensible, uninferable, unthinkable and indescribable. The essence of the Consciousness manifesting as the self in the three states, It is the cessation of all phenomena; It is all peace, all bliss and non-dual. This is what is known as the Fourth (Turiya).
items.statement: Turiya is defined in the Mandukya Upanishad as the Fourth state beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, unperceived, unthinkable, non-dual, and the cessation of all phenomena.
items.title: The Principal Upanishads (Swami Nikhilananda)

items.quote: For you, the Self, are proved to be free from change, and therefore perpetually the same on the ground that all the modifications of the mind without a single exception are (simultaneously) known by you. You regard this knowledge of all the modifications which is the reason for the above inference as that for your doubt. If you were changeful like the mind or the senses (which pervade their objects one after another), you would not simultaneously know all the mental modifications, the objects of your knowledge.
items.statement: Pure Consciousness is immutable and changeless because all mental modifications are known simultaneously without succession or partial awareness.
items.title: Upadeshasahasri of Sri Shankara - A thousand teachings (Shankara (Sankara) etc.)

items.quote: Work is for the purification of the mind, not for the perception of the Reality. The realisation of Truth is brought about by discrimination and not in the least by ten millions of acts.
items.statement: Action is meant solely for the purification of the mind, whereas direct perception of Truth is achieved solely through discrimination.
items.title: Vivekachudamani of Sri Sankaracharya

items.qualifiers: within Hindu religious tradition and Vedanta
items.quote: Among the many vital differences may be mentioned the fact that the birth of an ordinary mortal is governed by the law of karma, whereas that of an Incarnation is a voluntary act undertaken for the spiritual redemption of the world. Further, though maya is the cause of the embodiment of both an ordinary mortal and an Incarnation, yet the former is fully under maya’s control, whereas the latter always remains its master.
items.statement: An Avatar or Divine Incarnation differs from an ordinary mortal because their birth is voluntary rather than driven by the law of karma, they remain the master of maya rather than controlled by it, and they possess the unique power to bestow liberation upon others.
items.title: Vivekananda: A Biography

items.quote: He often said that to see the world alone, without God, is ignorance, ajnana; to see God alone, without the world, is a kind of philosophical knowledge, jnana; but to see all beings permeated by the spirit of God is supreme wisdom, vijnana.
items.statement: Seeing the world alone without God constitutes ajnana (ignorance), seeing God alone without the world constitutes jnana (knowledge), and seeing all beings permeated by the spirit of God constitutes vijnana (supreme wisdom).
items.title: Vivekananda: A Biography

items.qualifiers: when practiced consciously by yogis and saints
items.quote: There is a connexion between chastity and spirituality. The explanation is that through prayer and meditation the saints have transmuted the most vital force in the body into spiritual energy. In India this is well understood and yogis do it consciously. The force so transmuted is called ojas, and it is stored up in the brain.
items.statement: Transmuting vital bodily energy through prayer and meditation into ojas stored in the brain is the physiological and spiritual reason chastity is required across monastic orders.
items.title: Vivekananda: A Biography

items.qualifiers: comparative theological analysis by Swami Vivekananda
items.quote: The Buddhist command could only be carried out through monasticism; the Hindu might be fulfilled through any state of life. All alike were roads to the One Real. One of the highest and the greatest expressions of the Faith is put into the mouth of a butcher, preaching, by the orders of a married woman, to a sannyasin. Thus Buddhism became the religion of a monastic order, but Hinduism, in spite of its exaltation of monasticism, remains ever the religion of faithfulness to daily duty, whatever it may be, as the path by which man may attain to God.
items.statement: Buddhism functions primarily as a religion for a monastic order requiring renunciation, whereas Hinduism allows the realization of the Real within illusion through faithfulness to daily duty in any state of life.
items.title: Vivekananda: A Biography

items.qualifiers: standard structure of the first lesson of Tantra Yoga
items.quote: Thus, withdrawal has three steps: withdrawal from the external world, the body, and the thoughts. Then comes mantra ághát and mantra caetanya.
items.statement: In Tantra Yoga's Iishvara Pranidhana, withdrawal (mantra diipanii) consists of three successive phases: withdrawal from the external physical world (bhuta shuddhi), withdrawal from the body to a sentient point (asana shuddhi), and withdrawal from thoughts passing through the mind.
items.title: Rajadhiraja Yoga - Acarya Cidgananda Avadhuta

items.qualifiers: structural distinction in Rajadhiraja Yoga lessons
items.quote: The difference between the third and the fifth lessons is that the former greatly increases one’s capacity for retention and conception whereas the latter gives more joy and thrill. Also the third lesson is done only up to the Vishuddha Cakra while the fifth lesson is done up to the Sahasrára Cakra. So we can say very clearly that the third lesson deals especially with the five fundamental factors, whereas the fifth lesson deals with the five fundamental factors plus the mind and soul.
items.statement: The third lesson of Rajadhiraja Yoga (Tattva Dharana) focuses exclusively on controlling the five fundamental physical factors up to Vishuddha Cakra, whereas the fifth lesson (Cakra Shodhana) encompasses the physical, psychic, and spiritual realms up to Sahasrara Cakra.
items.title: Rajadhiraja Yoga - Acarya Cidgananda Avadhuta

items.quote: Truly speaking, the lessons themselves do not give liberation and salvation. Rather, it is the power of the Guru behind the lessons which serves this purpose. When the power is withdrawn from the lessons, they are as good as dead. Therefore, it is said: Gurushakti dáyakah na tantra na mantra (the Guru, and nothing else, is the giver of force, liberation and salvation).
items.statement: Spiritual practice and specific techniques are ineffective on their own for granting liberation unless empowered and animated by the Guru's grace and force.
items.title: Rajadhiraja Yoga - Acarya Cidgananda Avadhuta

items.qualifiers: when the practitioner is firmly established in second lesson
items.quote: If you can surrender all your actions to him you will not be responsible for the reactions. Do whatever you do, act in whatever manner you act, but surrender those actions completely to him. This is what second lesson teaches. If you are firm in your second lesson your reactions will gradually go on diminishing, and a day will come when your mind will be so well-established in that process that your actions will not bring any reaction.
items.statement: Surrendering all actions and their objects to the Supreme Entity through the practice of Guru Mantra (second lesson) prevents actions from generating binding reactions (samskaras).
items.title: When_The_Time_Comes

items.qualifiers: strict mandate for all spiritual aspirants
items.quote: Occult power is of little value, nor is it difficult to achieve. It is easy to achieve, and it is of little value because if one uses one’s occult power it becomes the beginning of one’s downfall.
items.statement: Spiritual practitioners should strictly avoid using or exhibiting occult powers, as displaying them exhausts spiritual strength, increases ego, and initiates spiritual downfall.
items.title: When_The_Time_Comes
